For the sake of favoring kings and out of a desire for the welfare of the world.

Various Vaiṣṇava duties that remove the sins of the worlds.

Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Devoted to Brahmanas, truthful, blessed, and the destroyer of all enemies.

Seated here at ease, O rulers of the earth, speak of your own doubts as you desire.
Thus addressed by the eminent descendant of Bhṛgu in the midst of the great seers, that leader of the Yadus—
Having bowed to the brahmins, the king went to his throne, which was variegated with a thousand jewels.

And all became bowed down and desirous of hearing the words of the chief of Brahmins. || 27 ||
Vajra said:
"O moon of the Bhṛgu lineage, tell me truly how you arose from the world;
the foremost of the assembly of brahmins and the chief of kings listen to your words. (28)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction to the Narrative," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. || 1 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa, the supreme refuge of all beings.
Accompanied by Lakṣmī, the bestower of boons, reclining upon the couch of Śeṣa. || 1 ||
The sole cause of the origin, maintenance, and destruction of this world.
He is knowledge and the object of knowledge, attainable through knowledge, and resides in the heart of everyone.
O King, I shall speak of the origin of the worlds; learn of it from me.
It pacifies all sins, bestows long life, grants heaven, and is auspicious.
Nārāyaṇa performs the creation, destruction, and protection of this world.
O protector of the earth, he for whom this entire great world acts [as his servant].
He who is celebrated in the Vedas as the twenty-fifth Puruṣa.
The sustainer, without beginning or end, infinite, the Supreme Person. || 5 ||
The opening of his eyes is the day of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin.
Likewise, a night is a nimeṣa, and that is proclaimed to be a kalpa.
But in the case of the infinite one, O King, no form exists as a human being.
Nor is there sound, nor smell, nor touch, O Lord of the Earth. (7)
It has no measure, nor does it have a beginning or an end; how could it?
With hands and feet on all sides, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere.
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, he stands encompassing all.
It manifests as the qualities of all the senses, yet is devoid of all the senses. || 9 ||
It is unattached yet the sustainer of all; devoid of qualities, yet the experiencer of the qualities.
And having attained that, those supreme persons who have become liberated in this world—
A good rebirth belongs to those who have attained perfection through yoga; therefore, everything arises from that.
Therefore, the unmanifest comes into being, and from that, the Self is also born. || 11 ||
From that [the ego] comes the intellect, from that the mind, from that the ether, and from that the wind.
From that [the Self] came fire, from that water, and from those [elements], it is said, the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) arose.
O King, there was a golden egg, and within it, indeed, was he himself.
The Lord first assumes a body for the purpose of creation.
The four-faced god Brahmā is always characterized by an excess of the quality of rajas.
Having assumed a body, he creates this world of the moving and the unmoving.
Within the egg is the entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans.
The seven worlds, along with the nether regions (pātāla), and the earth with its seven continents and oceans.
Having performed the creation, that Blessed One assumed a sattvic body.
In the Ocean of Milk, the Lord became Keśava, consisting of the coils of Śeṣa.
Accompanied by Lakṣmī, he always protects all the worlds.
Having entered into yogic sleep, he dwells within the bodies of all sentient beings.
For he indeed perceives the auspicious and inauspicious actions of all beings.
At the time of the end, becoming Hara, he again destroys the universe. ||18||
Assuming a body of the nature of darkness, the one of great fame acted thus as if in mere sport.
Then, at the time of creation, Brahmā [saw] the earth situated in the midst of the waters.
Having seen this, the Soul of Sacrifice, assuming the body of a boar, uplifts it.
In this world, he eternally becomes Brahmā at the time of creation and the high-souled Viṣṇu during its preservation.
And at the time of withdrawal, he attains the state of Hara; through union with the three times, he ordains the threefold [creation].
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Account of the Origin of Hiraṇyagarbha," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When the night of Brahmā had passed and the Lotus-born One had awakened,
Viṣṇu, desiring to create living beings, perceived that the earth was submerged within the waters.
He was auspiciously fond of sporting in the water, just as in former times at the beginning of the kalpas.
Assuming the form of a boar, he raised up the Earth.
He has the Vedas as his feet and the sacrificial ladles as his fangs; he is four-faced and possesses four mouths.
Agni-jihva (Fire-tongued), Darbha-roma (Darbha-haired), Brahma-śīrṣa (Brahma-headed), and Mahātapas (Great-austere). || 3 ||
The divine one whose eyes are day and night, whose limbs are the Vedas, and whose ornaments are the sacred scriptures.
With clarified butter for its nose, the sacrificial ladle for its beak, and the sound of Sāman chants for its great voice.
Dharma is great in truth, glorious, and honored for its power of action.
The wise Prāyaścittamaya was tall-kneed and possessed of great fame.
He has the Udgātṛ as his internal organ, the oblation as his characteristic mark, and the great medicinal herbs as the seeds of his fruit.
The wind is his inner self; the mantras are his bones, and the soma is his blood.
The Vedas are its trunk, the fragrance of oblations its scent, and it possesses great speed in carrying offerings to the gods and ancestors.
His body was the sacrificial hall, radiant and endowed with various initiations.
The yogin, whose heart is the sacrificial fee, is great and consists of the great sacrifice.
It was beautiful with the Upākarma and Iṣṭi rites, and adorned with the whirlpools of the Pravargya ceremony.
Accompanied by his wife Māyā, he indeed rose up like a great horn.
The earth, bounded by the ocean, together with its mountains, forests, and groves.
The Lord, who dwells within the single ocean, rescued her when she had fallen into the waters of the universal ocean.
Having lifted [it] up with the tip of his tusk, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
The primordial god, the great yogi, created the world once again.
Having understood this, the Boar, desiring the welfare of all beings, assumed that form.
In ancient times, the goddess Earth, who was situated in the midst of the waters, was lifted up.
Having raised up the earth from within the waters, that omnipresent and great-souled one assumed the form of a boar.
Listen, O lion among kings, to how that Lord made the division of the world accordingly.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Boar," in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The subtle particle of dust that is seen when the sun shines through a lattice window—
First, they declare the *trasareṇu* to be the smallest measure of those [units of measurement].
Eight *trasareṇus* should be known as one *likṣā* in terms of measurement.
Three of those black mustard seeds (rājasarṣapa) make three white mustard seeds (gaurasarṣapa). || 2 ||
Six mustard seeds and six barley grains make one middle-sized finger-breadth (aṅgula), and eight of those [finger-breadths] make one [hasta].
A śaṅku consists of twelve aṅgulas; two of those are called a hasta.
Four of those are declared to be a dhanus, and one thousand dhanus make a krośa.
Two *krośas* make a *gavyūti*, and four of those make a *yojana*.
In measurement of yojanas, it is three hundred thousand.

This world is proclaimed to be shaped like an umbrella, fixed upon its base.
The Lord himself is free from passion and devoid of all suffering.
Those people who have attained single-minded devotion go to that Hari.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Pātāla," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The Bhūrloka is the first, O King; listen as I speak.

The fourth, however, is proclaimed as the path of Vāyu, belonging to the Gandharvas.
The Vināyakas go in the fifth [house], and in the sixth are the herds of elephants.

On the outside, the egg is surrounded by water ten times its size.
The waters, increased tenfold, are likewise enveloped on the outside by fire.
And by the external wind, which possesses ten times the quality of fire.
The wind is likewise enveloped by space, which possesses ten times its own qualities.
And space is encompassed externally by the mind multiplied tenfold.
And the entire mind, O King, is enveloped by the intellect through its tenfold power.
And one's own intellect is shrouded on all sides by the ten-fold [obscuration].

O King, it is impossible to state the number [of beings] across, above, or below.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the World," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Vajra said:
And by the configuration of the entire circle of the earth, O Bhārgava.
Tell me the entirety of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) therein; I have a great doubt regarding that. ||1||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Indra among kings, in the center of the terrestrial sphere stands the great mountain Meru.
In its center, extending all around, it measures thousands of yojanas.
Jambūdvīpa, however, is proclaimed to be fifty [yojanas] in measure.
O lord of the earth, its further shore is a million yojanas away.
It is surrounded by that salt ocean.
The Lāvaṇa ocean is twice the size of Śākadvīpa. ||4||
And Śākadvīpa, O Great King, is surrounded [by it], without a doubt.
And the Ocean of Milk is also surrounded by an ocean of milk equal to itself.
Kuśadvīpa, in its yojanas, is twice the size of the Ocean of Milk.
Kuśadvīpa is surrounded by Ājyoda, which is equal in size to itself.
And Ajyoda is surrounded by Krauñcadvīpa, which is twice its size.
And Krauñcadvīpa is surrounded by an ocean of curd-cream (dadhimaṇḍoda) equal to itself.
It is then surrounded by the Śālmaladvīpa, which is twice its size.
Then the Suroda ocean is surrounded by the Gomedha sea, which is twice its size.
In the center of Puṣkaradvīpa, however, is a pavilion in the shape of the island.
In this world, there is a very great mountain renowned as Mānasottara.
It is proclaimed to be fifty thousand yojanas in measurement.
It was thus raised up, possessing peaks of various kinds.
On the summit of Mānasottara, in the eastern quarter of Meru.
The city of Śakra is renowned by the name Amarāvatī. || 11 ||
Likewise, in the southeastern direction from the fire, there is Prabhāvatī.
In the southern region of Yama is the city named Saṃyamanī.
In the south-western quarter is the domain of Virūpākṣa, characterized by his valor.
And in the western direction likewise is Varuṇa’s [city], Sukhaprabhā.
The city named Śivā is indeed situated in the northwestern quarter of Vāyu.

Even for the gods there is Ayodhyā; therefore, this city is named Ayodhyā after you.
It was provided with walls and moats, and beautified by the banks of the Sarayū river.
It was adorned with magnificent palaces and great highways well-apportioned for the devotees.
With ever-peaceful elephants resembling mountains of collyrium.
It was adorned by hundreds born from the lineages of gods and nāgas. || 3 ||
With horses that were fleshless-faced, possessed of excellent ears, and as swift as thought;
She was endowed with long necks and prominent collarbones, as well as large thighs and hips.
Their limbs were the color of the interior of a lotus, and their faces resembled the full moon.
Where there are thousands of courtesans skilled in the delights of conversation.
There is no such merit, no such knowledge, no such craft, and no such action.
Having reached Ayodhyā, one who seeks his favor departs disappointed.
It was crowded with hundreds of gardens and resplendent with social festivals.
They are healthy, heroic men, and free from all discursive reasoning. ||7||
It was constantly resounded with the sounds of lutes, flutes, and drums.
Its people were always joyful, and it was adorned with many jewels.
Possessing the great sound of the Vedic recitation, it was graced by throngs of the twice-born.
Her sins were destroyed by the wind enriched with the rising smoke of clarified butter.
The wind was made fragrant by the scattering of sweet-smelling incense.
It was always crowded with fragrant women in its market streets.
Where there is no person who is wretched, or soiled, or even emaciated.
One who is intent on censuring the Vedas, base, one who has broken the moral dam, and not an atheist. || 11 ||
And that great city is ten yojanas in extent in its middle.
It extends for three yojanas, situated along the bank of the Sarayū.
Furthermore, O hero among men, in this very Manvantara, it was constructed once again by that King Manu.
O Lord of the Yadu clan, by whom the entire world must be protected duly throughout a manvantara.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of Ayodhyā," in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra. || 13 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
By which Vaivasvata Manu that city was constructed.
Having ruled the kingdom for a long time, he consecrated Ikṣvāku [as his successor].
Having entrusted the burden to his son, he ascended to heaven in his physical body.
Residing there, he remains protecting the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile.
By him, this entire world must be protected throughout the whole Manvantara.
His son was Ikṣvāku, who protected the earth. ||3||
He was a knower of dharma, grateful, truthful, and one who had conquered his senses.
He was pleasing to behold for all beings and was skilled in discerning right and wrong policy.
He is devoted to Brahman, a refuge for all, and compassionate toward the poor and the helpless.
And he was endowed with the powers of destiny, counsel, and energy.
Possessing great energy in the sixfold policy, he addresses others with a smile.
He should employ punishment appropriately, neither being without punishment nor being one who delights in punishment. ||6||
One who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, who performs sacrifices, and who delights in austerity.
He possesses noble conduct, is beloved by all beings, and is indeed non-violent. || 7 ||
One who honors those worthy of honor is respected; one who worships those worthy of worship finds happiness.
Lust, anger, intoxication, pride, greed, and likewise joy. || 8 ||
By him, the six enemies that constantly arise from the body have been conquered.
Everywhere he was seen according to the prescribed rite—fortunate and pleasant to behold.
Possessing much grain, much wealth, and many elephants, horses, and men.
He whose eternal abode is Ayodhyā, who destroys the pride of the hosts of gods.
At that time, he protected all his subjects like his own children.
While that king was ruling, there was not even the slightest unrighteousness among men.
Whether he be dejected, or afflicted by disease, or short-lived, or suffering;
Whether he be foolish, or deformed, or unfortunate, or lacking in physical form; ||12||
In a single body, the specific cognition "I am" perceives the entire multitude of qualities as one's own.
The high-souled Prajāpati, the foremost of all the worlds, created that best of kings. ||13||
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ikṣvāku Dynasty," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
To Ikṣvāku was born a righteous son named Vikukṣi.
Kakutstha was his son, and Anenas was his son. ||1||
His son was the illustrious Pṛthu, and Viśvadāsa was his son.
He had a disciple named Śrāvastaka, by whom Śrāvastī was created. ||2||
Bṛhadaśva was his son, and Kuvalāśva was his offspring.
The immensely powerful Kuvalāśva attained the status of Dhundhumāra.
Having slain the large-bodied water-demon (jalarākṣasa) named Dhundhu in the water.
Vajra said:
How was Dhundhu, possessed of great splendor, slain by Kuvalāśva?
And who is this water-demon renowned as Dhundhu?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In ancient times, when the world was a single ocean and all moving and stationary beings had perished.
When the moon, sun, and wind have perished, and the planets and stars have been destroyed;
Having assumed the śeṣaparyaṅka posture, the Lord Janārdana fell asleep.
A beautiful lotus emerged from the navel of that god.
There, the auspicious four-faced god Brahmā himself was born.
There he remained practicing the Vedas while the god Janārdana was asleep.
In that same manner, the Vedas waited upon that embodied being.
As he was devoted to the recitation of the Vedas there, a drop of sweat was produced.
O King, having reached the lotus leaf, he became divided into two parts.
Therefore, two Daityas, fierce in their strength and composed of rajas and tamas, were born from him.
The two named Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who possessed great strength and prowess.
Then those two, fixed in their evil resolve, carried off the Vedas from Brahmā.
Then, when the Vedas along with their bodies had been slain, the Grandfather [Brahmā]—
That sinless one awakened the Lord of Gods, Padmanābha.
Then that god, having assumed the form of a horse-headed neck, awoke.
Resembling a hundred moons and adorned with various ornaments.
With his second body, he went to the depths of the netherworld (rasātala).
Having gone there with that horse-headed form, he brought back the eternal Vedas.
The Teacher of the World gave it once again to the Grandfather.
Then the Lord, assuming the form of Hayashiras, vanished from sight.
Then the two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, arrived at that place.
Viṣṇu created two bodies, remembered as Viṣṇu and Jiṣṇu.
Jiṣṇu fought with Madhu, and Viṣṇu indeed with Kaiṭabha.
Then, the Lord Janārdana was pleased by their excellent combat.
He spoke to those two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who possessed massive bodies.
"Choose a boon, O best of men; you two are unconquerable."
Then those two spoke to the lotus-eyed god Viṣṇu.
O Lord, may we have a son of great strength and prowess.
But when the son was born, those two who had formerly been [conceived] by Viṣṇu, the Victorious One—
And then those two heroes were slain, having indeed resorted to the water.
There they both shed fat, by which the earth became overspread.
Therefore, she is known in this world as Medinī by those who contemplate the ultimate reality.
Then, in the form of a boar, the earth was lifted up from there.
By that very God of gods, she was established in her former place.
Then, by the command of the God of gods, Brahmā brought forth creation.
Thus, at that time in battle, those two known as Madhu and Kaiṭabha were struck down by the best of gods.
They proceeded to the abode of Lord Viṣṇu and remained near him in the Ocean of Milk.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra. || 15 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, in this ninth division of this land of Bhārata.
It is heard that the ocean is filled with sand, known as Ujjānaka. || 1 ||
In the midst of that ocean, there was always the city of Dhundhuprasthapati.
At the end of that year, he releases a great sigh.
At that time, the earth, along with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembles;
and those living beings who are of little strength go to the abode of Yama.
When he has awakened, there remains but a small portion of the earth.
For the sake of food, that fierce and evil-minded water-demon performs [these deeds]. || 4 ||
At that very time, however, Uttaṅka was performing austerities.
At the conclusion of his ascetic penance, he beheld the high-souled Madhusūdana.
The divine Hari said to him: "O Bhārgava, choose a boon."
Uttaṅka, with palms joined in reverence, offered praise to Madhusūdana.
He said to the boon-granting god, "This alone is my boon."
That I have beheld the lotus feet of the God of gods.
The Blessed One said:
O scion of the Bhṛgu lineage, a boon must certainly be granted to you by me.
And by my grace, you shall indeed become free from old age and immortal. || 8 ||
Wherever you desire water, there it shall be for you accordingly.
And you shall likewise perform a great task for the gods.
"O sinless one, whoever constantly causes obstruction to this hermitage of yours,"
"O Kuvalāśva, go and slay that Dhundhu; do not delay!"
And I shall enter the body of this Kuvalāśva.
With my splendor, he shall slay him in the battle against Dhundhu.
For Dhundhu cannot be slain by one of little splendor, O best of the Bhrigus.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord, the Blessed One, vanished from sight.
And thus the great ascetic Uttaṅka also went to Ayodhyā.
Having been honored by Bṛhadaśva, he addressed Bṛhadaśva.
Utaṅka said:
O Indra among kings, how can you sleep so peacefully, seated upon your couch?
Having observed the life of Dhundhu, gird your loins now for the sake of worldly existence.
O King of kings, by my word, you indeed have the power to slay Dhundhu.
What is the power of kings other than exertion, and how could anything be difficult for you? (15)
O King, there you slew the massive-bodied Dhundhu, who was an oppressor of the twice-born.
Having heard the words of the sage, King Kuvalāśva spoke.
I have entered the forest and likewise renounced the staff of punishment.
Go there and slay that best of Dānavas, protected as you are by Uttaṅka.
Thus addressed and embraced by his father, he who was naturally affectionate [replied].
Accompanied by Uttaṅka, he went to fight the water-dwelling Rākṣasa.
And the righteous Keśava fought with that very Dhundhu.
With Utanka's consent, he subsequently struck him with the Brahmāstra.
Having slain that Rākṣasa, he then obtained boons from the gods.
Devotion to Kṛṣṇa, steadfastness in dharma, and likewise an imperishable residence in heaven.
O lord of men, having caused the son of Madhu and Kaiṭabha to be slain, [he departed].
He attained the state of Dhundhumāra and likewise graced the city.
When that best of Daityas was slain, the quarters became serene and the gods were filled with joy.
Then the world was freed from obstacles, and the king attained supreme fame. || 22 ||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Dhundhumāra," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From Dhundhumāra was born Dṛḍhāśva, and Haryaśva was his son.
Nikumbha was his son, and Suhita was his offspring.
Bhṛśāśva was his son, and Māndhātṛ was his offspring.
By the decree of fate, the king was born from his very womb.
Purukutsa was his son, and Trasadasyu was his offspring.
His illustrious son was Śambhu, renowned as Anaraṇya. ||3||
He who was formerly the conqueror of the three worlds was slain by Rāvaṇa.
Dṛśadaśva was his son; from him came King Vasumanas. || 4 ||
His son was named Tridhanvan; from him, Tryāraṇi is remembered [to have descended].
His son was Satyavrata, whom they call Triśaṅku.
Hariścandra was his son, and Rohitāśva was his offspring.
His son was King Harita; because he was tawny (hārita), he is called Cañcu.
Vijaya was his son, and Cālarka was his offspring.
Vṛka was the son of Alarka, and from him Bāhu was born.
He was beset by many vices, such as drinking, women, hunting, and gambling.
At that time, while that lord of men was thus occupied with his enemies in a state of calamity.
[The earth was overrun] by the Haihayas, the Tālajaṅghas, and all the hosts of Mlecchas.
The kingdom was seized by deceit; deprived of his realm, he went to the forest.
His virtuous wife followed him on foot into the forest.
It is said that her co-wife had previously administered poison to her while she was pregnant.
Then that auspicious forest-dweller gave birth to her son Sagara.
The king, having fathered a son, was joined with the work of time (died). ||11||
The queen, the daughter of Yadu, who was devoted to righteousness, ascended after him.
He was consecrated with all the ritual refinements by Sagara and Cyavana.
Likewise, he was led to the further shore of the entire collection of sciences and of the science of archery.
Having attained youth, he alone became the lord of men. ||13||
On foot and with his sword girded, he was there by the grace of Cyavana.
The scorcher of enemies slaughtered the Haihayas and the Tālajaṅghas. ||14||
Then, having reached Ayodhyā, he obtained a kingdom free from all obstacles.
Sagara, having obtained the kingdom with his fourfold army, [ruled]. ||15||
Having conquered all the mlecchas, he brought the kings under his control.
Having conquered the entire earth and obtained a kingdom free from thorns.
He honored Cyavana again and again with respectful hospitality.
Permitted by Cyavana, he took a wife.
That great-souled Sagara had two wives.
Accompanied by those two, the king performed austerities for the sake of obtaining a son.
At the conclusion of his ascetic penance, Hara spoke to the king, who was emaciated by his austerities.
One of them shall give birth to a single son who will perpetuate your lineage. ||19||
A second [wife] shall give birth to sixty thousand sons.
Having thus obtained the boon, the king went to his own city together with his wife.
The virtuous and powerful one begot a son and sons.
By both his deeds and his name, he was known as Prince Asamañjasa.
Exiled from the kingdom by his father, he was intent on doing harm to the citizens.
His son was named Aṃśumat, endowed with all excellent qualities.
He gratified his father and his father’s father, the lord of the earth.
The sinless one was attended by that grandson and by his sons, who possessed great heroism and prowess.
That high-souled one, the best of kings who had conquered his enemies, ruled over the entire earth while bringing joy to it. || 23 ||
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Legend of Sagara," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Those sons of Sagara, united and endowed with prowess, [set out].
By the turn of fate, thorns to the gods and Brahmins have arisen.
Distressed by their actions, all the gods [approached] the Grandfather.
They all said, "O Lord, we shall be oppressed by all the oceans joined together. ||2||
Thus addressed, Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, then [spoke].
He spoke to all the gods, who were provoked to indignation by the oceans.
But he who is the Lord of this world, the eternal Supreme Self—
That Vāsudeva, who is Kapila, will cause those gods to be slain.
Thus addressed by him, all the gods went to heaven.
At that very time, however, that lord of the earth, Sagara, [ruled]. || 5 ||
He was duly initiated for the horse sacrifice by those who had mastered the Vedas.
The sons caused the sacrificial horse to roam over the earth.
And while they were leading him away, that horse was likewise seized by Kapila.
Deluded, they do not know that the horse has been taken away by Kapila.
Even though they searched with great effort, they did not find the horse from which it had departed.
Having informed their father, they all buried them within the surface of the earth.
O King, within this ninth division of this land of Bhārata.
Then, those endowed with the strength of laborers performed the work of digging on all sides.
It was a hundred yojanas in width and reached down to the depths of the netherworld (pātāla).
To the north of the Himālaya mountain and to the east of the Vaiḍūryaparvata.
In the western half of the Golden Mountain and likewise to the north of the Salt Ocean.
And the heroic Himācala was wounded by them, O King, in two places on his body. || 11 ||
And a fragment of the Himalaya mountain was cast into the interior of the pit.

They saw the horse standing near Kapila.

Then the sage beheld those evil-minded ones as they were harassing them.

And all those who were thorns to the gods and the Brahmins have gone to hell. || 16 ||

Then, being pleased with him, the sage Kapila gave him a horse.
Then he spoke to Aṃśumān regarding the ancestors who were seeking water.
O King, you shall have a grandson, for I have been gratified by his ascetic penance.
That goddess Gaṅgā, whose girdle is the sky, will come.
By her, this ash of the evil-minded oceans was moistened.
When that time comes, the oceans shall go to heaven.
But when even the bone of another person falls into the waters of the Gaṅgā, [it attains liberation]. || 22 ||
For him too, there will be a journey to the world of the gods; of this there is no doubt.
Thus addressed, Aṃśumat quickly paid obeisance to the Teacher of the World.
Having approached, he yoked the Grandfather with the horse.
King Sagara also brought the sacrifice to completion. || 24 ||
For thus, O best of kings, was Khātaka surrounded by the intoxicated oceans.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Sagara," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having obtained the kingdom, the son of Dilīpa, a king of great splendor, [ruled].
Having heard that his ancestors were dwelling in hell, he quickly abdicated the kingdom for their welfare.
He then propitiated Gaṅgā with great austerity.
And by means of restraints, observances, and likewise by subsisting on leaves, O King.
For ten thousand years, the king performed intense austerities.
Then the great goddess Gaṅgā became serene and her fatigue vanished.
The righteous Bhagīratha, full of curiosity, also obtained a boon.
Then the goddess Lekhanadī spoke to that Bhagīratha.
The earth shall not be able to withstand my momentum as I fall from the sky.
Since they are not capable [of this], therefore quickly propitiate Śaṅkara.
For he, O lord of men, is capable of enduring the force of my fall.
Having spoken thus, the Goddess, the Sovereign Lady, then vanished from sight.
The virtuous Bhagīratha also performed most rigorous austerities.
For the purpose of propitiating the god Śaṅkara, the Great-Souled One.
At the conclusion of his ascetic penance, he of great splendor beheld the Lord of the Universe.
The God of gods said:
O King, I am pleased with your fierce austerity; [I grant you] whatever you desire.
I grant you devotion, as well as imperishable fame for your ancestors. ||9||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been addressed thus by the god, he worshipped Maheśvara.
The king, his desires fulfilled, went to the Ganges in his mind.
Having understood that it was presided over by Śaṅkara and what the king intended to do, [he spoke].
Then, O lotus-eyed one, the Gaṅgā fell from the sky.
Having learned of the descent of the Gaṅgā, Brahmā came to that place.
Placing before them the gods Yama, Indra, and Varuṇa, those beings of immeasurable splendor [proceeded].
The sages, nāgas, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and mahoragas.
Likewise, the hosts of Suparṇas and Kinnaras, as well as the hosts of Apsarases. || 13 ||
That expanse of the sky became crowded with hundreds of celestial chariots.
It was strewn with flowers and graced by gods and nāgas.
It was difficult to gaze upon due to its divine radiance, shining brightly with its ornaments.
The breeze was fragrant and pleasant, resounded by the music of celestial instruments.
A river fell from the sky through the midst of that cloud.
Having seized Śaṅkara with my current, I shall enter [the earth] after piercing through Pātāla.
Thus, with such a wicked disposition, she fell upon the head of Hara.
Having understood the goddess's cruel intention, the god who bears the Pināka bow—
The four-faced one placed that goddess within his mass of matted locks.
Having vanished, she wandered there for a long time as a river.
Whichever drops of hers fell and reached the earth, ||16||

The god also saw the king, whose senses were agitated by hunger.
Then Maheśvara quickly released her with the tip of his matted hair.
Then the Lord, having placed the Gaṅgā upon him, vanished from that place.

From that, the celestial river issued forth again, branching into seven streams.
Hlādinī, Hrādinī, and Plāvinī flow toward the east. ||22||
The Sītāvaktra and the Sindhu rivers flow toward the west.

In some places it flows with great velocity, and in others it creeps along slowly.
In some places its waters were turbulent with foam; in others, they were garlanded with whirlpools.
In some places there were surging waves of deep sound, and likewise in other places it was silent.
In some places it resounds loudly with the cries of swans; in other places it is filled with pairs of ruddy geese.
Its waters were agitated by garlands of waves, and it was adorned with heaps of flowers. ||25||
It is crowded with hundreds of aquatic creatures and bestows happiness upon the gods and siddhas.
Its waters are as sweet as nectar and rendered pure by contact with Hara. || 26 ||
Arising from the blow of Viṣṇu’s foot, it destroys all sins.
Having thus reached the Vindhya mountains, she entered the eastern ocean.
Having reached the underworld of terrifying appearance by means of the ocean, he entered it.
He caused that ash to be washed away by the great-souled oceans. ||28||
When the ashes were washed away, all those oceans went to heaven. ||29||
Thus the celestial river, possessing most meritorious waters and frequented by the best of sages, flows across the earth.
O King, the daughter of Jahnu is of great majesty; she has become a ladder for the journey to the third heaven.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Descent of the Gaṅgā," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Vajra said:
I have heard from you that you are the Bhāgīrathī, the Gaṅgā, the river of the gods.
For what reason is the Jāhnavī called "she who flows to the ocean" in the world? (1)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Lord of the Earth, there is a region named Pañcāla in the Middle Country,
which is always inhabited by those belonging to the various social classes and stages of life who are devoted to their own duties and actions.
There, the city Mahodaya was built by Kuśastamba.
It was strewn with all kinds of jewels and was renowned as Kānyakubja.
In that [lineage] there was a king named Jahnu, who was supremely righteous.
The fame of that illustrious one remains pervading the entire universe.
Once, that protector of the earth performed a horse sacrifice.
The river flowed toward the sacrificial enclosure of the consecrated king.
O best of the Yadus, he flooded [the land] with a torrent of water with great force.
When the sacrificial enclosure had been flooded, the king then spoke to the Gaṅgā.
"Receive now the immediate fruit of this arrogance toward the Gaṅgā."
I drink all your water, O beloved of the ocean.
Having spoken thus, the king drank all the water of the Bhāgīrathī.
O King, by means of great austerity as well as the power of yoga.
Then, having seen the Gaṅgā devoid of water, the distressed sages [lamented].
But being propitiated for the sake of Gaṅgā, he released her upon hearing [her words].
And then the king adopted Bhāgīrathī as his daughter.
Therefore, O delighter of the Yadus, she was called Jāhnavī in the world.
O King, when that monarch was exceedingly arrogant toward the Gaṅgā, [he was seized by the serpent].
O sinless one, he then flooded the sacrificial arena for the sake of fame.
Thus, O King, the daughter of Jahnu is declared by the wise to be the purifying Viṣṇupadī throughout the three worlds.
The daughter of Himācala, the lord of mountains; the wife of the ocean; the bestower of boons; she who is free from sorrow. || 12 ||
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Legend of Jahnu’s Daughter," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Vajra said:
For what reason is the Gaṅgā called Viṣṇupadī in the world by the wise?

By whom, having displayed his prowess, the kingdom of Śakra was then seized by force.
But the lord of the gods, having been deprived of his kingdom, went to Brahmā for refuge.
Brahmā too, taking Śakra with him, went for refuge to Hari.
Then he reported it to the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Brahmā, the auspicious four-faced one, [bestowed] the entire victory of Bāṣkali.

Atri was the son of Brahmā; his son was Saumya, and his son was Candra.
Budha was the son of Soma, and Purūravas was the son of Budha. || 1 ||
Śrutāyu was his son, and Nagnajit was the son of him as well.
His son was Kāñcana, and Suhotra was his offspring.
His son was the illustrious Jahnu, by whom the Gaṅgā became known as Jāhnavī.
His son was Suvrata, and his son was Cālarka.
His son was Balāka, and Kuśika was his offspring.
He, however, made his permanent residence in that most excellent city of Mahodaya.
At that very time, however, your father-in-law Cyavana—
Having perceived the intermixture of his own lineage with the Kuśikas, the one of great fame [acted].
For the sake of exterminating the Kuśikas, he went to King Kuśika.
Having been honored by Kuśika as well, he spoke these words to Kuśika.
O King, sinless one, I shall tell you what must be done, if you wish to listen.
And, O King, you must perform service together with your wife.
Kuśika said:
"This house is indeed yours; dwell here as you please, O Bhārgava."
"To the best of my ability, I shall perform service for you together with my wife. (8)
Ṛcīka said:
Desiring to serve that Cyavana while he resided in his home, he remained free from egoism.
He constantly honored him with the fulfillment of all his desires. ||9||
Cyavana did not perceive that many numerous days had passed.
Taking no food, the lord of the earth attended upon him along with his wife.
He sometimes eats food at the improper time, even when it is difficult to obtain.
"It is done," the king announces with all haste. ||11||
Sometimes he eats much food, and sometimes he does not eat for many days.
And with that man's wealth, he indeed gratified the twice-born.
Sometimes he even illuminates the fire produced within his father's house.
And once, he saw that bull among kings yoked to a chariot together with his wife.
He prods them with a goad along the royal highway according to his own will.
For him, this [person] is truly beneficial through action, mind, and speech. (14)
He practices with diligence out of a desire to do what is pleasing to Bhārgava.
When he did not see any fault whatsoever, O Bhārgava, [he spoke].
Then he granted him a boon, whatever boon was desired by his mind.
Cyavana said:
Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—for I am pleased with you, O sinless one.
O King, you have always served her with this sincere and faultless devotion.
Kuśika said:
If you are pleased with me, O enhancer of the lineage of the Bhṛgus!
"Let my lineage attain the status of Brahmins; this is the boon I choose. (18)
Cyavana said:
"This alone is certain to happen: that you choose me as your bride, O King."
"Brahminhood shall belong to you and to the lineage of your descendants. ||19||
O best of the twice-born, the duty of the Kshatriya is the one established by your lineage for us.
O Lord of Men, this shall come to pass; this is well known to me.
Having understood this, you who desire to raise up your own lineage, [should act accordingly].
For the sake of provoking your anger through various transformations, I dwelt in your house for a long time.
No transformation resulting from that was seen by me, as it was impelled by a future purpose.
Therefore, you have obtained from your mother this boon which is very difficult to attain. ||22||
A son named Kuśāśva shall indeed be born, who will be exceedingly righteous.
He, too, shall have a son renowned as Gādhi.
His son Viśvāmitra shall attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
Having created enmity with Vasiṣṭha through his great ascetic power, O King.
From the exchange of sacrificial porridge among the women, Viśvāmitra was born.
O King, may you be one who has attained liberation, having experienced [the fruits of] our lineage.
That which has been destroyed by you will become burnt, yet it shall possess its own particular excellence.
And together with your wife, you shall be free from old age. ||26||
When the brahmin had departed after speaking thus, the king’s desires were fulfilled.
He spoke to Sumukhī, who was free from old age and sorrow: "O blessed lady! (27)
O fair-eyed one, what man on earth has the power to fulfill these words of Cyavana?
In order to make that false, he chose this boon among others: "Your grandson shall become fierce in the world of men. || 28 ||
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Granting of Boons to Kuśika," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra. || 34 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus addressed, Satyavatī, when the time was fulfilled, [spoke] to the best of the twice-born.
She gave birth to Jamadagni, who was a knower of dharma and whose wealth was his asceticism.
And from him, she gave birth to Vātsya, a scion of the Bhṛgu lineage.
Then he begot eighty-nine sons, who were the founders of various lineages.
At that time, Gādhi’s wife also gave birth to a son.
He was renowned as Viśvāmitra, endowed with the splendor of a Brāhmaṇa.
That king was defeated in battle by Vasiṣṭha through the power of his wrath.
That righteous-souled one, firm in his vows, attained the status of a Brahmin through austerity.
Then King Prasenajit [gave] his daughter, Reṇukā, to him.
Jamadagni, of great asceticism, accepted her for the sake of a wife.
She attended upon him with devotion every day while he was in the forest.
Then once, during the summer season, when the sun had reached the meridian, || 6 ||
The great ascetic Jamadagni threw it for a long time for the sake of sport.
As beautiful-eyed Reṇukā was struck again and again by him with arrows.
Knowing what was right and obedient to her husband's word, she brought it.
Then, scorched by the heat of the sun, her lotus-feet were being burned.
And having reached the shade of a flowering tree, she stood there.
Having rested for a moment, she brought that excellent arrow to her husband.
When she had arrived, her husband Jamadagni, filled with anger, spoke to her.
"O blessed lady, why have you created this obstacle for me while I was playing with my arrows?"
"O blessed lady, you do not fear me, or perhaps you even despise me. (11)
Reṇukā said:
O observer of the great vow, she was scorched for a mere moment by the heat of the sun and fire.
Being unable to proceed, I have rested; therefore, you ought to forgive me. || 12 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard the words of Reṇukā, Jamadagni, of great asceticism, [acted].
Then, his anger aroused, he prepared to discharge arrows at the sun. || 13 ||
At that very time, however, Divākara appeared in the form of a brahmin.
Having arrived quickly, the radiant one addressed Jamadagni.
Sūrya said:
O Brahmin, it is my very nature that I am of the essence of fire.
And since I act according to my own nature, you ought not to be angry with me. || 15 ||
"I shall become your son through her alone, O best of the twice-born."
I shall perform the work of protection and bring about the great welfare of the worlds. || 16 ||
And this wife of yours, Renuka, who knows the dharma, is now [here].
"O lady of excellent complexion, please accept this parasol and pair of sandals from me. (17)
Out of compassion for him, O Brahmin, [I gave] an umbrella as well as sandals.
In this world created by me, these two shall exist eternally.
The gift of an umbrella and sandals shall be the most excellent in the world.
By the gift of an umbrella and sandals, a man shall go to heaven. || 19 ||
Thus addressed by Sūrya, Jamadagni, the great ascetic, [replied].
Having worshipped the Sun, he received the entire speech of Savitṛ.
Then, when the sun had set, the virtuous goddess, the daughter of the Sun from of old, [departed].
Reṇukā gave birth to Rāma as her youngest son.
Tama, Anūpa, Vasuṣeṇa, Vasu, and likewise Viśvāvasu. || 21 ||
Among them, Rāma, who was born last, was Viṣṇu assuming a human form.
When the God of gods was born upon the earth through a portion of himself, the earth then became truly at peace.
And that earth considered the suffering of the sons of Diti taken away as her own, as well as that of human beings. || 23 ||
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Birth of Rāma," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then Rāma, the scion of the Bhṛgu lineage, having transcended childhood, [proceeded].
The highly illustrious one remained constantly serving his father. || 1 ||
At that very time, however, when Rāma had gone to the forest.
The highly resplendent King Citrāṅgada came to the forest.
He, whose splendor was equal to that of the king of the gods, dwelt together with the beautiful women.
Seeing him, the beautiful Reṇukā conceived a longing for worldly enjoyments.
She went in her mind to that king, who resembled the god of love.
At that very moment, however, she was deprived of her Brahmanic luster.
But seeing her deprived of her fortune, Jamadagni, the great ascetic, [spoke].
Out of anger, he said to those sons, "Let your own mother be killed! || 5 ||
Then, having all reflected upon the supreme reverence due to their mother, they [acted].
They did not obey their father's word at all; consequently, that descendant of Bhṛgu cursed them.
You shall become like animals, devoid of right consciousness.
Taking up a load of sacrificial fuel, Rāma brought delight to his father. || 7 ||
Then, having arrived at the hermitage, his father urged him on.
O Rāma, do not delay; abandon this wretched mother.
Thus addressed by his father, immediately upon those words, he...
Then Rāma severed his head with a sharp axe.
Then his father, the best among the upholders of dharma, was gratified.
Jamadagni said:
"O son, when I am pleased, you shall obtain the power to die at your own will."
And as long as the Vaiṣṇava splendor remains within you, my son.
At that very moment, no one shall be your conqueror in battle.
And Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, shall be righteous in nature.
Viṣṇu, having assumed a human form, was born in the lineage of Raghu.
When he shall be united with that splendor of Viṣṇu, then indeed [it will come to pass].
You have performed your duty and are liberated, and he too shall become disciplined.
"Therefore, my son, from now on you must not bear weapons."
O hero, except for the protection of those in distress, or for the sake of women and Brahmins.
And choose another boon as you desire, my son.
Rāma said:
O best of gurus, I shall describe the arising of the Mother.
And likewise, there was a lack of mindfulness regarding her, and likewise a lack of mindfulness regarding his brothers. ||15||
Jamadagni said:
"Let it be so, O illustrious one, through such great ascetic power."
Propitiate Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, who is blue and red.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When this was said, Renuka, with her beautiful smile, rose up.
All the brothers of Rāma were likewise released from their curse.
Thus addressed by his father on Himavat, the best of mountains, Rāma—
Possessed of great splendor, he performed austerities with the desire to propitiate Rudra.
At that very time, however, the gods, led by Indra, [arrived].
Terrified by the fear of the son of Siṃhikā, they went to Śaṅkara for refuge.
The gods said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before you!
We have all been cast down from our positions by the sons of Siṃhikā.
Then, relying upon the sons of Siṃhikā, the Daityas by the hundreds of thousands [attacked].
They all dwell there constantly; exert yourself in their destruction.
Mahādeva said:
Let all the deities listen, as well as the Dānavas, those thorns in the side of the gods.
"For I shall be slain by Rāma, since he regards them as mere men."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When the hosts of gods had departed, the god of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, [remained].
Having summoned Rāma Bhārgava, he spoke these words.
Mahādeva said:
O son, slay the ill-behaved Asuras, the sons of Siṃhikā.
You alone are capable of slaying them; no one else exists who possesses such power.
Rāma said:
O Destroyer of Bhaga, grant me the entire collection of celestial weapons.
By means of which I shall slay those Dānavas of wicked conduct.
Mahādeva said:
O best of the Bhṛgus, what use have you for weapons? You are Viṣṇu; you are not a mere mortal.
Even when you are distracted, they are not capable of fighting in your presence.
Rāma said:
I shall slay all those unassailable sons of Siṃhikā.
O illustrious Tripurāri, [I am] strengthened by your command. || 27 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus addressed by the Destroyer of Tripura, Rāma, whose power was equal to that of the Three-eyed One, [acted].
Taking up a sharp axe, he went to where those foremost of enemies were stationed.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Command of Maheśvara to Rāma," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
At that very time, however, there were most terrible portents involving wood.
Very great portents occurred in the abode of Siṃhikā’s son.
The earth, together with its forests and groves, trembled while making a great sound.
A great meteor fell from the center of the solar disc.
Likewise, the moon and the sun were eclipsed by darkness at an improper time.
And likewise, terrifying clouds rained down blood in great abundance. || 3 ||
The weapons, shedding tears repeatedly, emitted smoke.
The sun was surrounded by a halo having the color of Indra’s bow.
He was served during both twilights and throughout the entire night by the moon.
The son of Siṃhikā was also the husband of the daughters of the great-souled Śālva.
Having assailed the Kṣatriya power at its very birth, the great planet Ketu remained stationed there.
Fierce great winds blew, agitating the ten directions.
The sun appeared with a headless trunk for its body, and the deer were filled with cries.
They clung to the tips of the banners of the evil-minded Dānavas. ||7||
For terrifying flocks of carnivorous birds were wheeling to the left.
Even though it was well-supplied with dry fuel, the sacrificial fire did not blaze up. ||8||
The bodies of the lords of the Dānavas did not shine forth, O Yādava.
An inversion of heat and cold was also observed even among the seasons.
The trees exuded blood, and their ornaments fell shattered to the ground.
Donkeys were born among the cows, and cats among the mice.
The trees have blossomed out of season; the great trees have borne fruit out of season.
Without rain, the great rivers rushed with force in the opposite direction.
Having observed a multitude of most terrible and terrifying portents, the king was seized with fear.
Then Śālva, accompanied by the Daityas, summoned the son of Bhṛgu and held a consultation with him.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Portents," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having then reached that vast assembly hall, variegated with jewels, |||
Sālva, the son of Siṃhikā, spoke these words to Śukra: || 1 ||
Śālva said:
"O Blessed One, these portents of terrible appearance are being seen."
Proclaiming the great battle and even the terrible destruction.
Nor do we see any enemy with whom we shall have to fight.
Because you possess omniscience, you know this; therefore, tell it to us who ask.
Śukra said:
In ancient times, Siṃhikā propitiated the god Brahmā through her ascetic penance.
For she obtained from the thirty gods the invincibility of her own sons.
By you, who are inspired by the granting of boons, through my vidyā—
All the thirty gods, having been utterly defeated, went to Śaṅkara for refuge. || 5 ||
Therefore, for the purpose of slaying you, Viṣṇu has assumed a human form.
Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, who is fierce in battle, has been dispatched.
That god of great splendor was always [divine], but now he has indeed become human.
There is a terrible fear even of humans; fight, O best of Asuras!
Śālva said:
O Blessed One, Madhusūdana is the lord of all the gods.
Therefore, we have heard of no other deity whatsoever who is higher than Him.
For what purpose did that one of great splendor [serve] the high-souled Śaṅkara?
O best of the Bhṛgus, acting according to his command, he seeks to slay the son of Siṃhikā.
Śukra said:
For whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Dānava,
When there is the rise of unrighteousness, he then creates himself anew.
Sometimes among the Daityas and gods, and sometimes among human beings.
Then, at one time, having understood the relative strength and weakness of the task among the animals, [he acted].
When he is among the gods, then he acts like a god.
And when the god acts like an animal among animals, then [he is so].
When one exists in the human state, then one behaves like a mortal.
Having attained human form, [he worshipped] the Destroyer of Tripura through austerity.
O King, he propitiated Hara within his own body.
But he, a man of great asceticism, placing the command of the best of gods before him, [set out].
Marked by Rāma for the purpose of slaying you, he is coming here.
Therefore, an alliance with Śakra is pleasing to me.
And let Triviṣṭapa belong to the gods, O best of Asuras.
Dwell in your abode in Pātāla, free from all anxiety.
I shall restrain Bhārgava by means of Śaṅkara.
And otherwise, you shall dwell as those rejected by man. (17)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been addressed thus by Śukra, the Daityas and Dānavas understood [his intent].
Highly incensed, they spoke these words to Śukra, the descendant of Bhrigu's lineage.
The Daityas said: "The entire world, both stationary and moving, is established in one place."
If one should fight against him, even there no fear exists. ||19||
How, being afraid of a mere human, shall we abandon heaven to our enemy?
"We shall conquer that Śaṅkara by whom this twice-born man has been sent."
Śukra said:
The entire world, both stationary and moving, was gathered together in one place.
In one [aspect] he is the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu; he excels the world.
He cannot be conquered in battle, nor indeed is he the god Maheśvara himself.
Therefore, all of you great Asuras, having abandoned your ordinary intellects, [should act accordingly].
Make peace with the god Śakra, the slayer of enemies.
Janārdana, the God of gods, is ever intent upon the task of Śakra.
By whom the Daityas were struck down—those of former times and those even more ancient.
Śambara, Namuci, Śambu, and Kārtavīrya, who had committed offenses;
Hiraṇyakaśipu, Keśin, Hiraṇyākṣa, and Madotkaṭa. || 24 ||
Madhu, Kaiṭabha, Viṭa, Dhūma, and Atikopana.
Hayagrīva, Niśuṇḍa, Sunda, Candrārkalocana,
Candrārkamardana, Candrahartṛ, and Raṇapriya.
Sūryaśatru, Jitāmitra, Yajñaha, and Yajñatāpana. || 26 ||
Meghanāda, Mahāroma, Meghavāda, and Bhayānaka.
The Dānava Daśagrīva, Śatagrīva, and Mahāgrīva. ||27||
Kālaka, Kālakeya, Kālanemi, and Sulocana.
Kāla, Kālakalpa, Makarākṣa, and Janāntaka. || 28 ||
Antaka, Keśamanobhīma, Devāntaka, and Narāntaka.
Krodhaha, Bahunetra, Mahākāla, and Jalāntaka. ||29||
Ekalavya, Sādhāra, Durmukha, Durdhara, and Vaḍi.
And Indutāpana and Rambha, who were dear to Raṇacaṇḍa and Hara. || 1.38.30 ||
Kirīṭin, Gajavaktra, Mahāsāla, and Vilohita.
Hrāda, Anuhrāda, Prahrāda, Vṛkṣa, Rakṣa, and Radāruṇa. || 31 ||
Śatabha, Śalabha, and the great asura Kūpana.
Vipracitti, Śiva, Śaṅkarāya, and likewise Śaṅku. || 32 ||
Ayaḥśiras, Aśvaśiras, Bhīmadakṣa, and Guhāśaya.
The great asura was possessed of speed, bearing a banner, gracious, yet fierce in his form. || 33 ||
Puṣkara, Puṣkala, Sālva, and Aśvapati as well.
Kumbha, Nikumbha, Śatada, Saṃgraha, and Gaganapriya. || 34 ||
These and other renowned sons of Diti were arrogant in battle.
All have obtained boons and are heroes; all have cast away their anger. || 35 ||
All the kingdoms of the thirty-three gods were brought under their control by those arrogant in their power.
They were slain by that god out of a desire to do what was pleasing to Vāsava.
Some were in human form, and others in the form of animals.
And some were slain in the form of gods by him of immense splendor.
Śālva said:
I know the majesty of that god of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
"O Bhārgava, considering my own death certain, I shall fight with him."
Death at the hands of a superior is better than victory over an inferior in battle.
The kingdom of those whose hands have been destroyed by Viṣṇu shall flourish once again. || 39 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus addressed by the lord of the asuras, that venerable Śukra, the foremost of the Bhṛgus, [spoke].
Having learned that all the Daityas were destroyed, he went to another desired quarter.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Śukra and Sālva," within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When Śukra had departed after speaking thus, Gaviṣṭha spoke these words.
O King, let the word of Śukra be carried out without hesitation.
"Indeed, most terrible dreams that increase fear are seen at the end of the night, O Lord, constantly portending your destruction. (2)
In a dream, I saw you wearing red garlands and smeared with red unguents.
Traveling on an camel, a porpoise, and likewise on a boar; ||3||
And other Daityas, smeared with oil, mounted upon donkey-vehicles.
O King, you saw mountains falling down; they were a cause of fear.
Some wore black garments, while others ate kṛsara.
Some were seen stuck in the mud, and some had gone to lie upon ashes.
Some are dragged toward the southern direction by a naked woman.
A certain woman, dressed in red garments, was being led toward the southern direction.
Some kings dance, and others likewise laugh.
Some were seen by me with shaven heads, and some were clad in saffron-colored robes.
Some were mounted on the shoulders of Caṇḍālas, while others were perched upon Kiṃśuka trees.
And you, O Bhava, were accompanied by the entire army of elephants, horses, and infantry.
Having reached a very turbid pond, he sank into a pool of cow dung.
And I beheld Rājaśrī intent upon embracing Śakra.
O King, an alliance between you and Śakra is pleasing to me.
"O King, protect your life; for one who lives attains blessings."
Sālva said:
O sinless one, as soon as the Blessed Viṣṇu was heard of by me as an enemy, [I acted].
O Lord, having heard that very thing, I likewise renounced the kingdom.
Sacrifices were performed, austerities were practiced, and a kingdom free from thorns was established.
The enemies were placed upon his head, and his friends were protected.
All our dependents have been supported; therefore, we have fulfilled our duty.
Having met his death at the hands of Govinda, he shall regain his kingdom once more.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these very words of the king, Gaviṣṭha then considered them to be most improper.
Then he became silent, his mind firmly resolved, and he considered the Daityas as already destroyed in battle.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Dreams," in the first section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
At that very time, however, [the encounter] of the high-souled Śālva [took place].
And he was seen with only his head remaining from his elder brother.
The king, well-known as Rāhu, paid him homage.
Having been honored by the king as was fitting, he sat down and spoke these words.
Rāhu said:
For enmity with the powerful Viṣṇu does not please me.
From whose wrath I, Anaṅga, the destroyer of the enemy's forces, was born. ||3||
And it was through his grace that he attained the status of a planet.
O son of an asura, what is the use of praising his other deeds?
Śālva said:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear how it was by that great-souled one.
O Hero, you were made bodiless; and how was the Lord of Planets (Rāhu) made so? || 5 ||
Rāhu said:
In ancient times, the gods, together with Indra, desiring immortality,
went to Keśava for refuge.
The gods said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, destroyer of the afflictions of the worlds!
We are no different from mortals; therefore, may you be our protector in that matter.
The Blessed One said:
O gods, you ought to make an effort in churning the Ocean of Milk.
By joining together with the Dānavas, you shall then attain even greater prosperity.
Rāhu said:
Thus addressed by the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, all the deities [spoke].
Having joined together with the Dānavas, they churned the abode of Varuṇa.
O King, she rendered assistance to them in that task.
Without the assistance of Viṣṇu, neither the gods nor the asuras are capable [of success].
Having become Ananta, he is then a portion of Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Having uprooted the temple with his two arms, he hurled it into the ocean.
Then Janārdana, having become Akūpāra, assumed the form of a tortoise.
He quickly held Mount Mandara, which had entered the Ocean of Milk.
Having thus joined the serpent Vāsuki with his own splendor, he [said]:
O Dānava, he assumed the role of the eye in each respective task there.
Then the gods and the dānavas suddenly churned the ocean.
Where the mouth was, there the Daityas were; where the tail was, there the gods were.
The Daityas were born from Vāsuki while the great ocean was being churned.
And he himself held the mouth of the Naga king with his hand. || 15 ||
Having turned his face toward the sky, Janārdana, the God of gods, [spoke].
Indeed, O King, by the poisonous breath from her mouth— || 16 ||
Otherwise, there would have been the destruction of the hosts of Daityas.
The waves of the milk ocean, resembling the Himalayas, reached the very heavens. || 17 ||
They flew up as he was being churned by the gods and the Dānavas for the sake of slaying Bala.
The peaks of Mount Mandara fell into the great ocean.
Hundreds and thousands of delightful objects, variegated with jewels. || 19 ||
And trees fell by the hundreds, and deer fell by the thousands.
Filling the three worlds with its roar, the ocean resounded.
Clad in the ripples of milk, with white clouds as his garment;
That Mount Mandara shines, adorned with various minerals,
its cloud-like garments fluttering violently as they are filled by the wind.
The mountain, with its cave-mouths bowing down, was like the ocean with its intoxicated elephants.
With waterfalls for tears, a great roar, and mighty arms raised like mountain peaks.
That best of mountains weeps incessantly at the very loss of its abode.
Thinking, "All these great things are to be enjoyed by the gods."
While the divine musical instruments were being played, that Mount Mandara seemed as if it were dancing.
For thus was the great-souled Ocean of Milk being churned.
A terrible poison appeared, possessing a radiance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.
By the mere appearance of which the gods and dānavas were despondent.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Division of the Nectar," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.

O Lord of Daityas, he attains satisfaction through righteousness just as it does for human beings.
That which ought to be said by an elder brother, who is a friend desiring one's welfare.
O Lord, that which has been spoken by you was uttered as if by a god; it does not please me.
Therefore, O illustrious one, go; you shall see me again in heaven.
Having attained another body, he was perceived by means of the divine eye.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus, having heard these words of Śālva and having understood them to be appropriate for the occasion, [he spoke].
Without saying anything at all, the high-souled Rāhu, the foremost of the worlds, departed for heaven. ||21||
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Words of Śālva," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 44 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When Rāhu had not yet reached the sky, King Śālva entered the assembly hall.
A messenger sent by Rāma, Akṛtavraṇa, has arrived. || 1 ||

Akṛtavraṇa said:
"O Śālva, I am a messenger sent by Rāma, whose actions are performed without effort."
Having heard Rāma's words, then do as you desire.
Rama, the descendant of Bhrigu, released by Tryambaka, has spoken to you.
O Lord of Daityas, grant me a moment in battle for a fight with you.
Having banished Vāsava from heaven and having constantly conquered the gods in battle, he [ruled].
O evil-minded one, reap the fruit of this terrible misconduct!
I never strike one who is careless or trusting.
Therefore, a messenger has been sent by him; for that reason, remain firm in battle.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus addressed, Śālva then spoke these words to the brāhmaṇa.
O Brahmin, I never arm myself for the sake of Rāma.
But with the entire army arrayed and clad in armor.
"I shall conquer Mahādeva, by whom Rāma was sent away."
Accompanied by his arrayed army and desiring victory for Mahādeva.
If Rāma fights me, I shall slay him in battle.
Therefore, go as you please and report this to Rāma.
Having received these words from that high-souled Sālva, he—
Having been informed by the words of the Sālva king, he went to Rāma, who knows the dharma.
Having gone, he reported to Rāma the deeds of the son of Siṃhikā.
At those words, Rāma also went to the city of the Daityas out of anger.
When that messenger of Rāma had departed, Śālva urged on the Daityas.
"Arm yourselves; we shall conquer Bhaga-sūdana along with his host."
Then all those Dānavas were urged by the words of Śālva.
Having equipped themselves for battle, they departed from their own homes and arrived at the palace gate.
By the trumpeting of elephants and the sound of conchs and kettledrums, ||14||
A great and tumultuous noise arose at the palace gate.
Having offered oblations into the fire and bathed, O Sālva, he then honored the twice-born.
He mounted the rutting elephant as the sun ascends the peak of a mountain. || 16 ||
Seeing the lord of the Daityas emerged, the lords of the Daityas, whose pride was equal to that of Time itself, [advanced].
Then they said to him, "Invincible in battles, conquer Śambhu by seizing him in combat. (17)

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Departure of Śālva," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara, concerning the battle between the descendant of Bhṛgu and Rāma.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:

Wolves, jackals, tigers, cats, donkeys, and hares. ||4||

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Observation of Ill Omens in the Army of Śālva," in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
He was resplendent with a mass of matted hair that had the color of the tips of flames of fire.

The support of all the gods, whose radiance is illuminated by ascetic power.

A single hero, alone, adorned with a hundred thousand [ornaments].

Resplendent with a black antelope skin as his upper garment, he was exultant in his strength.
It was as if colored by the affectionate glance of Pārvatī. || 4 ||
He was resplendent with his staff-like arms, which shone like radiant golden rods.
With a sharp battle-axe that possessed the luster of the stainless sky. || 5 ||
He was an ascetic, invisible to the sight, resembling Yama, the Ender of Time.

At dawn, it was stealing away all splendors like the orb of the sun.
Tall, with limbs the color of gold, and wearing a white sacred thread.

Unassailable, irresistible, difficult to overcome, and a destroyer of life.

When Rāma came within the range of their vision from all sides, the Dānavas [were struck with fear].
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from those who were slaying him alone in battle.
Having lost his Brahminhood by wielding weapons, he has fallen from his own path.
"Kill this man of wicked conduct! they said to one another.
Thus, as those many assailants were rushing forward.

With maces, swords, nooses, bhuśuṇḍī missiles, and iron balls.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Vision of Paraśurāma in Battle," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, in that battle, he was being struck down by the army of Siṃhikā’s son.

With their heads severed by axes that have sharp edges and points, and are difficult to behold.

Arising from the bodies of Daityas pierced by the tips of battle-axes.

Of the Dānavas being slain repeatedly by Rāma.

With all his limbs covered by arrows, he was drenched in blood.

Likewise, hundreds of weapons were released from the arms of the Daityas.
In the battle, he who was fierce in combat severed [it] with the tip of his axe. || 15 ||
As they were being cut to pieces, fire burst forth from them.

Having shaken off the mass of causes, he is like the fierce sun dispersing a mass of clouds.
The destroyer of the splendor of the Daityas appeared once more.
Brahmā, together with the hosts of gods and the high-souled sages.
O Yādava, he honored that battle with shouts of "Excellent! (sādhuvāda).
And they have witnessed battles fought with the bow again and again.

This battle of Rāma with many is unprecedented.
"Ugra is the name for one whose weapon is the battle-axe," thus the gods spoke. || 21 ||
Then Rāma, too, was being honored with heaps of celestial flowers.
In the battle, he severed the heads of the Daityas by the hundreds in the fray.
Bhārgava, whose limbs were smeared with the blood of the Daityas and who possessed swift prowess.
Then, O Yādava, he sees it as resembling a whirling firebrand.
By this fierce one, who wanders in battle with the splendor of the fire of time (Kālāgni).

He wrought a terrible slaughter, like the fire of universal destruction risen up.
He saw elephants with their trunks severed and other elephants drenched in blood.
Having descended to the earth, we do not see them, for they have darkened the intermediate spaces of the directions. || 29 ||
For thus did he fight in battle, possessing the splendor of the fire of time.
Millions and hundreds of millions of the lords of the Dānavas were slain.
The earth is not capable of enduring their blows.
Even though his limbs were pierced by their blows, Rāma did not tremble at all.
Having seen the distress caused by the blows and the great asuras slain,
The hosts of Daityas fled to Śālva for refuge in the battle.
Seeing that the sons of Diti were few in number, nearly destroyed, and intent upon their own welfare, Śālva—

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Sālva Army," in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the highly energetic Sālva, with his swift elephant, [advanced].

He brought to a standstill the lord of serpents, who resembled the peak of a great mountain.
He, who delighted in battle, stood before that Śālva.
He held in his hand an axe, its body smeared with blood, stained and impure.
Bearing [it], he moves like Viṣṇu, making the entire world free from blemish.
An elephant [was used] for Rāma, who desired to mount the back of an elephant.
The swift one took away his momentum with straight-knotted arrows.
His prowess was turned away by the multitude of arrows discharged by the Sālva king.
In battle, the hosts of Daityas covered Rāma with excellent weapons.
In that battle, Rāma was completely covered by a great mass of missiles.
Then, with eyes closed, he hurled his axe at Śālva.
The Sālva [beheld] that battle-axe approaching him with great speed in the fray.

Terrified by Rāma’s lion-roar, the leader of the elephant herd [fled].

Possessing great speed, he seized [it] with force, desiring to bring about the end of the Dānavas.
Having seen Rāma with his axe and Sālva struck down, [he was filled with fear].
Those Daityas who remained after being slain entered the abode of Varuṇa.
At that very time, however, the gods, led by Indra, [arrived].

O King, he dwelt in heaven, protecting the three worlds. || 19 ||
Even Mahādeva, on a chariot yoked with lions, [approached] Bhārgava.
Having taken it, he departed swiftly for Kailāsa, the best of mountains.
And with oil, Hara performed a thorough cleansing of his limbs.
By which means, O noble-minded ones, Rāma became strong and free from wounds. || 21 ||
Having attained victory that was present before him, he was free from wounds and endowed with splendor.
Śaṅkara spoke these words to Rāma, the best among strikers. 22.
Śaṅkara said:
O Rāma, Rāma, O highly fortunate one, I have been thoroughly gratified by you.
Therefore, I shall grant you this unsurpassed collection of divine weapons.
O Bhārgava, you alone on earth are capable of wielding celestial weapons.
Your fortitude is incomparable; your courage is unsurpassed.
O son, remaining here, perform the yoga of the weapons very gradually.
O Rāma, having mastered all weapons, you shall go to your own father.
And as for that divine axe, O sinless one, which was given to you by your father—
From this day forward, your cast-off hand shall once again be reunited with you.
And this is merely an illustration; it shall be so for you as well.
I shall sever your doubts; be at peace, my son.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus addressed, the high-souled Rāma, who had conquered the pride of his enemies, felt his desires completely fulfilled.
He dwelt there together with the Pramathas, training himself in all the divine weapons.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Śālva," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. || 49 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The Brahmāstra, the Vaiṣṇava, the Raudra, the Āgneya, and the Vāsava.

Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, variegated with various minerals.

In the constant and beautiful sound produced by the cascades of the Gaṅgā.

I do not see any other god whatsoever who is superior to you.
The gods, together with Indra, always worship your linga.
The hosts of ṛṣis praise you and meditate upon you again and again.
They worship the Supreme Lord, the giver of boons, with such devotion.
In the creation, sustenance, destruction, and protection of this world.
I consider you alone to be the cause; everything is established in you.
"O Lord of Gods, upon whom do you meditate? In this regard, I have a great doubt."
Tell me that, O Blessed One, if I am worthy of your favor.
O Foremost One in the World, having gained this confidence through your gracious presence, I have said this.
Having prostrated with my head before you, the one worthy of praise, I ask, my soul filled with curiosity.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "Rāma’s Question," within the *Śaṅkaragītā* in the *Paraśurāmopākhyāna*, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the first section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*. 51.
Śaṅkara said:
O lotus-eyed Rāma, this further question has been asked by you.
O scion of the Bhrigu lineage, you alone are worthy to hear this from me.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, that which is my supreme abode—
That which is the imperishable, unmanifest, and beyond which nothing higher exists.
He is knowledge and the object of knowledge, attainable through knowledge, and is seated in the hearts of all.
I meditate upon you, Janārdana, the lotus-eyed one.
O Rāma, this secret word has been told to you exactly as it is.
Those devotees who worship that unborn God do not suffer defeat.
To that Lord, unborn and unmanifest, the ultimate refuge of all beings. || 4 ||
Nārāyaṇa is indefinable, the cause of the cause of the world.

Possessing ears everywhere in the world, he stands encompassing all.
It manifests as the qualities of all the senses, yet it is devoid of all the senses.
It is unattached in every respect, devoid of qualities, yet the experiencer of the qualities.
He exists both outside and inside all beings, and is both the unmoving and the moving.
Because of its subtlety, it is unknowable; that which is far away is also near.
Undivided, yet existing as if divided among those who are divided.
And that which is to be known is the true wick, which is both devouring and powerful.
That is said to be the light of even the lights, and the supreme beyond darkness. ||9||
The beginningless supreme Brahman is said to be neither being nor non-being.
He who is the source and the transformation of all beings, the creator of the worlds.
I meditate upon that God, beyond whom there is nothing higher.
All this triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is merely a product of will.
I meditate upon that God, who is the God of gods.
In whom all is contained, from whom all proceeds, who is all, and who is everywhere.
And I meditate upon that God who is eternal and consists of all things.
To Viṣṇu, the lord of yogins, Padmanābha, the victorious, the master of the universe; || 13 ||
I meditate upon Jagannātha, the wide-eyed one, the teacher of the world.
The pure one, whose station is purity, the swan, the supreme, the highest lord.
With my whole being, I take refuge in that Prajāpati, the Self.
In whom all beings abide and into whom they enter. || 15 ||
They exist as subordinate qualities within the Lord of Beings, like clusters of gems upon a thread.
When that eternal, extended thread is perceived, one remains like a bird [released from its snare]. || 16 ||
The universe, woven from both the existent and the non-existent, resides within the Universal Form of the Architect of All.
Hari, who has a thousand heads, a thousand feet, and a thousand eyes.
They call him the god Nārāyaṇa, who is the supreme refuge of the universe.
The most minute among the minute, and the most massive among the massive.
The most venerable among the venerable, and the best even among those who are excellent.
Or that which is found in the Vākas, the Anuvākas, the Niṣads, and the Upaniṣads; || 19 ||
They praise the one of true deeds as the Truth itself within the truthful Sāman hymns.
He who is fourfold in nature through his four forms, established in goodness, the Lord of the Sātvatas.
Whom the gods worship with divine and secret, supreme names.
He who is free from desire and devoid of expectations beholds himself as one whose impurities have vanished. || 21 ||
Having sacrificed to Govinda for the sake of infinity, one beholds Him established within the self.

[He saw] that one Adhokṣaja who has manifested himself in many forms. || 23 ||
Those who are devoted to no other and are observant of ritual duties worship [Him], the granter of all desires.
That which they call the treasury of the worlds, in which all living beings are contained.

The Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, who is beyond reasoning and unknowable.

I take refuge in that Prajāpati, who transcends the entire collection of the sense organs of the intellect.
To him who is indeed the creator of the universe, the lord of all that moves and stands; || 29 ||

He whose mouth is fire, whose head is heaven, whose navel is space, and whose feet are the earth.
