Mṛgā, Mṛgamandā, Haribhadrā, and Manoharā. || 19 ||
And Bhūtā, Kaśipā, Daṃṣṭrā, Sarasā, and likewise Surasā.
And the beautiful woman Irā gave birth to all grasses and herbs.
O knower of dharma, listen as I describe that fivefold [nature] to you.
Trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, bark-fiber species, and various kinds of grasses; || 21 ||
These beings possess internal consciousness, yet they are enveloped by terrible darkness.
O descendant of Yadu, these are the presiding deities of these [elements].
The auspicious Irā, daughter of Dakṣa and knower of dharma, gave birth [to them].
Prādhā gave birth to the Apsarases; hear their names from me.
She was irreproachable, well-proportioned, delicate, and fond of compassion.
Manūnā, Subhagā, Sahajanyā, and Menakā. || 24 ||
Ghṛtasthūlā, Ghṛtācī, Viṣūcī, and Pūrvacity as well.
And there were the Apsaras Pramlocī and likewise Nimlocantī. || 25 ||
In this very context, O Lord of the Earth, there are likewise others.
I shall describe your birth from the Apsarases; listen as I speak it.
She was created by Viśvakarman for the destruction of Sunda and Upasunda.
Taking up every single sesame seed, Tilottamā [was adorned] with all kinds of jewels.
By circumambulating whom the four-faced one and the wielder of the Pināka bow were born.
The glorious thousand-eyed Śakra, wielder of the thunderbolt and destroyer of Pāka.
The remaining hosts of gods, beholding him with their faces turned in circumambulation as they wandered about, [praised him].
When the rite was completed, that excellent woman reached the world of the Sun.
Desiring to behold the beauty of form concentrated in one place, the Grandfather [Brahmā]...
He gave her the name Ahalyā, for she was the most beautiful woman in the three worlds.
And Brahmā, the auspicious four-faced one, gave it to Gautama.
For whose sake Śakra was made castrated by Gautama. ||31||
Likewise, the auspicious Urvaśī was born from the thigh of Nārāyaṇa.
With her mind fully surrendered, she chose as her husband the king born of Budha,
named Purūravas, who was peerless in beauty upon the earth.
Even today, she remains having attained heaven together with him alone. || 33 ||
She was renowned as Āhūti, and likewise there were auspicious Apsarases.
Created by Brahmā with his mind, they were celestial women, enchanting to the heart.
The sons of Manu are remembered as being pure and possessing the brilliance of a mass of lightning.
And the sons of Mṛtyu were timid; they are known as the Bhūmijās, born from the earth. || 35 ||
And those known as Amṛtas were likewise produced during the churning for nectar.
From Vahni were born those named Sudā, and likewise from Soma were born the Bhekurayas.
Likewise, those born from the rays of the sun are declared to be long-lived.
Likewise, they are named as having originated from sacrifice, and likewise from the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda, and from the iṣṭis.
Those celestial nymphs born from Vāyu are celebrated by the name Sudās.
Thus, these many thousands of hosts of Apsarases are to be known. || 38 ||
They were indeed the wives of the gods and the sages, as well as their mothers.
And all the auspicious Apsarases are fragrant and free from outflows. ||39||
From the touch of them, his vital energy is nourished and he experiences great bliss.
Vinatā gave birth to the Rudras who indeed drink the soma juice.
Likewise Aṅgāraka, Sūrya, Nirṛti, and Khaga.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Dhūmaketu, and likewise Dhvaja; || 41 ||
The sacrificial ladle, the lord of men, the skull, and then the small bell.
These eleven Rudras of great power have been described to you.
And she gave birth to two sons for them, a yakṣa and a rākṣasa.
O King, from whose lineages the yakṣas and rākṣasas were indeed born.
And whoever should recite this lineage of great souls with discipline in the presence of Brahmins and deities, [shall attain the highest goal].
He shall obtain offspring, as well as abundant prosperity, and after death, an auspicious destination.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Creation of Kaśyapa," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*. || 128 || || cha ||
Vajra said:
And how was Urvaśī born, and how did she become the daughter of Budha and a mortal woman?
Tell me how that goddess made a mortal her husband. || 1 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Sādhya and Dharmasuta are said to be the two ṛṣis Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
O descendant of Yadu, those two who were formerly kings—both of them [are here].
The two portions of Viṣṇu, possessed of great heroism, were always devoted to ascetic penance.
Then they [saw] their delightful hermitage, with its fragrant branches and trees.
It is called Badaryāśrama; it is auspicious, cool to the touch, and pleasant.
One Gaṅgā carries warm water, while another carries cool water.
It is delightful with its golden sands and garlanded with golden lotuses.
There that beautiful jujube tree stands, always laden with flowers and fruit.
There, those two tigers among sages devoted themselves to severe austerity.
Both are the lords of the entire world for the sake of the existence of all the worlds.
While the two of them were thus performing penance, ten Apsarases appeared before them due to their practice of silence.
Having come together and resolved to create an obstacle to their asceticism, they acted accordingly.
Having reached that place, they were adorned with various ornaments and decorations.
O King, there is no one in the three worlds who is more gentle than the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Upon beholding them, a man would fall under the sway of desire.
Gathering flowers and sporting at their pleasure. || 9 ||
Then Nārāyaṇa beheld all those women with the eyes of young deer.
Having understood the inner disposition of those women, the best among the knowers of the Vedas—
Having conquered anger, possessed of great splendor, having conquered desire, and knowing both material prosperity and dharma.
Having taken the juice of the mango tree, which kindles passion. || 11 ||
From his two thighs, he fashioned the auspicious Apsaras Cārvangī by means of Citra.
That [ornament], which excels in various modes of decoration, was fashioned upon the thighs by Citra.
At that very moment, she became a woman with long, wide eyes.
Neither a goddess, nor a Gandharva woman, nor an Asura woman, nor a Pannaga woman. ||13||
Such was that excellent woman in this triple world.
Upon seeing her, all ten of the Mauneya Apsarases were filled with shame.
They departed as they had come, O King; Purandara heard of that.
And out of curiosity to see her, he came to the hermitage of Badarī.
The wielder of the thunderbolt fell at the feet of the two to be converted, who were ever established in the Dharma.
And he beheld her of auspicious limbs, like another goddess Śrī.
Then the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the one to be accomplished, spoke to him while laughing.
"O knower of dharma, may this woman born from my thigh become Urvaśī. || 17 ||
Lead her to the third heaven, and let her become a beautiful Apsaras among the celestial nymphs.
When this had been said, having attained joy and having saluted those two sages, [he departed].
Then [he beheld] the goddess with the eyes of a young deer, who was not dependent on him [for her protection].
And he gave her to the Gandharva Tumburu as his pupil.
Then, on one occasion, she danced before Śakra.
Transgressing the instruction of Tumburu, she of the lovely smile—
That Gandharva cursed her: "O auspicious one, you shall dwell among mortals."
Having left this world of the gods together with Mānuṣa, O sinless one.
Having thus worshipped that human being for some time, O lady of pure smiles.
Having arrived there in the third heaven, you shall then practice it from that point.
With him alone, O fair-faced one, you shall rejoice in the third heaven.
The duration of the period known as that of the Manu Vaivasvata is now stated.
Thus cursed by him, O best of kings, she fell from the world of men, O King, due to that preceptor.
She dwelt together with the king; and from that place, having likewise attained heaven, she remained there with him.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Birth of Urvaśī," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 129 ||
Vajra said:
O Brahmin, having abandoned Nāka, how did Urvaśī go to the son of Budha?
And where did she see that unconquered lord of men? || 1 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In the first Dvāpara age of yore, the mind of this son of Vivasvat [was directed].
When the war between the gods and the asuras had occurred, and when the churning for the nectar of immortality had taken place.
That very lord of men, who had performed his duty in that battle.
At that time, he was seated upon half of Śakra’s throne, possessing a form beyond compare.
The large-eyed woman beheld him being worshipped by the gods.
Then the daughter of Nārāyaṇa [spoke] to that son of Budha, the lord of men.
Having seen him, she became unwell, struck by the arrows of desire.
From that time forth, that beautiful woman [resided] in the auspicious groves of Mount Meru.
Concealing her true disposition, that passionate woman passes the time.
She was constantly thinking of that lord of kings, who was ever like the god of love himself.
She neither eats nor sleeps; when she is exhausted, she sleeps.
Then, she with eyes like blue lotuses beheld him in a dream.
And she forms whatever desires she has directed toward that king.
Deluded by that dream, she somehow beheld them in her dream.
Sometimes she plays with the king, and sometimes she is entreated by him. || 9 ||
O Indra among kings, she sometimes speaks while asleep and wakes up while speaking.
She was grasped by the neck by the king, and the lord of the earth was likewise grasped by her.
Having seen this in her dream, she fell into a state of delusion through sleep.
In that very same way, he awakens when the noose of his arms is fashioned. || 11 ||
When she sees him situated in a dream, she falls into a state of delusion for a long time.
Having made it into a painting on a cloth, he sometimes gazes upon it.
Thus, having perceived that the king had lost all interest in her, she whose slender body was most beautiful—
Upon seeing Rambhā, whose pale and emaciated cheeks were like bare walls, he spoke to her quickly. || 13 ||
O fair-limbed one, though you were concealing your emotion with effort, you have been discovered by me, O lady of beautiful brows.
This heart of yours belongs to that high-souled one, the lord of men, who is invincible in battles.
A hero among men named Purūravas, renowned throughout these three worlds for his virtuous deeds.
He shines with beauty surpassing that of Kāma, and he excels even Śakra in valor. || 15 ||
O hero among men, there is no one equal to you in generosity, nor even in those incomparable virtues that truly exist.
In this battle between the gods and the asuras, five million asuras were slain by him.
Keśin, Viśāla, Madana, Ugra, and Mahābala were likewise slain by him.
He was the grandson of Candra and the son of Budha; his mother was the nurse of that son of the Sun.
Abandoning pride, O young woman, go to that renowned king of wide eyes.
There is no effort on his part to attain you; indeed, the gods are very difficult to reach. || 18 ||
For you, O large-eyed one, are a ground unattainable by the desires of both gods and asuras.
O slender-limbed one, even the bed of lotus stalks, though smeared with sandalwood paste, has been made distressful by you alone.
Climb onto his lap, O beloved one of golden hue, and be freed from all suffering.
"Come, come quickly, O you of excellent practice; let us go to the palace of that lord of men."
The king obtained from his maternal grandfather the city known as Pratiṣṭhāna.
Having been addressed in this way, she who was the color of refined gold, realizing the truth, became filled with shame. || 21 ||
She said to Rambhā, "Friend, you have spoken the truth; that opinion is indeed very appropriate to me."
O you with eyes like those of a young deer, let us go this very day into the presence of that lord of men.
If today [I were to see] that lord of men, whose eyes are like blue lotuses and whose face has the luster of the full moon...
I do not see him of the broad and long arms; therefore, I shall go to my inevitable end.
O Rambhā, when a person says that the five [objects] alone are the arrows of desire, then enough with such falsehood!
Piercing me incessantly with volleys of arrows, he does not cease for even the duration of an eyeblink. || 24 ||
This body, though revolving in the midst of the fire of desire, does not turn to ashes.
By the moon-like face of that very king, which resides within my heart, it is protected.
O large-eyed one, lead me this very day into the presence of that lord of men.
Having spoken thus piteously, Rambhā took the large-eyed woman by the hand.
Then, having leaped up into the air with her intellect, she went joyfully to the king's palace.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Urvaśī and Rambhā," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then Urvaśī departed in haste together with Rambhā.
Afflicted by desire, she then beheld Nārada upon the path to the Siddhas.
He was traveling along the path of the perfected ones, having come down from the world of the gods.
Having honored Nārada, the fair-browed lady departed with great haste.
He was traveling along the path of the perfected ones, having arrived from the world of the gods.
Having worshipped Nārada, the fair-browed woman departed with great haste.
Nārada said to Rambhā: "O Rambhā, who is this female companion of yours who has set out?"
Out of fear of her curse, Rambhā reported everything to her.
Nārada spoke to her again: "Listen further to my words."
This Urvaśī has lost her affection for that lord of men, a mere mortal. || 4 ||
Due to the curse of Tumburu, she shall dwell there out of delusion, as is fitting.
O auspicious one, you should carry out my word exactly as it is virtuous.
By virtue of that agreement, the cool-eyed Urvaśī remained with him.
And hear from me the agreement that must be made with her by the king. || 6 ||
In former times, that auspicious woman indeed adopted two rams as her sons.
O fair-eyed one, that [liṅga] should be installed permanently near the bedchamber.
In that same manner, she should likewise take only ghee as her food.
O Rambhā, King Purūravas should not be seen naked in that manner. ||8||
Likewise, sexual intercourse must not be performed with one who is unwilling.
Moreover, when even a single agreement was broken, the lovely-eyed woman [acted]. 9.
If she remains with the king, she will become like a stone.
"Let it be so," Urvaśī said to Nārada, together with Rambhā.
Having spoken thus and having honored the sage, he set out once again.
The brahmin Nārada then departed for the city of Vaiśravaṇa.
And Urvaśī, together with Rambhā, beheld Pratiṣṭhāna.
It was resplendent with a golden rampart that had the color of the sun.
It was resplendent with four white gate-towers made of silver.
And it was likewise beautiful and delightful with arches made of coral. || 13 ||
A beautiful great royal road through a well-divided vast forest.
It was adorned with various moats and lotus ponds.
It was adorned with white palaces that scraped the sky.
It was filled with brave and wealthy people, divine, and inhabited by noble men.
It was crowded with merchants and adorned with various kinds of merchandise.
Born from the lineage of Airāvata, they resembled moving mountains. ||16||
It was accompanied by many thousands of most enchanting elephants.
And with horses born from fire, equal to the wind in speed. || 17 ||
Then, intoxicated men were seen here and there in the gardens.
With the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, clay drums, and war-drums; ||18||
And the sounding of various musical instruments resounded throughout every house.
It resounded with the voice of Brahmā, a great sound, and the music of lutes and flutes.
It was crowded with joyful and well-nourished people, and entirely free from all afflictions.
He was accompanied by thousands of women whose complexions were like the color of lotus filaments.
And with women who were dark-complexioned, O Great King, as well as those who were fair as a reed.
It was filled with those wearing various garments and originating from various lands. ||21||
And by men of many forms, who were skilled in the arts, indeed in great numbers.
In the middle of that city, she beheld the palace of the king.
In the midst [of it], like Kailāsa, the best of mountains, stands amidst the Himālaya.
It was filled with thousands of beautiful houses belonging to illustrious householders.
With broad [limbs] as white as nectar and possessing a radiance equal to the rays of the moon.
In some places with jewels, in some places with gold, and in some places, O protector of the earth, with silver.
With stairways made of jewels and coral, adorned with nets of pearls;
In some places they were rich with garlands of flowers, and in others they were adorned with Vaijayantī banners.
Not far from it was a vast forest, resembling the Caitraratha grove.
The large-eyed lady beheld the king’s delightful pleasure-grove.
It was provided with various kinds of trees bearing flowers, areca nuts, and fruits.
With various lotus ponds and enchanting pleasure-mountains. || 27 ||
And likewise with delightful palaces, as well as with beautiful clusters of jewels.
Having seen that grove of plantain trees, she spoke these words to her friend: || 28 ||
O beautiful-eyed one, in this delightful and dense pleasure grove of the king, [I have been wandering].
"Concealed by illusion, we two shall dwell here until the setting of the sun."
Then, having gone there and informed that lord of men of what you intend to do, [you should act].
I, however, shall lead you into the presence of that king.
Having spoken these words, the friend urged Urvaśī forward.
And when that divine Rāma had descended from there, they entered the pleasure-grove, which was delightful with beautiful flowers.
In that pleasure grove, Urvaśī mentally desired the time of sunset. || 31 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Descent into the Krīḍāvana," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. || 131 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Knowing that Rambhā and likewise Urvaśī desired the setting of the sun, she acted accordingly.
Indeed, for the sake of diversion, he showed that forest to her. ||1||
O fortunate one, behold this beautiful campaka tree with its lovely blossoms.
It is strewn on all sides with flowers that match the color of your limbs. ||2||
And behold this pomegranate tree in bloom, O lovely-eyed one!
This [lip] which bears the beauty of your lower lip with its flowers. ||3||
Behold the beautiful mango tree, which has the very form of the arrows of Kama.
And where the [feeling] self-arisen within that Great-Souled One had taken root. || 4 ||
By means of those delightful [lotuses] that bestow beauty upon your two cheeks.
O lady of beautiful limbs, O auspicious one, look at the Madhūka tree covered with flowers.
It is enriched with lovely fruits that resemble your breasts.
Behold, O gentle one, the palmyra tree that increases the joy of the mind.
O beautiful one, look at the plantain tree with its stalks resembling your thighs.
She was golden-hued, with all her limbs beautiful, fashioned by Viśvakarman.
Behold this enchanting, unbound creeper, rich with blossoms.
She was graced by bees resembling the mass of your hair.
Behold this kunda bush with its beautiful blossoms resembling your teeth.
It was beautified on all sides by enchanting flowers, O large-eyed one. || 9 ||
And behold this lotus-pond, made beautiful by its blue lotuses.
With blossoming flowers resembling your eyes, which gladden the mind and heart.
"O fortunate lady, behold the lotus pond, filled with blossoming lotuses."
[It was filled] with golden filaments tipped with diamonds, rich with the fragrance of your breath.
Behold these royal swans frequenting the banks of the lotus pond.
Their gait is as captivating as yours, O well-trained one.
And by those holding sprouts fashioned from the tips of your fingers, O gentle one.
Behold this pleasure-mountain, adorned with many kinds of trees. || 13 ||
On the pleasure-mountain, there was a cuckoo perched upon a mango tree, increasing the passion of love.
This [bird] warbles with a sound that is as enchanting as yours.
Behold the river of cool water flowing forth from the pleasure-mountain.
O gentle one, your mind is equal to this pure water as it flows along.
The vast forest was full of many wonders, gentle, and beautiful to behold.
"O large-eyed one, do you not see that the sun is setting? (16)
But knowing you to be under the sway of desire, the Sun, as it were, out of compassion—
O beautiful lady, the god who bears the rays of the moon is now approaching his setting.
O beautiful one, even hard leaves become like tender sprouts.
Deeply colored by the eightfold heat, the branches of the trees shine intensely.
The sun indeed makes the peaks of the mountains red.
O large-eyed one, having accomplished his task at the close of day, he went to his setting.
Behold the western quarter, O beautiful one, which is reddened by the time of twilight.
Like a passionate woman suddenly embracing another passionate woman.
Now, O lady born of the best of the twice-born, the twice-born are endowed with their religious observances.
Devoted to the path of the virtuous, they worship at the time of twilight.
The twilight followed the sun, even though its lord had set.
Like a virtuous woman toward her beloved, she became filled with bashfulness, O high-minded one.
O lady with beautiful thighs, behold the earth as you are about to travel through the darkness.
O woman of excellent complexion, it was equal to the interior of a bumblebee or a tamāla tree.
For everything was pervaded by darkness; nothing shone forth at all.
O lady with eyes like lotus petals, by means of this impurity, the entire world has been made uniform.
For at this very hour, O friend, we have been brought under the sway of Love.
Wearing blue garments, the lovely women, beautifully adorned, proceed. ||25||
Behold, O fortunate one, the auspicious orb of the moon has risen.
It possessed a luster equal to the faces of women intoxicated by wine. || 26 ||
Having ascended slightly into the sky, O friend, it has indeed turned white.
Behold the moon, O fair-browed one, which brings delight to the eyes.
Having entered the darkness of this world, the moon, which resembles the quality of purity (sattva), shines forth.
He shines, stainless, in the gentle sky of pure white luster. ||28||
The beauty of your cheeks is worthy of one struck by the arrows of Love.
The moon, emitting a web of moonlight, bears it on both sides. || 29 ||
O woman of excellent complexion, I shall grant this boon with a silver pitcher as bright as the moon.
Under the guise of moonlight, the goddess Earth shines as if she were gleaming with silver.
O auspicious lady, look at the night-lily in full bloom once the moon has risen.
It was adorned with flowers resembling your smile.
"O auspicious one, this is a Cakravāka bird separated from his mate, longing for the red lotus."
Afflicted by great sorrow, O large-eyed one, he enters as if into a white [sandalwood paste]. || 32 ||
From this moonstone house, she possesses a radiance equal to the rays of the moon.
Drops of water fall, touched by the rays of the moon. || 33 ||
Embraced by the moon, the night cast off her veil of darkness.
O large-eyed one, the beautiful woman [clings] to her garment like a lover to his beloved.
At the rising of the moon, when the moon-faced one appeared like the moon itself in this pleasure-grove of the king of men.
Behold him and offer hope for his life; driven by your own good fortune, he has suddenly entered here.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Moonrise in the Grove," in the first section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been addressed with these words by Rambhā, she saw that the king had arrived.
Then Queen Urvaśī became both thrilled and filled with trepidation.
A great wonder occurred when she beheld the king, O lady of auspicious countenance.
And his body, with its hair standing on end, appeared covered in perspiration. || 2 ||
Then Rambhā said to her, "Listen, Urvaśī, to my words:
there will be no small task for this king upon his arrival here. (3)
This king has entered the forest at night without a companion for his comfort.
"Let us listen, while remaining hidden, to the words of this king."
Then the daughter of Nārāyaṇa said to Rambhā, "So be it."
Then, with their bodies concealed by illusion, they approached the king.
Then his friend questioned the king, whose every limb was beautiful.
He was always highly esteemed by the king, virtuous, and exceedingly righteous.
The friend said:
O Indra among kings, from the very moment you descended here from the third heaven.
And from that time forward, O giver of honor, you have been seen by me to be unwell.
O King, I have understood that this lack of composure of yours was caused by desire.
Tell me that secret of yours, O best among the foremost of men, if it is not [to be told].
Purūravas said:
There is nothing whatsoever that is secret from you, even at any time.
"O gentle one, I shall tell you the cause of my own ill health."
The beloved daughter of Nārāyaṇa was auspicious and peerless in beauty.
I have seen the excellent Apsaras known by the name Urvaśī.
From the moment that lovely-limbed woman appeared, from that very instant, my friend, [my heart has been captivated].
My mind is churned by desire, and thus it finds no peace. || 11 ||
Nor do I perceive any means for its attainment, O best of the twice-born.
That excellent woman is auspicious and difficult to obtain even for the gods.
Thus, O friend, my time has passed while I was overwhelmed by suffering.
Today, that woman with lovely-smiling eyes has been enjoyed by me in a dream.
For in this moonstone chamber, she is indeed struck by the arrows of Love.
At the rising of the moon, the lovely-faced one, the sole beauty of the three worlds, [appeared]. 14.
For the sake of diversion, O friend, it is exceedingly captivating to the mind.
Then, at the rising of the moon, he reached a house made of moonstone slabs.
Therefore come, O gentle one; there is [a place]—enter the beautiful house.
I am diverting my heart, which has been brought under the sway of the god of love. || 16 ||
The friend said:
Just as you have seen it in your dream, so shall it surely come to pass today.
That passionate woman, her limbs overwhelmed by desire, will also come to you.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, he then entered a house made of moonstone.
Then, having been brought under the sway of passion, he sat down upon that spot.
Having heard that, Urvaśī, together with Rambhā, was filled with joy.
Then Rambhā also revealed herself to the king.
Then Rambhā, overcome by passion, said "Victory! to the lord of the earth.
She stood before him, as if illuminating his house with her splendor.
Then the king said to her, "Welcome to you, O lovely-faced one."
Adorn yourself, O lady of beautiful limbs, upon this auspicious jeweled throne.
While she was seated upon the jeweled throne, he was astonished by her arrival.
Then he, whose eyes were as red as lotuses, spoke to that fair-faced woman.
O Rambhā, Śakra’s city shines eternally because of you.
O beautiful lady, she was like the night of the full moon when accompanied by the hare-marked one.
You are the ornament of his assembly, and you are the true disciple of Tumburu.
O beautiful one, all the women have been overcome by you and are sleeping.
All women in the most beautiful heaven have been surpassed by you.
Even though you behold with a thousand eyes, O destroyer of ripeness (Pākahā), [you do not see me].
O lady of beautiful limbs, O fair-faced one, he is not satiated anywhere.
Therefore, O fortunate one, tell me the reason for your coming here.
Rambhā said:
Listen attentively, O King, to the reason for my arrival.
O Indra among kings, having heard that, carry out my word.
There dwelt the goddess, the daughter of Nārāyaṇa, who was the most beautiful in the three worlds.
O protector of the earth, my friend is the lovely-limbed one named Urvaśī. (28)
Having seen you in the abode of Mahendra, she was deluded by desire.
The foolish woman finds no peace, crying out "Alas! Alas! again and again. || 29 ||
She, however, is severely tormented by the arrows of the bodiless god for your sake.
Within a few days, that auspicious woman became nothing but her beauty.
With her cheeks grown exceedingly thin, her mind was entirely surrendered to you.
Her limbs tormented by passion, the beautiful woman cast aside her pride.
Eager for a sight of you, she has set out together with me.
O auspicious lady, it was there that Nārada spoke to you as you were setting out.
But you must dwell there, O fair-faced one, according to the agreement.
As for those two rams which were conceived by you as being your sons; || 33 ||
If he should always place it near his bed.
O beautiful lady, that king, with all his limbs lovely, must not look upon her naked. (34)
Nor should he commit sexual intercourse with you against your will.
Likewise, O fortunate one, dwell there always subsisting on ghee. || 35 ||
If even a single moment has passed while [the king] is away from his royal domain, [then...]
If you do not abandon it, O gentle one, you shall become like a stone.
These rules of conduct were declared by Nārada to me, my friend.
Therefore, accept them and enjoy the company of that fair-faced woman.
Purūravas said:
O beautiful Rambhā, by your words today, I have been as if filled with nectar.
"O lady of auspicious countenance, having fallen into the power of death, I have been restored to life. (38)
O Rambhā, for her sake, Madana has also rained down showers of arrows upon me.
The fair-browed woman torments his heart day and night without ceasing. || 39 ||
Therefore, revive me quickly and show me that excellent woman.
O auspicious lady, I shall abide by that agreement which you shall propose to me.
Know that the agreement which was uttered by Nārada has been fulfilled.
For me, who am submerged in this great ocean of desire where there is no place of refuge. ||41||
Become a raft, O large-eyed one; become a giver of life, O beautiful woman.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having been addressed thus by the lord of men, Rambhā then vanished from sight.
Then, accompanied by Urvaśī, she revealed herself to the king.
Having said "Victory! to the lord of men, the daughter of Nārāyaṇa then—
She stood before that high-souled king, filled with shame.
Upon seeing her, that king of great splendor was filled with joy.
With her entire body covered in horripilation, she cannot be described.
Taking her by the hand, he placed the bashful girl upon his lap.
Likewise, Rambhā also occupied a most enchanting jeweled throne.
Then the king, with a joyful mind, spoke these words: ||46||
Purūravas said:
"O Urvaśī, today the god of love is pleased with me in this forest of boons."
Today, O fair-browed one, I have come to know myself through my own self as being superior even to Śakra.
Even upon gaining sovereignty over the three worlds, O auspicious one, how could I have any delight in it?
O fair-eyed one, having obtained the state of being obedient to your command today, [I shall act]. (48)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
While the king was speaking thus, the beautiful-faced Rambhā departed.
In an instant, accompanied by the ram, she returned once more to the presence of the king. || 49 ||
Having presented two rams to the lord of men, he addressed these words to the king:
Rambhā said:
I shall go to Laṅkā, O king of kings; there dwells the lord of my life.
The illustrious son of Dhanada stands waiting for me.
O Lord, he is known by the name Nalakūbara and is renowned throughout the three worlds.
And just as this auspicious friend of mine does not feel any longing.
O sinless one, you must likewise act for the sake of your heavenly companions.
Purūravas said:
I shall strive to act accordingly; be at peace, O Mānadeva.
Taking these jewels, depart as you please.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been addressed thus, Rambhā then [acted] for the sake of pleasing the king.
Taking the jewels, he went through the air to the great city of Laṅkā.
Having obtained Urvaśī, the lord of men also took his pleasure together with her.
Just as the powerful Pākaśāsana, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, [is aided] by Śacī. || 55 ||
Having laid down his burden upon the chief of ministers, O foremost of the Yādava lions, he took delight with her.
Accompanied by Lakṣmī, the Blessed One Ananta is like that god who is the protector of the world.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Meeting of Urvaśī and Purūravas," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In various palaces as well as in houses made of jewels.
In delightful flower-houses as well as in cloth-pavilions. || 1 ||
In the most excellent jewel-chambers as well as in the painted halls.
And in the inaccessible places of the mountains, and on the sandy banks of the rivers.
And likewise among the blooming lotus ponds and the blue-lotus ponds.
And likewise upon most excellent couches, as well as upon beds of flowers.
And he thus delighted that goddess in those places so beautifully prepared.
O King, in houses filled with many jewels and emitting the fragrance of incense, ||4||
But he took delight with her again and again in the Manasa lakes.
He never grew weary of delighting that woman of excellent form.
And her face is more beautiful than the moonstone on nights when the moon is present.
That lord of men, the ruler of people, drank of it according to his desire. ||6||
On nights when the moon had vanished, his face alone provided radiant illumination.
In that region, the lotus-eyed king took his pleasure with her.
She, however, fulfilled the king's desire day after day.
She, with her long eyes, appeared as beautiful as one never seen before. ||8||
She was dearly beloved by the king, and the king was twice as devoted to her.
By her that king is pleased, and by him that excellent woman is also pleased.
Their limbs were smeared with excellent sandalwood paste, and they were adorned with various ornaments.
The couple remained delighted, adorned with various jewels.
Sometimes the king himself adorns her.
And being adorned by her, he attains unsurpassed joy. || 11 ||
They both rejoiced greatly, delighted by those various boons.
They both beautified each other's hair with flowers.
Urvaśī is a flower that has blossomed and has likewise been woven together again.
The best of kings bore it upon his head with love.
The marks that the lord of men fashioned by means of leaf-cutting—
And she, of lovely smiles, bore them upon her forehead.
Thus did the king sport with that slender-waisted woman.
There were five sons; learn their names from me. || 15 ||
First is long-lived, then wise, and after that, another who is free from disease.
The fourth had a lifespan of ten thousand years, and the fifth had a lifespan of one hundred years. || 16 ||
Thus, as that enchanting time passed, she indeed gave birth.
Then the chief Gandharvas, having gathered together, were deeply anxious, being deprived of her.
Then, those of undaunted spirit set out for the world of the Lord of the Gods in order to reach him, where they then performed [their task].

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Enjoyment with Urvaśī," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
They made an effort to bring Urvaśī and performed an excellent mantra.
Then the Gandharva named Ugrasena spoke this mantra: || 1 ||
Ugrasena said:
At that very moment, Urvaśī, adorned with beautiful ornaments, stood there.
But she, having transgressed the agreement, will indeed abandon that king.
I know that time; O sinless one, I shall go there.
"I shall perform your task with my companions; of this there is no doubt. || 3 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, he went to the place where that king was staying.
And at night, O lord of men, he carried off my ram by means of his illusory power.
Having learned that the ram had been stolen, the queen spoke thus to the king:
"O protector of the earth, my son the ram has certainly been carried off by someone. (5)
And the second has been carried off by a king; bring that son back to me.
Thus addressed by her, the king, still naked, then acted out of agitation.
Rising up, O bull among men, he began to search for the two rams.
Then that dark-eyed woman saw the king naked.
Having recollected the words of Nārada, she vanished from sight.
Then, filled with sorrow, she also went into the presence of the Gandharvas.
Having attained heaven, the large-eyed lady remained eternally devoted to the king.
Even with her body overcome by desire, the beautiful woman passes the time.
Terrified by the fear of the sage’s curse, she was brought under the sway of passion.
That woman of beautiful hips remained constantly devoted to her husband, intent solely on sighing.
Without having reached the pair of rams, the lord of men turned back.
Not seeing the queen on her bed, he then remembered the agreement.
Having realized that he had abandoned himself and having remembered his own vow, he [acted].
Nevertheless, the king, afflicted by the arrows of desire, remained thus in the lonely forest.
He searches for her everywhere like one who is mad, she who possesses such beautiful limbs.
Then the king was alone in the desolate place, separated from his beloved.
The Great Being lamented like some wretched creature.
Purūravas said:
"O large-eyed one, where have you gone, leaving me here all alone? (14)
How shall I enter the city of Pratiṣṭhāna without you?
O beautiful one, having abandoned their vital breaths, they will depart from my body.
O lady of beautiful countenance, I am unable to follow you with my body.
For you, O lady with tremulous glances, are dearer to me than my very life.
"Abandoned by you, O woman of excellent complexion, I shall surely give up my life."
Where are you? Where am I? Where shall I go? What shall I do? Whither shall I go? || 17 ||
Who can show my beloved to me, who am tormented by desire for refuge?
Whom indeed shall I question in this solitary place? To whom might she be known? || 18 ||
Or rather, who could find safety for me, were it not for one who might show me my beloved?
This remainder of the night has passed for me while separated from my beloved.
The goddess Urvaśī has vanished from me, like a star.
At the touch of the rays of the dawn-god, the moon abandons its splendor.
At the end of the night, my body is emaciated like mine, being deprived of him.
For this morning twilight is now recurring; having bathed, the twice-born [should perform their rites]. (21)
Surely those who have conquered their senses remain joined to their religious observances.
For here rises the sun with its crimson orb. || 22 ||
The God is equal toward all beings; he is the destroyer of the sins of all.
And now this sun has risen and shines brightly in the cloudless sky. (23)
Like a single blooming great lotus in a pure lake.
Knowing that the sun had risen, the lotus-eyed woman [approached].
When opened, it perceives everything; without it, it remains closed.
This day has begun with a sharp sun, increasing the power of desire.
The summer heat torments me especially without her.
Whom shall I ask, she who is of beautiful form and possesses the luster of refined gold?
"She has been seen by me"—what will anyone say to me regarding that queen in the forest?
This lordly elephant approaches, bearing what resemble her two breasts.
I ask this well-faced elephant about his two firm temples.
Indeed, that pair of thighs of yours has become like a pair of tusks. || 28 ||
If you know that Urvaśī has gone, tell me.
This elephant has departed from fear of this high-souled lion. || 29 ||
Without giving me an answer, I shall ask Siṃha in the forest.
O Lion, where is she now—she for whom you alone are her equal?
"Urvaśī is my beloved; if you know [her whereabouts], let it be told."
"How has this lion gone away from me without even giving me an answer? (31)
Having seen her, tell me, O Bimba, [of] the goddess whose lips are like the bimba fruit.
Even by this [means], the fair-toothed woman did not speak when questioned by me.
O peacock, if you know the girl with the eyes of a young deer, [tell me].
"Tell me now about Urvaśī; where does my beloved abide? (33)
The fire of desire burns within the body, while the sun burns it from without.
Afflicted by heat, these lions dwelling in mountain caves are sighing.
With their tongues thrust out, their limbs hanging limp, and their mouths agape again and again.
And herds of female buffaloes lie in the waters of the lotus pond.
Others lie down in the waters stirred up by the sun, with only the mud remaining.
And this cātaka bird, afflicted by thirst, gazes repeatedly at the sky. || 36 ||
I am exceedingly thirsty for water, just as I am for Urvaśī.
These elephants, tormented by the heat, are going toward the clusters of lotus ponds.
And with water released from well-trained hands, they sprinkle themselves by their own selves.
And other elephants, despondent, [clung] to the trunks of the great trees. || 38 ||
They bring heat at midday, repeatedly emitting sprays of water.
These birds, tormented by the heat, [seek refuge] within the spaces between the branches and leaves.
And they indeed enter [the city] at the time of midday for the sake of protection.
For these young birds are perched upon the branches of the tree.
With eyes whose corners are blood-red, they enter here repeatedly and with great intensity.
And these herds of deer in the great forest have abandoned the act of eating.
They stand in the shade of trees, repeatedly ruminating.
Searching for my beloved, I am exceedingly delighted by this victory.
I shall now rest in the shade of this śirīṣa tree.
The flowers of this tree are as delicate as her limbs.
This śirīṣa tree is delightful, bringing joy to the mind and heart.
But this śirīṣa tree, deprived of her, torments me. (44)
The sun is setting; where shall I go for the night?
The thousand-rayed sun has set; the most dreadful night has arrived. ||45||
I shall spend this night under this great nyagrodha tree.
In that excellent palace constructed by the supernatural power of Urvaśī, the king [resided]. || 46 ||
Well-honored with all objects of desire, he sports together with her.
Surely that person knows me, even though I am in the city of Pratiṣṭhāna.
At present, no one knows this condition of mine.
A certain person from the countryside was always dear to me. || 48 ||
O Sleep, resort to my eyes; O Dream, surely [show] a fair-faced woman.
I shall indeed attain that gentle lady, who increases the joy of my heart. (49)
How is it that the risen moon causes me such pain?
Having previously been defeated by his face, he now provokes me.
O Moon, strike my body as you wish, now that it has been deprived [of its life].
But having obtained a husband through you, show me the state of being his co-wife. || 51 ||
Alas! I am ruined, I am destroyed, being separated from Urvaśī in the forest.
O grandson of Candra, show mercy; reveal my beloved to me.
O Lord Śaśāṅka, cool-rayed one, who captivates the eyes of men!
I cry out to you today; show me my beloved!
Even while my gaze was still unsated, that beautiful woman departed from me.
O large-eyed one, show me that Urvaśī who has vanished from sight.
When shall I drink the nectar of her lower lip, which is like unto ambrosia?
When shall I behold her again, she who resembles the interior of a lotus? (55)
When shall I [behold] my beloved, whose pair of arms are like lotus stalks and whose face is like a lotus?
Embracing her whose eyes are like blue lotuses, I shall cast off the torment born of the bodiless god of love.
O young girl, become the refuge for me, who am pierced by the arrows of the bodiless god of love.
Grant me your sight, O lady of beautiful brows; what other refuge could I have? ||57||
For me, seized by the delusion of desire, you alone have been my refuge.
Furthermore, O fortunate and sinless one, may you alone be my refuge.
This night, though drawn out, seems to me like a hundred years.
Where shall I go to search for that pitiless woman who has acted so toward me?
O woman of excellent complexion, I do not know her anger even in a dream.
Today, that fortunate woman has departed, abandoned by me who am struck down by fate.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Lamenting thus, the king, having abandoned food, wandered about until,
O monarch, he reached Kurukṣetra after twelve days.
Then, exhausted and overcome by hunger and thirst, he sat down upon a banyan tree on the bank of the lotus pond, which was adorned with lotuses.
There too, overcome by passion, he lamented.
When indeed will that face, which rivals the moon, and the smile of that lovely-eyed woman [be seen again]?
Lifting up [her face], I, tormented by thirst, shall drink her lower lip as a traveler on a road drinks water found with great difficulty. (63)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Purūravas’s Lamentation," in the first section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Urvaśī too, of beautiful limbs, was tormented by the god of love.
Then she spoke of her own condition to Nārada, who was without a king.
Then Nārada said to her, "O fortunate one, go to the king."
O beautiful one, even his condition will be great when he is deprived of you.
Having spent one night with the lord of men, O woman of excellent complexion.
Go to the heavenly world; from there, you will indeed attain the highest good.
Thus addressed by Nārada, she was surrounded by many female companions.
The fair-faced woman went to bathe at a fig tree on the bank of a lotus pond.
At that very time, however, the king was overcome by sleep.
Disregarded by the Apsarases, O King, he fell asleep there.
"Today I shall go to the king," thought Urvaśī then, filled with joy.
Then, surrounded by her circle of friends, she played there in that water.
The king, having cast off his sleep, lamented again for a long time.
Accompanied by her friends, she heard the king lamenting.
Then that beautiful woman revealed herself to the king.
And the woman of excellent limbs spoke everything exactly as it had been told by Nārada.
There, that fair-faced woman dwelt for that night together with him.
At the end of the night, she spoke these words to the king, who was unconscious.
Urvaśī said:
Abandoning delusion, O lord of men, seek to propitiate the Gandharvas.
"O gentle one, request me on their behalf; then you shall obtain it without delay."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, O King, the monarch departed for heaven right there.
He performed extensive austerities with a mind focused solely on that.
Then, when the year was complete, at the time of the sun's rising, [he spoke].
Placing Nārada at their head, the Gandharvas revealed themselves.
The Gandharvas said:
Choose a boon, O Indra among kings, whatever you desire, O mighty-armed one!
For we, all of us possessing the splendor of immortals, shall indeed grant you our service.
Purūravas said:
If you are well-disposed toward me, O sirs, and if this boon is pleasing to me, [then grant it].
"Urvaśī, who possesses beautiful limbs, is here; let her be given to me by you. (14)
The Gandharvas said:
"O King, O mighty-armed one, take this full vessel from the fire."
Therefore, having divided this fire into three parts, perform the sacrifice free from all anxiety.
By means of the procedure prescribed in the Vedas, you shall attain the state of a Gandharva.
In this Manvantara, you are the one who establishes the ritual procedure preceded by the three sacred fires.
He will appear in the world as a teacher and a lord of the earth.

For by the jewels that have arisen from it, even the three worlds are adorned.

One who is not deficient beholds the mountain, which is not deficient in its wealth of jewels.
Where ascetics attain perfection through their austerities and penance.
And he who, by the mere sight of him, destroys all impurities.
[They were] like birds terrified by the falling into a great abyss. 16.
Carried by the wind, there was constant rain in some places and in others, rain only at certain times.
In some places, its peaks were exceedingly lofty, yet remained unclimbed by clouds.
It is joined with a mind that is impassable due to the poisons of the sun's constant heat.
[It was] with dense clusters of branches from great deodar trees.
It was adorned with regions possessing the forms of all the worlds.
Its great peaks were covered with snow, and its waterfalls cascaded down steep precipices.
The water there was inaccessible except by sound, and the caves were blocked by snow.
Upon merely beholding that ground of her beautiful hips, that lord of kings, possessed of great majesty, [was struck with wonder].
He wandered about right there, filled with joy, and then he sat down at a certain spot.
Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of Himavat," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
A most enchanting region of that very lord of mountains.
Inaccessible to other humans, he arrived there by the power of destiny. || 1 ||
From this country issued the Irāvatī, the best of rivers.
And that region was dark like a cloud, with numerous clusters of trees.
With *sāla*, *tāla*, *tamāla*, *karṇikāra*, and *śālmali* trees;
And with nyagrodha trees, as well as aśvatthas, śirīṣas, and śiṃśapā trees. || 3 ||
With śleṣmātaka, āmalaka, harītakī, and vibhītaka;
And with delightful sandalwood trees, wood-apple trees, and red sandalwoods. ||4||
With banyan trees, mahiṣakas, kākṣotas, aśvakarṇas, and likewise arjunas;
With *hastikarṇa* trees, along with *panasa* and well-flowered *kovidāra* trees. ||5||
With great devadāru trees as well as with kālīyaka trees.
With lotuses, sandalwood, bilva, kuṭaja, and yellow sandalwood. || 6 ||
And with *prācīnāguru* woods, as well as *sthūṇika* and *samaśaṇḍika* woods.
With dates, coconuts, priyāla, āmrātaka, and iṅguda fruits; ||7||
Likewise with Terumānas, Vaṭas, Bhanyas, Kāśmīras, and Phalins.
With nutmegs, betel nuts, katphala fruits, and lavalī fruits. || 8 ||
With mandāra, kovidāra, and kiṃśuka trees, and with the rays of their blossoms.
With Palāśa, Śamī, Sūllāsa, Vetasa, and Amlavetasa trees; || 9 ||
With red datura, oranges, iṅguda, and priyaṅgu;
With red Aśoka trees, as well as Aśoka trees, Āruka trees, and Cirāruka trees; ||| 1.151.10 ||
Likewise with mucukundas, kunda flowers, āṭarūṣas, and parūṣakas.
With hosts of Kiṃkaras, Kirātas, Ketakas, and Saketakas; ||11||
With śobhāñjana, añjana, mukūlaka, and nikocaka;
With trees possessing most excellent, beautiful, and well-filled garments, as well as with superior seats. || 12 ||
With enchanting mango trees that took the form of the arrows of Manmatha.
O King, likewise with yellow jasmine and white jasmine. ||13||
With *jāti* and *campaka-jāti* flowers, as well as with *tumburu* and *udumbara* fruits.
And with māṣa beans, ucca fruits, salakucas, tilas, balakas, and śambalas. || 14 ||
Likewise, with beautiful flowers and choice varana trees, which are beloved by women.
And with *bakula* trees thick with flowers, as well as *pāribhadraka* and *bhadraka* trees. ||15||
With Dhārākadambas, Kuṭajas, Kadambas, and Girikuṭajas;
With lovely *kakubha* trees that pervaded all directions. || 16 ||
With *karkandhu* and *badara* trees, and with *nīpa* trees as brilliantly radiant as lamps.
With red *pālīvat* flowers, white pomegranates, and *caṇyaka* trees; ||17||
And with the creepers of *pippalī* and *nāgavallī*, respectively.
Likewise with clusters of marica and with navamallika. || 18 ||
With excellent circles of grapes and circles of atimuktaka flowers.
And with auspicious, fruit-bearing creepers of cucumber and gourd. || 19 ||
And in some places with the spreading vines of kūṣmāṇḍa and likewise with those of alābu.
And with the spreading tendrils of the *cirbhaṭa*, with *paṭola* gourds, and with *kāravellaka* cucumbers.
With karkoṭaka creepers, spreading vines, eggplants, and bṛhatī fruits.
With white water-lilies, radishes as the principal [ingredients], and likewise various kinds of potherbs. ||21||
Likewise, with all varieties of *suvarcalā* and with mustard seeds as well.
With *kākolī*, *kṣīrakākolī*, *chatrā*, and *aticchatrā*;
with *kākamācī*, *mahābuddhī*, *śaśā*, *karddala*, and *kandala*.
Likewise, with kṣīrika vegetables and also with kālaśāka; || 23 ||
Likewise, with all types of pulse crops and grains, without exception.
And with various medicinal herbs that were indeed blazing. || 24 ||
Likewise, with bulbs, vidārī, and tarūṭa, combined with sweet substances.
[The city] was filled with those who had heard [the news], with the remnants of the Śaṭīs, and with the Rājakṣayakas and Vāstukas. || 25 ||
O lord of men, [these verses] are conducive to long life, conducive to fame, and conducive to a beautiful complexion.
[With those mantras] which destroy the fear of old age and death, and likewise those which destroy the fear of hunger. || 26 ||
And [these are] many times productive of good fortune and aphrodisiac.
And with rattan canes, bamboo creepers, as well as hollow bamboos; || 27 ||
In some places with kāśa grass resembling the moon, and likewise with thickets of reeds;
With lovely groves of *kuśa* grass and with groves of sugarcane that were enchanting to the mind. || 28 ||
With cotton cloth, with bark-fiber cloth, and with beautiful fine silk.
And likewise, with excellent and captivating groves of plantain trees. || 29 ||
Likewise, with regions resembling emeralds and covered with lush grass.
Together with *irā* flowers and portions of saffron.
With tagara, ativiṣā, māṃsī, granthiparṇī, and surāgada;
And with golden flowers, as well as with earthly flowers and others. || 31 ||
And with fresh jambīrikā, bhūstṛṇa, and likewise with sṛmuka.
With ginger, ajamoda, kuṭheraka, and priyāluka; || 32 ||
And likewise with water-born lotuses of various colors and fragrant scent.
Resembling the rising sun and likewise resembling the full moon.
With [hairs] the color of refined gold and resembling the flax flower.
And with other land-lotuses resembling parrot feathers, arranged in their respective parts.
It was strewn with flowers of five colors, as well as many other varieties.
With flowers resembling the moon, which produce joy even for those with evil views. || 35 ||
Likewise, O King, with auspicious red lotuses shaped like flames of fire.
With blue lotuses, along with kahlāras, durjātaka, and kaśerukas. || 36 ||
With lotus-bulbs, lotus-stalks, water-melons, and night-lotuses belonging to the Rākṣasas.
With all kinds of roots, fruits, and flowers, both aquatic and terrestrial.
And with various kinds of wild rice, O lord of men, which are the food of sages.
That is not grain, nor that is a crop, nor that is a vegetable, nor that is fruit. || 38 ||
It has no root, no bulb, and no flower, O lord of men.
That which originates in the world of the Nāgas, and that which originates in the world of the gods; || 39 ||
And that [suffering], O Yadava, does not arise from a continuous connection where it does not exist.
All flowers and fruits were always present, appearing perpetually through the power of the seasons.
That Maheśvara was seen by you as he had gone for the sake of performing ascetic penance.
And there he likewise beheld birds of various forms.
Peacocks, woodpeckers, and sweet-voiced cuckoos;
Likewise, [he saw] kadamba ducks, swans, wild cocks, and water-fowls. ||82||
Kṛkaras, barkas, śyāmas, tittiris, and kapiñjalas;
The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were like water-fowl, cormorants, sparrows, parrots, and cranes. || 43 ||
Sparrows, ruddy geese, āṭakas, ṭiṭṭibhas, and saṭas;
The Putrapriyas, Lohapṛṣṭhas, Gonandas, Girivartakas, and Vartakas; || 44 ||
Pigeons, kāmalas, śārakas, and jīvajīvakas;
[He saw] the Lāva, Vartaka, Tīra, Rakta, Dharma, and Prabhadra [countries]. ||45||
Cockatrices, variegated-crested birds, lapwings, and wagtails;
The sons of the sages along with the Arītas, the Kukkuṭas, and the Kāṣṭhakukkuṭas. || 46 ||
Laṭvāṃllas, iṣuṅgas, gokṣveḍas, and likewise kuṅkumacūḍakas;
The Bhṛṅgarājas, Añchārapādas, Bhūliṅgas, and Piṇḍimālavas; ||47||
[He saw] the *maṃjūlīyaka*, the *dātyūha*, the *gopaputra*, and the *vañjula* trees.
Likewise, he saw Bhāradvāja birds, blue jays, golden birds, and Rajanīyaka birds. ||48||
Indeed, these and many other charming flocks of birds [were there].
[He saw] beasts of prey of various forms, as well as deer and great wild animals. || 49 ||
Tigers, maned lions, leopards, sharabhas, and wolves.
Bears, hyenas, bandhūka trees, langurs, and monkeys; || 1.151.50 ||
From the world of Śaśa, he created the śaśaplānas, the māyavas, and the cats; from Śuna, [he created] the dogs.
Mṛṣikas, nākulas, kācas, siṃhas, noḍras, and suromakas. || 51 ||
Likewise, he saw intoxicated elephants, buffaloes, gayals, and bulls.
As well as those that move, those that creep, and likewise those with hooves and those with claws. ||52||
And likewise, goats, rams, antelopes, and even wild asses.
Ruru deer, antelopes, monkeys, crabs, and wild animals.
And those that are blue, as well as the mahānīlas, the karālas, and the mṛgamārdakas. ||53||
[He slew] the Śvadaṃṣṭras, Rāmas, Śarabhas, Koḍas, Kākas, Paśus, and Aṃbaras. ||54||
Some were formidable, some wore garlands, some had black tails, and others were ruddy.
Camels, elephants, boars, horses, donkeys, and mules; 55.
Seeing these [allies] and those who were hostile to one another, the Lord of Madra [reflected].
Living without conflict in that forest, he attained supreme peace. || 56 ||
In ancient times, O King, Atri was the foremost one in that hermitage.
By his grace, it is always occupied by both stationary and moving beings.
Those who are intent on harming do not injure one another as much as those who are harmful injure each other.
All the carnivorous creatures there subsist on milk and fruit. || 58 ||
They were created there for the sake of pleasure by the great-souled Atri.
O King, there the cows themselves [graze] in the low-lying areas among the rocks.
They flow with milk that is divine and resembles the taste of nectar.
In some places the queens of the king, and in others the king himself, were present in their respective portions.
O Yādava, in one place the rocks were completely filled with milk, and in another with curd.
Beholding this, the lord of the earth attained supreme joy.
There are divine lakes there, and rivers with pure water.
And divine lotus stalks, cool and in their respective portions. || 62 ||
And the mountain caves are pleasant to inhabit, O Yādava.
There is no falling of snow there for five yojanas in every direction. || 63 ||
It exists in the valleys at the foot of the mountain and also upon its peaks.
There too, O King, was the white peak of that lord of mountains.
There, the clouds, gathering together, constantly cause a fall of snow.
And there is another peak there, where the waters are thick and dense.
They constantly rain down stones upon the peak of Mount Khara.
That hermitage was captivating, wherein the very grounds fulfilled all desires.
Because they are to be enjoyed by the foremost of the gods, these trees are always laden with fruit.
It was constantly sung over by bees and served by celestial women; it was immortal.
It brings about the destruction of all evils, like a great mine within a mountain.
And monkeys were playing here and there in various places, O lord of men.
There, heaps of swans were fashioned, possessing a luster equal to the orb of the moon.
And all around that hermitage were mountain caves blocked by snow.
It was surrounded by stone enclosures and was always inaccessible to human beings.
The great king Purūravas was one who had previously propitiated the Lord of the Gods.
Then, by the grace of the God of gods, he arrived at that hermitage.
Then he beheld that hermitage, which dispelled all fatigue, was enchanting, and adorned with hundreds of captivating flowers.
And that auspicious deed, which bestows prosperity, had been performed by Atri himself; then the King of Madra beheld him.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Hermitages of the Great Sages," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Therein are those two great peaks, Mahāśṛṅga, Mahāvarṣa, and Mahāhima.
But between those two, the third peak is exceedingly lofty. || 1 ||
It was perpetually scorched by the sun, consisting of heated stones, and always devoid of living beings.
Below that, in the southern region and the western part.
The opening was beautifully visible, encircled by a jasmine creeper.
Upon seeing him, the lord of the earth entered, filled with curiosity.
And the lord of the earth [traversed] a space of one nalva, which was extremely dense with darkness.
Having traversed a distance of one nalva, [he saw it] blazing with its own radiance and ornaments.
Then, it was exceedingly lofty, profound, and perfectly circular.
There the sun does not shine, nor does the moon radiate its light. || 5 ||
Nevertheless, that day and night possess the appearance of daylight and luminosity.
It was more than a krośa in extent and was resplendent with lakes. ||6||
Surrounding that lake, however, was a stone-paved terrace clinging to the mountain.
It was adorned with trees made of gold, silver, and even coral.
With various mani-jewels and flowers, radiant with the weight of their own luster.
In that lake were lotuses with petals of ruby.
Likewise, the fragrant nets of diamond filaments are exceedingly beautiful.
With leaves made of emeralds and blue lapis lazuli, O lord of the earth.
And likewise, O King, all the pericarps were made of gold.
In that lake, the ground was not at all covered with mud.
It was filled with various jewels and served as a refuge for aquatic creatures.
Of cowries, mother-of-pearl shells, and conch shells, O lord of the earth. || 11 ||
And of crocodiles, fish, and pīṇḍas, together with tortoises.
Therein were thousands of emerald fragments and diamonds.
O King, there were rubies, sapphires, and great blue gems.
Beautiful topazes as well as karketakas. ||13||
And likewise, the fragments of Turuṣka and the portions of Śeṣa.
And also of Gajāvarta, which is the principal, and of the one called Rudhira. || 14 ||
And likewise from sun-stones, moon-stones, pīlu, and bhallātaka.
Of Jyotīrasa, Ramya, and Śaṅkhaka, respectively. || 15 ||
Of emeralds, beryl, and likewise of crystal;
And the dust of gomedaka, pittaka, and emerald. || 16 ||
Likewise, O King, [the fragrance] of beryl, saugandhika, and royal gemstones.
And likewise for Khañja, Mukhya, and also Brahmamaṇi. ||17||
Of the finest pearls, which bear the form of stars.
And that water, being pleasantly warm, destroys the cold through bathing. ||18||
In the midst of that lake was a beautiful slab of lapis lazuli.
O King, it was likewise measured by that standard, and it was two hundred bows in length.
It was square and beautiful, fashioned by Atri through his ascetic power.
In the region at the gate of the cave, there is a golden Ketu.
That region, O Indra among kings, is located on that enchanting island.
Likewise, O King, there was a beautiful lotus pond on that rocky surface.
It possessed very cool and pure water and was adorned with aquatic flowers.
O King, it was as pure as the sky, square-shaped, and captivating to the mind. || 22 ||
That water of hers was sweet, light, cool, and fragrant.
It does not emaciate the body in that way, yet it fills the belly as well. ||23||
It bestows supreme satisfaction and great happiness upon the body.
And in its center, by means of ascetic penance, he [constructed] a well-made, auspicious palace with an entrance of golden arches, composed entirely of all kinds of jewels.
A silver palace, beneficial and resembling the rays of the moon. ||25||
Delightful, with stairs made of lapis lazuli and stars as pure as coral.
The great wheel of sapphire was adorned with gold. ||26||
With great pillars of ruby and likewise altars of emerald.
It was strewn with networks of vajra-rays, beautiful, and captivating to the sight. ||27||
In that palace resides the Blessed One, Janārdana, the God of gods.
He lies upon the coils of the serpent Śeṣa and is adorned with every ornament. || 28 ||
One [should place] the knee bent against the god of gods, the wielder of the discus.
And the second, O King, likewise has his two feet resting upon the lord of serpents.
His feet rest upon the lap of Lakṣmī, while he is stretched out upon the coils of Śeṣa.
He was beautified by his forearms and elbows resting upon the coils of the lord of serpents.
The Lord, who bore the head of a deity placed upon the back of his own finger.
One belongs to the God of gods, while the second is fully extended.
It is beautifully adorned with the wrists resting upon the knees drawn together.
And the hand, slightly contracted, is placed at the region of the navel. ||32||
Now hear of his third arm, and likewise his fourth.
It has the flower of one's own continuum as its essence and creeps along toward the region of the vital breath.
His feet were being massaged by Lakṣmī with her hands, which resembled full-blown lotuses.
Adorned with a garland of living beings, a crown, necklaces, and armlets.
And likewise, the god was adorned with finger-rings.
It was radiant with the beautiful crests of gems set upon the hoods of the lord of serpents.
Then Atri established himself in the practice of remaining unknown to all beings.
It is constantly worshipped as the object of the Siddhānta and is adorned on all sides with flowers. ||36||
His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes and incensed with celestial incense.
Always with delightful, prepared, and offered cow's milk products along with fruits.
The front and sides were beautifully adorned, and the god possessed a most excellent headpiece.
Likewise, having seen him facing westward, that lord of men paid him homage. ||38||
Having gone to the ground upon his knees and his head according to the prescribed rite.
He then praised Madhusūdana with a thousand names.
Then, having risen, he circumambulated him again and again.
Having seen that beautiful hermitage, the king dwelt there in that retreat.
For she had taken refuge in a certain vast and most enchanting cave.
He performed austerities in that very place, worshipping Janārdana.
With various kinds of flowers, fruits, and roots, along with dairy products, [he always offered worship].
Constantly bathing at the three periods of the day, he was devoted to the worship of the sacrificial fire.
Constantly sustaining his life with the waters of Devavāpī.
Having renounced all food, that lord of men [departed]. || 43 ||
The king passes his time dwelling in the cave that is without support.
Thus, for him who had abandoned the practice of eating food and subsisted on water alone, [the following occurred].
No illness comes upon his body; that is truly wonderful. ||44||
Thus that king, devoted to asceticism, was constantly worshipping the best of gods.
There, in that hermitage which was like heaven, he dwelt for some time, experiencing no suffering.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Hermitages," in the first section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having gone to the hermitage, the king abandoned food and all personal attendants.
Together with the Gandharvas, he beholds the Apsarases through their playful diversions. || 1 ||
Having gathered a profusion of flowers and likewise having strung them into garlands,
Having first offered it to the god, he likewise gave it to the Gandharvas.
While they were intent on gathering flowers and sporting at their pleasure.
Even while seeing various kinds of movements, he does not see them.
Some, intent on gathering flowers, were entangled in a network of creepers.
Abandoned by their circle of friends, they were rescued by their beloved.
Some women had their eyes overwhelmed by the nectar-like fragrance.
Their eyes were cleared of dust by the wind of their beloveds' sighs.
A certain beautiful woman, having gathered flowers, gave them to her beloved.
And with those [flowers] woven together by her beloved, she shone, having fashioned a crest-ornament.
Having herself gathered and woven them, she made a crest-ornament for her lover.
She, who increases the passion of love, considered herself as one who had accomplished her purpose.
In another dense bower, there was a creeper with particularly beautiful blossoms.
A certain woman was thus led into private by her lover, who desired to sport with her.
Gathering flowers from the creepers bent down by her beloved.
One among them all considered herself superior in every virtue.
In some places, the king saw [them] individually among the lotus ponds.
The charming celestial women were being sported with by the Gandharvas.
And one woman of pure smiles sprinkled her beloved with water.
In the same way, another woman, though being struck, attained sexual delight with her lover. || 11 ||
But the beautiful woman, overcome with distress, struck him.
The woman of beautiful hips was seen, her breasts dancing with her breath.
With her mass of hair loosened by the blow of the beloved’s water-sprinkling, she fastened it back.
With her face agitated by her breath, she shines like a lotus plant surrounded by bees. || 13 ||
In a forest of lotuses covered with flowers resembling their own faces.
A certain woman, having been concealed, was found after a long time by her beloved who had searched for her with great effort.
Under the pretext of bathing, a certain mature woman bathed excessively under the guise of cooling herself.
She performed the embrace of her lover, which had been long desired by her mind. || 15 ||
Her garment was fine, wet with water, clinging to her limbs, as she smiled with a pure radiance.
Holding the people there in her power, she made them full of passion.
Another, having been drawn by her beloved into the water with the charms of perfumes and garlands, [remained there].
Seeing her lover fall from the breaking garland, she laughed for a long time.
A certain woman had a nail-mark on her knee-crevice given by her friend as she was submerged [in water].
In her agitation, she too, while seeking her beloved, sank down into the water. || 18 ||
A certain woman, having turned her back to the sun, was shedding water from her hair.
She was seen by her husband on the surface of a stone slab, his eyes afflicted by desire. ||19||
The beautiful garland has been removed, and the saffron from her breasts has been transferred [to another].
The water of that lake took on the luster of a beloved woman exhausted at the end of lovemaking.
And by the hosts of well-bathed gods, gandharvas, and celestial nymphs.
He beheld Janārdana, the God of gods, being worshipped.
And in another place, the king beheld women situated within bower-houses of creepers.
Adorning their own limbs, with their minds fixed upon their beloveds. ||22||
A certain woman, her hand busily occupied with a mirror, [heard] what issued from the mouth of her messenger.
Hearing her lover's words, she appeared with a face exceedingly weary. ||23||
A certain messenger, being in a hurry, caused a reversal of her ornaments.
Performing these acts, her consciousness possessed by the god of love, she did not wake up at all.
Adorned with heaps of fragrant flowers scattered by the wind.
In one place, on a patch of dark green grass, she saw some women drinking;
in another, a certain excellent woman was herself making her lover drink.
A certain woman of beautiful form drank [the wine] offered by her lover's hand. ||26||
A certain woman [beheld her reflection] accompanied by blue lotuses reflected in her own eyes.
Having drunk, she asked her lover: "Where have those great lotuses gone? (27)
"Surely you yourself have drunk them," she was thus addressed by her lover.
Having realized the truth, she remained ashamed for a long time due to her own foolishness. ||28||
A certain fair-browed woman [drank] what was offered by her lover, the remainder of what had been drunk by her beloved.
She drank the beverage, which was full of exquisite flavor and increased the passion of love. ||29||
Then, at their drinking parties, that bull among men [was present].
He heard various songs blended with the sounds of stringed instruments.
And at the time of dusk, they [worshipped] Janārdana, the God of gods.
O King, they always dance before various musical instruments.
When only one watch of the night had passed, he emerged from the mouth of the cave.
They come together with their beloveds to their own homes, which have been fashioned by their own supernatural power.
Their surfaces were honored with various perfumes, and they were fragrant with diverse scents.
[They saw] various and wonderful couches adorned with heaps of flowers.
Thus, on that mountain, he beheld the sports of the apsarases.
The great king performed penance, his mind dedicated to Keśava.
The hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases went to that king and spoke to him.
O King, O crusher of enemies, you have reached a land comparable to heaven.
For we shall indeed grant you the boons desired by your mind.
"Take them and go home, or else stay here. || 36 ||
Purūravas said:
All of you possess unfailing vision and immeasurable splendor.
Grant a boon this very day; show favor through Madhusūdana.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then King Purūravas was told by them, "So be it."
There he dwelt happily for a month, worshipping Janārdana.
O King, he was always beloved by the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
That person was satisfied with the king’s action, which was free from greed.
In the midst of the Maghas, that king then entered the hermitage, which was variegated with thousands of jewels.
O King, subsisting there on water alone, he dwelt for a month until the end of the bright fortnight of Phālguna.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of Water-Sports," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
At the end of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, King Purūravas saw [this] in a dream.
He heard the auspicious words spoken by that very God of gods. ||1||
When this night has passed, you shall be reunited with the minister.
By meeting him, O King, you will have accomplished your purpose.
Having thus seen this dream, that royal sage of vast prowess [reflected].
At the time of dawn, having bathed according to the rules as before, he remained unwearied.
Having accomplished his purpose, he worshipped Janārdana according to his desire.
The righteous one reported that dream to the God of gods.
Then he heard a voice uttered from the image of the deity.
It is even so, O protector of the earth; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. || 5 ||
Having thus attained serene faith in Janārdana, the God of gods.

Terrible, frequented by thieves, and infested with crawling reptiles. || 1 ||
And for one who is constantly diligent, the path brings about the supreme destruction of burning afflictions.
Therefore, O Keśava, tell me of a very brief rite for the worship [of you].
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Therefore, O King, the anointing of the temple of the deity is even more important.

He shall be liberated from rajas and tamas; there is no doubt in this matter.
O King, however many grains of dust a man might sweep away, [so many years shall he dwell in heaven].

Then, having attained another birth, he reaches an unsurpassed home.

O King, [they were] pleasant-spoken, heart-pleasing, and beautiful in form.
And she was surrounded by many women who possessed beautiful lineages.
And he attains a firm state of householdership there upon the surface of the earth.
And while living, he never undergoes a fall from that state.
All those who are his kinsmen there shall all be long-lived.
For him, mental afflictions and physical ailments neither arise nor persist. ||16||
Death never occurs within his house.
There, in that house, that illustrious man lived for the rest of his life filled with joy.
He has no fear arising from thieves, nor any fear caused by disease.
Nor would there be any fruit for him from [the gift] born of a king of serpents. || 18 ||

O lord of men, this propitiation of Viṣṇu, the best of gods, is easily accomplished.
I have thus explained to you the specific distinction regarding the fruitfulness [of practice] for those devoid of wealth and those possessed of wealth. (23)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Fruit of Smearing [the Ground]," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.

Go to Cyavana, the descendant of Bhṛgu; from him you shall obtain a son.

In the morning, he went on foot to the auspicious hermitage of that Cyavana.
Having worshipped Cyavana, he was in turn honored by Cyavana.
The best of kings told him both his vow and his dream.
Even Cyavana, of great ascetic power, [acted] with respect to the hosts of sages.
Unperceived by the lord of men, he offered his daughter as a libation of water.
And Bhārgava placed that water contained within the pitcher.
Then, when midnight had arrived, that lord of the earth became afflicted by thirst.
Then, in the midst of the sages, he spoke these words to the sages who were sleeping.
"O Brahmins, I am severely afflicted by thirst; give me water! (19)
No seer, impelled by the destiny of what was to be, heard of him.

Having been addressed thus, he honored the brahmins and went to his own home. || 26 ||
Having burst through the king's side, he was born resembling the rising sun.

As soon as he was born, Indra placed his forefinger into his mouth.
Upon reaching her, he abandoned his childhood state at that very moment. || 28 |||||
Then Śatakratu, that lion among kings, touched the belly of the king.

Thinking, "He shall sustain me," he became renowned throughout the three worlds as Māndhātṛ.

O Yādava, she too was the wife of that Śūdra, fallen from heaven.

Yuvanāśva, however, chose her, who was endowed with the auspicious marks of Māndhātṛ.

Yuvanāśva went from the forest to the woods, and from the woods even to heaven.

In the netherworld, in the sky, on the mountain, and in the ocean, [the power] of the Great-Souled One [prevails]. || 36 ||
O King, his movement was as unimpeded as that of a wheel.
That righteous-souled one became a universal monarch (cakravartin) and likewise a devotee of Viṣṇu.
