Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Māndhātṛ," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Vajra said:
But that king Māndhātṛ, O Brahmin, the lord of the world, was [conquered] by me.
It is heard that he was slain by Lavaṇa with the trident of Maheśvara. || 1 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The Vaiṣṇava splendor is indeed invincible and is eternally present within all living beings.
They all go to destruction, being utterly overwhelmed by the splendor of Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, there is nothing whatsoever in this world that is indestructible.
But without that great Vaiṣṇava splendor, O King, [it cannot be accomplished].
O King, his splendor is always extremely difficult for embodied beings to withstand.
Therefore, O giver of honor, being deprived of that, they go to their destruction.
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-Lion, and then the Dwarf;
Brahmā, Śambhu, as well as Arka, Candramas, and Śatakratu.
These and others like them were likewise endowed with the splendor of Viṣṇu.
And by the inference from the "elephant's shadow" (gajacchāyā), they are deprived of their splendor.
And all those, deprived of their splendor, shall meet their death.
Whatever exists in the world is gross and consists of the five elements.
O best of kings, you should know that everything is subject to destruction.
But know that to be indestructible by which all this universe is pervaded.
That which is devoid of the quality of fragrance and destitute of form and touch;
It is devoid of sound, tasteless, the Lord of all, and all-pervading.
It is devoid of qualities, yet transcends those qualities; it is both near at hand and far away.
It manifests as the qualities of all the senses, yet it is devoid of all the senses.
With hands and feet extending everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on every side.
The God who possesses the qualities of all the senses, the Supreme Lord in every respect. ||11||
That alone is indestructible, within whose belly the entire universe resides.
Some call that Lord of the universe "Sadāśiva. ||12||
Others call him Vāsudeva, and still others call him Time itself.
Others say it is God, and others say it is inherent nature.
Others say it is karma, and likewise others say it is the person (puruṣa).
And those people who know the Vedas likewise know him by the name of Praṇava. || 14 ||
That is one, unborn, unmanifest, and indestructible, O lord of men.
Except for that one Lord, the entire world is like an embryo within [him].
This true nature of the Lord of the universe has been described by me to you, O moon of the Yadu dynasty.
Without devotion, it is not possible for even an intelligent man to speak of or comprehend it.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of the Puruṣa," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Vajra said:
The manifestations as the Boar and others belong to the Lord of All, the Infinite Self.
All those who are aggregates of the great elements are subject to birth and death. || 1 ||
If this is so, O best of the Bhṛgus, what is the distinction between them and living beings?
Cut through this doubt for me, for my curiosity is indeed great.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O protector of the earth, all living beings are bound by the fetters of karma.
They are always born and they always die, being entirely dependent on others. || 3 ||
By the bonds of action, both auspicious and inauspicious, which are constantly impelled by the Lord.
O King, they are endowed with happiness and suffering resulting from actions performed in other births.
But Vāsudeva, O Yādava, is righteous-souled in his various manifestations.
By his own will, he ordains his birth as well as his death.
And actions do not stain the Lord, even during his manifestations.
Even while constantly engaged in actions, he remains unstained by them, like a lotus leaf by water.
O Yādava, there too, one experiences the fruits born of one's past actions.
O King, fearing the violation of established boundaries, she manifests falsely before men.
For whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Yadava,
When there is the rise of unrighteousness, he creates that very self. || 8 ||
Among gods, animals, and humans, as well as among gandharvas, serpents, and birds.
Likewise, having understood the relative strength and weakness of the effects even in other birth-places (yoni), [one should act accordingly].
Whenever and in whatever womb he manifests due to a cause.
Then, conforming to its source, it acts in the world in accordance with that.
O King, although the Lord of the Universe was capable of withdrawing the world at that time, he did not do so.
O Yādava, he indeed kills those who are to be slain through means that correspond to their own origin.
The Supreme Person likewise [dispels] the darkness within the heart, as well as the darkness of night, which is embodied.
He alone, of stainless luster, brings destruction upon the worlds.
By that divine form, the darkness within the heart of the world was destroyed.
And by means of its form as light, the most terrible darkness of night was destroyed.
He has always manifested in embodied form in order to destroy darkness.
And the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas, O Indra among kings, were embodied darkness.
Even for the Daityas who were as barren as barren women, Janārdana remained within their bodies.
He does not relinquish his bodies, and by means of skillful means, he seeks to destroy them. || 15 ||
He was beloved by the gods, his teachers, and the twice-born.
He is devoted to propitiation according to the method prescribed in the scriptures. || 16 ||
And for him, there is nothing whatsoever that remains to be done in the three worlds.
Yet, among all actions, there exists nothing that has not been attained nor anything yet to be attained. // 17 //
He is omniscient, all-seeing, and the Lord endowed with all powers.
Nevertheless, O King, he continues to study, perform sacrifices, and practice austerities.
For the purpose of establishing the bounds of conduct and out of a desire for the welfare of the world.
O King, he performs his duties like a weak laborer. || 19 ||
Whatever a superior person practices, that very same thing other people also do.
Whatever standard he sets, the world follows that.
Relying upon this cause, one always engages in actions.
Viṣṇu, though manifested through appearance, is just like any other ordinary being.
And he constantly prays for boons from both the gods and the sages.
And he, the giver of boons, O Pāṇḍava, honors their excellent gifts as well.
Therefore, O men, this [manifestation] is superior to the delight in [mere] appearance.
Deluded by his illusory power, they do not perceive the Supreme Person.
Thus, even though he has manifested himself by uniting all that is moving and unmoving, he remains as such.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, the powerful Lord of the universe [acted]. ||24||
Even when it has entered into manifestation, that [mindfulness] is considered to be all-pervading.
And there is freedom everywhere; no deliberation need be made on this point. || 25 ||
This is the great distinction between you and other living beings, O Lord of creatures.
I have spoken thus concerning that all-pervading god, the Self-existent One.
O best of the Yadu lineage, some have been projected by meritorious karmas.
The god enters into them completely with that splendor.
They were possessed by the splendor of that god, the Supreme Lord.
In that same way, they perform their duties while being honored by the great seers.
Thus, at that time, they were indeed cast down by that Vaiṣṇava splendor.
They come under the power of destiny, according to what is pleasing to Him alone.
And whoeversoever are seen in this world endowed with splendor, [they have all derived it from you].
O lord of the earth, you should know that their splendor is indeed Vaiṣṇava.
That which is in the moon, that which is in the fire, and that which is in the sun, the lord of the world;
One sees all that splendor; know it, O King, to be Vaiṣṇava.
And whatever super-sensory power belongs to those headed by Agastya, [that too is within his reach].
O King, that [power] residing therein should indeed be known by you through the splendor of Viṣṇu.
Whatever being possesses grandeur, beauty, or even power—
Understand each of those things indeed as being joined with the splendor of Viṣṇu.
Of Brahmins, of gods, of virtuous women, and likewise of cows.
Know that power of Viṣṇu, O Lord, to be the sustainer of the worlds.
Those kings, endowed with the Vaiṣṇava splendor, [ruled] the earth.

For them, however, there are seven jewels here upon the surface of the earth.
Elephants, horses, chariots, and jewels, as well as the jewel of a wife. ||42||
In the same way, there is the weapon-jewel and likewise the treasure of the gem-jewel.
And their four modes of movement are likewise unimpeded.
In the netherworld, in the sky, on the mountain, and in the ocean, O lord of the earth.
The ocean stands with its waters solidified at the departure of universal monarchs.
Furthermore, the earth and likewise the mountains become their path.
The earth provides a cavity for those who are about to go to the netherworld.
Likewise, their horses do not falter in the sky.
By means of sacred learning, austerity, sacrifices, heroism, and the power of weapons. || 46 ||
O lord of men, they surpass all other living beings.

Of Arjuna, the lord of men, who was united with the splendor of Hari.

Having presided over a certain body by means of that terrible splendor.

By his own splendor, he effects the withdrawal of that fiery energy.
O King, there is no one else in the world who can pacify the splendor of Viṣṇu.
In his incarnations, I have described this very nature of you, the Lord of the universe.
This is the supreme secret of the sages, the nectar of knowledge that destroys all impurities.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of Manifestation," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Vajra said:

In the month of Māgha, under the Maghā asterism, one should worship the left arm of the God.
Under the constellation Uttarāphalgunī, one should worship the left shoulder.
During these four waning phases, one should perform the ritual bath with cow’s urine.
Likewise, the worship of the God of gods is performed with red flowers and other such offerings.
A man should perform [this rite] with clarified butter, and offer sesame seeds to the twice-born.
Likewise, there is the gift of copper, followed by the consumption of cow's urine.
Then, the wise man should take his meal consisting of sacrificial food (haviṣya). || 9 ||
One should worship the right shoulder of the deity in the month of Caitra under the Citrā constellation.

And on the right side of the waist, one should worship Jyeṣṭhā during the Jyeṣṭhā constellation.
And likewise, in the month of Āṣāḍha, during the Vaiśvadeva rite, one should touch the right knee. 51.1.
During these four months, a bath with milk is prescribed.
And there shall be worship with yellow flowers and other offerings for the God of gods, the Wielder of the Discus.
One should perform the fire sacrifice with śāli rice, and barley should be given to the twice-born.
And silver should be given in such a manner that the act of eating is accomplished with food.
Likewise, O lord of men, it should be performed in every month of Śrāvaṇa thereafter.
One should worship at his feet him to whom this entire world belongs.
The Guptam [is worshipped] in the month of Bhādrapada, and then the Hṛdayam in Āśvina.
The worship of the head should be performed during the month of Kārttika and under the asterism Kṛttikā.
During these four months, bathing with curd is prescribed.
Likewise, the worship of the God of gods is performed with white flowers and other such offerings.
An oblation should be performed with milk, and ghee should be given to the twice-born.
Likewise, O King, the act of eating should be performed with gold and curd. (17)
O King, the mantra named Ananta should be recited during all months.
One should designate the fire-offering rites for the deity by that very name. || 18 ||
At the conclusion of the vow, food must be given to the Brahmins.
O lord of men, one should give gifts to the Brahmins according to one's ability. (19)
Within a year, one attains all of one's heart's desires.
By those desiring sons, by those seeking a livelihood, and by those longing for servants, wives, and wealth.
And those who make requests should cultivate strength, health, and prosperity.
O Great King, this vow is meritorious and is the supreme means of securing well-being.
This is called the Ananta-vrata, which destroys all impurities.
In former times, King Yuvanāśva performed this very vow.
He obtained a son, Māndhātṛ, who was a universal monarch (cakravartin).
O Indra among kings, Kṛtavīrya’s wife was likewise Śīladharā.
By means of this vow, she obtained a son endowed with a thousand arms.
[He saw] the universal monarch named King Kārtavīryārjuna. || 24 ||
The Blessed One, Mādhava, entered Yama with his own splendor.
Salutations to you, Kārtavīrya Arjuna, the great-souled one. || 25 ||
And to the Lord of the earth consisting of seven islands and oceans.
When this much has been spoken, it corresponds to the merit of a prastha of sesame seeds. ||26||
O King, that which was duly given by you to a self-restrained Brāhmaṇa...
Indeed, as soon as he was born, an auspicious wind blew forth. || 27 ||
The sky became free of dust, and the entire world attained joy.
Having assumed human form, the Daityas sought refuge with the king. ||28||
Then, by the hundreds and thousands, they fearlessly took up their positions.
O King, in that land where the people are prosperous, the earth is oppressed by their weight.
O King, with his body soiled by the water, he sustained himself with great difficulty.
O lion among kings, this ancient vow, which grants sons, has been recounted by me to you.
This should be performed on earth by those desiring sons; it removes sin and increases righteousness.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Ananta Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe this other matter: the worship of the lunar mansions according to the months.
Whatever fruit a person attains from the God of gods— || 1 ||

This vow is completed by three fast-breaking meals. || 2 ||
Likewise, O King, the breaking of the fast here is proclaimed to last for four months.
O King, listen to the procedure for each month regarding the breaking of the fast.
And one should always perform the ritual bath with the water of the five products of the cow.
Worship with flowers and other offerings should be performed with whatever materials have been obtained as they are available.
First, for four months, the food offering (naivedya) here consists of kṛsara.
Likewise, the middle group of four should be performed with barley gruel. || 5 ||
In the fourth and the third [offerings], the food offering (naivedya) should consist of milk-rice (pāyasa).
O Indra among kings, the wise man should feed the Brahmins with that very same food.
Restrained in speech and well-composed, one should eat the food offering at night.
He should remain self-restrained during that night, likewise sleeping on the bare ground.
One should continue to act in this manner until the Kṛttikā constellation occurs in the month of Kārttika.
There, O King, having worshipped the Lord of Gods according to the ritual for commencement, || 8 ||
A vessel filled with ghee, together with gold, [should be given] to a twice-born man.
Food must be given, especially to the Brāhmaṇas. || 9 ||
Having observed this vow for a year, that best of men—
And having obtained a dwelling, she rejoices; so too does a woman, O Yādava.
Stable prosperity, a mind devoted to dharma, strength, good fortune, vigor, and steadfastness of character.
One should maintain a very long-term aspiration for the third heaven; this vow is exceedingly meritorious for men.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Worship of the Lunar Mansions by Month," in the first section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In this regard, I shall relate to you a story that destroys all sins.
Having relied upon the conduct [of the gods] in heaven, [there is] the worship of the months and constellations. || 1 ||
O Śakra, I do not know anything at all that was practiced by those in the past.
Know me, O best of gods, to be a contemporary of yours. 2.
This renowned Śāmbarāyaṇī is a perfected one who possesses such knowledge.
Thus addressed, Śakra, the slayer of Bala, then questioned him.
And she related the great former deeds of Śakra as an Indra.
She has passed away hundreds and thousands of times through the Śakras who have gone before.
O Lord, he recounted there his deeds in other kalpas as well.
Śāmbarāyaṇī said:
And those who were the heirs and kinsmen of all the Śakras.
All have been destroyed by that powerful Viṣṇu.
All the Śakras were likewise endowed with that Vaiṣṇava splendor.
They surpass all other beings; therefore, they possess a perfection of qualities.
By means of charity, sacrifices, heroism, austerity, and strength.
By means of sacred learning and righteousness, [he subdued] the gods, daityas, and great serpents.
And those highly fortunate sages as well, O best of kings.
And all that was performed by them was rendered most pure by the Self-born One himself.
For this reason, they have repeatedly suffered defeat at the hands of their kinsmen.
They are lords of all, endowed with the power of heroism, established in the Dharma, and the foremost beings in the world.
Then, having relinquished their offices, they all gradually attained the state of being companions of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Śakra’s Deeds," in the first section of the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Indra said:
At which time those six Indras of immense splendor had passed away.
O auspicious lady, I desire to hear their life stories in detail.
Salute Śakra, Manu, and likewise the sons of Manu, O auspicious lady.
As well as the gods, the seven sages, and likewise his heirs and kinsmen. || 2 ||
Likewise, the gods [heard] of the slaying of Śakra and of those others by Janārdana.
I wish to hear all this from you, O beautiful one; you know everything.
Śāmbarāyaṇī said:
The first mind-born son of Brahmā is remembered as Manu.
And these ten sons of his are renowned, O Lord of the Three Worlds. || 4 ||
Agnīdhra, Atibāhu, Medhā, Medhātithi, and Vasu.
Jyotiṣman, Dyutimān, Havya, Savana, and Satra. ||5||
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
And Vasiṣṭha of great splendor—these are proclaimed as the seven sages (ṛṣis). ||6||
Those known as Jayā, those known as Ajitā, and likewise Śukrā and Yāmā;
These twelve groups consist of four who drink the Soma.
Among those gods, there was one who became their Indra, named Viśvabhuj.
At that time, the terrible Asuras were her heirs and kinsmen.
Among them, there was a king known by the name Bāṣkala.
From whose hand both worlds were formerly seized by Vāmana.
But Pātāla was taken by the two of them in succession, O Lord of the Gods.
That man who possessed a son named Keśin, who was exceedingly powerful.
The evil-minded one, having assailed Śakra, seized the three worlds once again.
Viṣṇu, whose vehicle is the foremost of birds, summoned him to battle.
With his discus, he split it in two out of a desire for the welfare of the three worlds. ||12||

Thus was the foremost of the destroyers of cities, whose power was equal to Time itself, slain by that great-souled lord of the gods, who is without peer, for the sake of Śakra’s pleasure and for the welfare of the worlds. 13.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the First Manvantara," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the Śāmbarāyaṇī-vākya of the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Śāmbarāyaṇī said:
Immediately after that, there was a Manu named Svārociṣa.
He had sons of great fortune who were lords of the earth's surface.
Caitra, Kaviruta, Kṛtānta, Vidyut, and Ravi.
Bṛhadgraha and Nabhas, possessed of great strength and prowess. || 2 ||
Likewise, his vital energy (ūrjas) is his life-breath (prāṇa), and the bull (ṛṣabha) is likewise immovable.
And with his teeth, he proclaimed the seven Ṛṣis who possess the power of the Śakvarī verses.
The twelve Bhūṣitas have been declared, as well as those who are the Pārāvatas.
Their lords were Indra and the high-souled Vipaścit, who was renowned throughout the world.
At that time, the terrible Asuras were her heirs and kinsmen.
At that time, their king was Purukutsa, who possessed superior strength.
Attached to what was displeasing to Śakra, he went to the forest for the sake of hunting.
Relying on his great prowess, he struck down the rutting elephants.
That elephant, the minister of the king, slaughtered the monkeys in the forest.
He, of immense stature and the hue of black collyrium, with his hand raised, struck like a mountain.
He forcibly struck down that foremost of Daityas, who was otherwise unslayable in battles by both gods and asuras. || 7 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of the Second Manvantara," within the account of Śāmbarāyaṇī to Indra, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 177 ||
Śāmbarāyaṇī said:
Learn from me the sons of Auttama, the third Manu.
Aja, Paraśu, Devadeva, Vṛdha, and Naya. || 1 ||
Devāvṛdha, the peerless Mahotsāha, and likewise Gaja;
Vinīta, Suketu, Sumitra, Subala, and Śuci. || 2 ||
Beyond this, O sages, I shall now declare those seven who were indeed present at that time.
Rajobāhu, Urdhvabāhu, Savana, and he who is Anagha; || 3 ||
Sutapās and Śakti—these are proclaimed as the seven sages (ṛṣis).
They are self-controlled, consuming their own portions, independent, truthful, and destroyers of the wicked. || 4 ||
Five groups of deities have been declared, and each of them consists of twelve.
Among them, there was a Śakra named Sucitti, the conqueror of enemy cities.
At that time, the terrible Asuras were her heirs and kinsmen.
Among them there was a powerful king known by the name Pralamba.
That ocean, which carries its waters, was intent on doing what was displeasing to Śakra.
Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a fish, swallowed one who was even more powerful.
But the world’s conduct proceeds through the form of the "law of the fish," wherein one treats an enemy in a foreign land as if he were the fire of cosmic destruction.
He struck him, who was as large as a mountain peak and insatiable with arrows, in the midst of the ocean.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Third Manvantara," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Śāmbarāyaṇī said:
Learn from me the sons of Tāmasa, the fourth Manu.
A man with well-formed knees and shanks is free from fear; likewise, such a man attains renown. (1)
For Avikṣit was fond of his servants, Prasthila had a firm quiver.
Kṛta and Kṛtagandha were the sons of the Tāmasa Manu.
The sages are Vana, Kaṭhīyān, Gātra, Caitra, and Agni.
Jyotirvāsas, Pṛthu, and Kārya are proclaimed as the seven sages (ṛṣis). || 3 ||
They are proclaimed as Satya, Supāda, Suriha, and Hara.
These four groups of deities consist of twenty-five members each. ||4||
The truths also have two divisions; they are proclaimed as the Satyas and the Viśvas.
Twelve truths have been specified; thirteen are declared to be universal. ||5||
Among them was the highly energetic and powerful Śibi, who was like Indra.
At that time, the terrible Asuras were her heirs and kinsmen.
Those for whom the lord King Bhīmaratha, possessed of great splendor, was their sovereign.
By whom, having propitiated Brahmā, immunity from being slain on dry land was chosen.
From that time forward, that evil-minded man avoided water.
He saw in the desert a tortoise that appeared as large as a mountain.
The evil-minded one, filled with curiosity, climbed upon it.
Having taken up the one who had mounted it, the Lord Hari, who possesses a great body, [departed]. || 9 ||
Assuming the form of a tortoise, he entered the waters of Pātāla with great speed.
Having brought water from the netherworld (pātāla) and immersed him in it, he slew him.
Having stepped upon that massive body with his great tortoise-like form.
Thus, that enemy of the incomparable Lord of Gods was forcibly seized by the tortoise in the water.
The foremost of all the gods was struck down by that peerless Lord of All.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fourth Tāmasa Manvantara," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Śāmbarāyaṇī said:
Learn from me the sons of Raivata, the fifth Manu.
He is the Great Purāṇa, worthy of honor, present in every limb, the supreme slayer of enemies, and pure. || 1 ||
Calabindu, Nirāmitra, Ketuśṛṅga, and Dṛḍhavrata.
I shall tell you of the sages who were the sons of Raivata Manu.
He is the Vedic revelation, the arm of the Vedas, the one with uplifted arms, and likewise the Yajus.
Hiraṇyaroman, Parjanya, and likewise Satyanetra. || 3 ||
And likewise the Ābhūtarājasa gods, who are possessed of great wisdom.
The Vaikuṇṭhas and the Amṛtas—these are the four classes of deities.
In each group, fourteen gods are said to reside.
Among them was Indra, named Vibhu, whose valor was renowned throughout the world.
At that time, the terrible Asuras were her heirs and kinsmen.
Among them was the great lord named Śambhu, possessed of immense splendor.
By him, death was chosen over the world of Brahmā from his grandfather.
Once, [he saw] a massive-bodied creature that dwelt within the waters of the ocean.
As soon as he saw the swan, the evil-minded man seized it and mounted upon it.
Having taken him up as soon as he had ascended, he went to the world of Brahmā.
There, the Blessed Lord Hari slew him in the form of a swan.
Thus was that great-souled one slain by that peerless Haṃsa, the Lord of All.
Possessing great strength, with a body as large as a mountain, he was the destroyer of gods and invincible in battles.

Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fifth Raivata Manvantara," in the dialogue between Indra and Śāmbarāyaṇīya, within the conversation between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 180 ||
Śāmbarāyaṇī said:
O Vāsava, hear now of the sons of Cākṣuṣa Manu, the sixth.
Ūru, Pūru, Śatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyavān, and Dhṛti. || 1 ||
O sinless one, [there were] Agniṣṭut, Atirātra, and likewise Sudyumna.
Haviṣmān, Unnata, Śrīmān, Sudhāmā, and likewise Vijaya. || 2 ||
Abhimāna, Sahiṣṇu, and Madhuśrī are remembered as the sages.
The Āḍhyas, Prasūtas, Bhāvyas, Lekhas, and likewise the Pṛthukas. || 3 ||
And at that time, five groups of eight [deities] of the dwellers of heaven were proclaimed.
Among them, there was a powerful Indra named Manojava. || 4 ||
At that time, the terrible Asuras were her heirs and kinsmen.
Among them, there was a king named Mahāmāla, who possessed superior strength.
Once, that man of evil intent went to the forest for the sake of hunting.
There he beheld a captivating horse, resembling the rays of the moon.
The evil-minded one climbed it, desiring to kill the deer.
Then the horse, taking him who was mounted upon it, galloped away with great speed.
Having gone to the far shore of the ocean, he hurled [the weapon] upon the evil-minded one.
As soon as he was hurled, that evil-minded one was carried away by the wind.
And having not obtained water, he is parched by the wind.
Even today, that one of great splendor remains on the exterior of the Lokāloka mountain.
But that wicked one [was granted] by Svayambhū the boon of freedom from death.
Having resorted to the path of the wind, he is not deprived of his vital breaths.
Thus that terrible one, arrogant because of the granting of the boon and thinking "I am immortal," committed an offense.
Assuming the form of a horse, Viṣṇu cast [the weapon] into the flow of the wind for the sake of the gods and the twice-born.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Sixth Cākṣuṣa Manvantara," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Śāmbarāyaṇī said:
Then there was another, Bhaviṣya, and Manu Vairasvata as well.
I shall now proclaim to you the illustrious sons of the seventh [Manu]. ||1||
Ikṣvāku, Nābhāga, Viṣṇu, and Śaryāti as well.
Likewise, Prāṃśu and the high-souled Diṣṭa both grew in stature.
Karūṣa, Pṛthudhra, and Sudyumna were the sons of Manu.
Atri, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, Jamadagni, and Kaśyapa. || 3 ||
Gautama, Bharadvāja, and Viśvāmitra as the seventh; |||
For the gods are proclaimed to be the forty-nine Maruts.
The two Aśvins are specified, as well as the ten Viśvedevas.
The ten Aṅgirasas are indeed gods; thus, there are nine groups of gods.
Among them was Śakra, known by the name Mojaṃbī, the destroyer of enemies.
Nevertheless, those Daityas who were his kinsmen and relatives were likewise fierce.
Among them, there was a king named Hiraṇyākṣa, who possessed great strength.
In former times, Hari slew him with a body that was half-man and half-boar.
That lord of the Daityas, who was terrifying to the hosts of gods, possessed great strength and a body as large as a mountain.
Hari, assuming the form of a boar-headed being, forcibly struck it with his discus. ||8||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Seventh Vaivasvata Manvantara," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Śakra said:
O highly fortunate lady, those who will be the Manus in this kalpa—
O Śakra, [protect] their sons—the ṛṣis and gods—who are your heirs and kinsmen.
Proclaim all of this, including his slaughter at the hands of Kṛṣṇa.
She is considered by me to be like the Omniscient One, possessing divine knowledge.
Śāmbarāyaṇī said:
[Listen to] the sons of the future eighth Manu, Sāvarṇi.
I shall tell you, O Śakra, of those possessed of great strength and prowess.
Vijaya, Avarīvan, Nirdoha, Satyavāk, and Kṛti.
He was both wandering and unassailable, and he possessed perfect mastery over speech.
Now learn from me the sons and the sages of Sāvarṇi Manu.
Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, Vyāsa, Gālava, and then Dīptimān. || 5 ||
Likewise, Rishyashringa and Rama are celebrated as Rishis.
The Sutapas, the Amṛtābhas, and the Ātreyas are the three groups.
All these great-souled ones were accompanied by twenty hosts of gods.
For those whose Indra shall be Bali, the best of the Dānavas.
On your account, the Lord of the Thirty-three was bound by the God of Gods.
O Vāsava, his heirs and kinsmen shall not exist.
By him, the state of Śakra must be assumed for a Manvantara free from all obstacles.
This gift was entrusted to him by the God of Gods, O great Asura.
He becomes the king of the three worlds during the interval of the Manu Sāvarṇa.
When that Manvantara had arrived, the powerful one whose abode is the snowy mountain [was born].
There will be a rākṣasa of evil conduct named Nānola.
Having obtained a boon from Brahmā, he was fierce and intent upon the destruction of the three worlds.
The righteous Viṣṇu, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, will slay him.
With his hundred-spoked wheel, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
With fangs formidable and a fierce, hideous appearance, he has the luster of black collyrium and inspires terror in the three worlds.
Having torn asunder the entire world with his discus, the Lord, the Maker, rendered it free from fear.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Eighth Sāvarṇi Manvantara," in the dialogue between Śakra and Śāmbarāyaṇī, within the conversation between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 183 ||
Śāṃbarāyaṇī said:
Now hear of the sons of the ninth Manu, Brahmaputra.
Dhṛtiketu, Dīptiketu, Pañcahasta, and Nirākṛti. || 1 ||
Pṛthuśravas, Bṛhaddyumna, and Ṛcīka—this is the host of the great.
Learn from me also of the sons of Brahmaputra, who were sages.
Medhātithi, Dyuti, Savana, and Vasu.
Jyotiṣmat, Havya, and Satya are proclaimed to be the sages (ṛṣis). || 3 ||
Pārā, Marīcigarbhas, and Svadharmans—these are the three.
The twelve groups have been declared, of whom Indra shall be the lord.
The powerful one named Vibhu, possessed of great splendor, is the lord of all the gods.
Those who will be his heirs and kinsmen shall be righteous.
One known as Kālakakṣa shall become their king.
In that Manvantara, there will be a king named Vasunābha.
But his son was Vāsudeva, the lord of the earth, who was born from you.
He will be a universal monarch of great splendor, known by the name Padmanābha.
In the battle between the gods and the asuras, [he encountered] Kālakākṣa, who was fierce in combat.
The one of great splendor, Padmanābha, will slay him who cannot be killed by men. || 8 ||
With an arrow adorned with gold and empowered by the Brahmā-weapon, he struck him who was fierce in battle.
Having slain the Asura of power equal to Time himself, that king shall destroy the fear of the world.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manvantara of the Ninth Son of Brahmā," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, within the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, in the conversation between Śakra and Śāmbarāyaṇī.
Śāmbarāyaṇī said:
Now hear of the sons of Manu, the tenth son of Dharma.
Sukṣetra, Uttamaujas, and the heroic Bhūriśoṇa. || 1 ||
Śatānīka, Nimi, Mitra, Vṛṣasena, and Jayadratha.
Bhūridyumna and Suvarman were the sons of Manoḥ, the son of Dharmaputra. || 2 ||
Āpomūrti, Haviṣmān, Sṛtikṛt, and likewise Avyaya.
Nābhāga, Pramita, and likewise the Saurabha sages. || 3 ||
Likewise, there are groups of deities numbering one hundred, known as the Prāṇas.
He shall become powerful; Indra shall be his peace. || 4 ||
The Asuras who exist shall become his heirs and kinsmen.
And their king shall be a great asura named Bāli.
Viṣṇu will strike him with his mace of terrible speed.
In the battle between the gods and the asuras, out of a desire for the welfare of the gods.
When the mighty Indra, the best of gods, was struck by the blow of that mace by him, the supreme deity.
This entire triple world shall become free from all defects and frequented by gods and brahmins.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manvantara of Daśama, the Son of Dharma," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, within the dialogue between Śakra and Śāmbarāyaṇī, in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Śāmbarāyaṇī said:
I shall now declare the sons of you, Rudra’s son, who are eleven in number.
To those who are constant in dharma, highly fortunate, and the ultimate refuge of the three worlds.
Sarvartuga, Suśarman, Senānīka, and Puroddhata;
Kṣemadhanvan, Dṛḍhendradhanvan, Cādarśa, and likewise Puṇḍraka. ||2||
These are indeed known as the sons of Manu; now learn from me concerning the sages as well.
Haviṣmān, Vapuṣmān, Varuṇābdhi, and Nistara. ||3||
Viṣṇu and Agnitejas are proclaimed as the seven sages (ṛṣis).
The Nirmathyas, the Rathayas, and the Kāmagas—these are the three groups.
Likewise, thirty deities are recorded in each individual group.
Their Indra will be named Vṛṣa, who will possess great strength.
The gods who are here shall indeed become his heirs and kinsmen.
Among them, however, there will be a powerful king named Daśagrīva.
Viṣṇu, having assumed a feminine form, will slay him.
Then, in the battle between the gods and the asuras, he pierced him through with the tip of a spear.
Him, who was unslayable and invincible to men by the Self-born One;
Having gone there by the power of her asceticism, Viṣṇu will cause him to be slain.
His natural form has the luster of a blue lotus and the color of refined gold, with well-rounded knees and thighs.
Having suddenly assumed a form far more beautiful than that of women, he, the slayer of enemies, confronted the fierce foe of the gods.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Eleventh Manvantara," in the dialogue between Śakra and Śāmbarāyaṇī, within the conversation between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 186 ||
Śāmbarāyaṇī said:
Now hear about the sons of Manu, the twelfth son of Dakṣa.
Devavān, Anupadeva, Devaśreṣṭha, and Vidūratha. ||1||
Mitravān, Mitradeva, and the heroic Mitrāsena.
Mitrabāhu and Suvarcas were the sons of Manu Dakṣasāvarṇi. || 2 ||
The seventh was Dyau, as well as Dyuti, Tapana, and Sutapas.
Tapas, rati, and tapasvin—the seven sages (ṛṣis) are thus proclaimed. || 3 ||
The Suśarmas, the Sutapas, the Haritas, and likewise the Rohitas;
There are five groups called Sutārās, each consisting of ten qualities.
And the powerful Indra among them was Ṛtadhāman, whose nature was righteousness.
The Asuras who exist shall be his heirs and kinsmen.
And among them there will be a king known by the name Naraka.
And he was invulnerable to the strength of both women and men due to a boon granted by Svayambhū.
Then Hari, having become a eunuch, will cause him to be slain.
The Great-Souled One assumed the form of a eunuch before the great Asura Devāntaka, whose power was equal to that of Time itself.
Having destroyed this entire world, that Blessed One, the Creator, is devoid of fear.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Genealogy of Manu, the Twelfth Son of Dakṣa," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Śāmbarāyaṇī said:
Learn from me the sons of Trayodaśa, the Manu Raucya.
Citrasena, Vicitra, Naya, Dharmabhṛt, and Dhṛti. ||1||
Sunetra, Vṛkṣavṛddhi, Sunaya, Dharmaya, and Dṛḍha.
These are the sons of Manu Raucya; hear from me, O sages, their names.
He is steadfast, imperishable, free from anger, and devoid of worldly anxiety.
The Emanation Body and the Reality-Perceiving Body are proclaimed to be twofold. ||3||
The Sutrāmaṇas, the Sudharmas, and the Śubhakarmas as well.
O Śakra, these three hosts of deities were then proclaimed. ||4||
Then, in each group, there were eleven auspicious gods.
And at that time, Bṛhaspati will be their Indra among the gods.
O Vāsava, those who will be his heirs shall be his kinsmen.
A wicked-souled one named Tiṭṭibha will become their king.
Even for him, death shall come from Janārdana, the God of gods.
And he constantly assumed the form of a peacock, which preys upon serpents.
But that evil-minded one, in the form of a serpent during the war between the gods and asuras, [acted].
Having waged war, he likewise rendered all the hosts of gods devoid of energy.
While the gods were rendered powerless, he assumed the form of a peacock.
Janārdana, the God of gods, will slay that wicked one.
He is the great mass, the crested one, the high-souled one, whose beautiful throat is like a blossomed blue lotus.
Having slain that Dānava there in battle by force, he will indeed make the three worlds joyful.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Thirteenth Raucya Manvantara," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Śāmbarāyaṇī said:
Hear from me the sons of Manu Bhautya, the fourteenth.
In the waves, there is indeed the destruction of distinctions, as well as the powerful submergence into the depths.
Abhimānin, Pravīra, Jiṣṇu, and likewise Saṃkrandana.
Tejasvin and Sulabha—these were the sons of Bhautya Manu.
Agnīdhra, Atibāhu, Māgadha, and likewise Śuci.
Ajita, Yukta, Go, and Śakya—these seven are proclaimed as the sages (ṛṣis). || 3 ||
The Cākṣuṣas, the Kaniṣṭhas, the Pavitras, and likewise the Bhajiras.
The groups of gods advanced in age are said to be five times seven [thirty-five].
Their Indra was named Śuci; his heirs and kinsmen were these.
Whoever shall become kings, for them there will be great happiness.
Then that battle between the gods and the asuras lasted for a thousand divine years.
At the end of that [age], there will be a most terrible [conflict] with that great Asura.
Keśava will destroy that which is established in the illusion of darkness (tāmasī māyā).
He mounted a divine elephant that resembled a moving mountain.
Madhusūdana made [the earth] level with its uprooted mountains by means of his discus.
He will slay that evil-minded great Daitya as he stands upon his chariot.

The planetary spirits, the spirits of the deceased, and likewise the spirits of the ancestors; || 34 ||

"I have destroyed this evil one entirely; let him be restored to health, just as was the word of Hari. (58)

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Pacification of Harm to Sentient Beings," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Origin of the Yakṣas," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.

Mārkaṇḍeya said:

Having saluted Rāma’s feet with his head and joined his palms in reverence. || 11 ||

With the sounding of conchs and kettledrums, and with the noise of small drums.

He is Dharma incarnate; he is the best among those who possess truth.

Whatever deed has been done by him now that Rāma has gone to the forest.

By one who constantly lived nearby, wearing matted hair and bark garments, and enjoying [his presence].

Listening to the excellent words uttered by the sage, Rāma’s younger brother went to Rāma’s house.
It is strewn with brave, noble, and learned men, like the immeasurable ocean filled with jewels.

Thus ends the two hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of Bharata’s Departure," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Yādava, when Bharata had departed from his home, seeking to set out on his journey.

The pursuit of the high-souled prince Bharata.

Taking up various forms and many goods, let them indeed go forth.
Poison-doctors, surgeons, as well as physicians who treat internal diseases;
Laborers, architects, wayfarers, and tree-planters. || 9 ||
Well-diggers, plasterers, and likewise those who work with bamboo;
And whatever merchants there may be, as well as beautiful basket-makers. || 1.203.10 ||
Likewise, those who perform manual labor and those who live by their clothes.
Peacocks, partridges, blue jays, and those that are pheasants; || 11 ||
Dyers, ivory-carvers, and likewise those who subsist on ivory;
And those who work with castor seeds and cane, as well as those who make beautiful mats. || 12 ||
And those made of brass, as well as those made of copper.
They were makers of birch-bark scrolls, sword-smiths, and sellers of molasses and rum.
O Lakṣmaṇa, there were those who raised sheep, those who raised buffaloes, and weavers.
And whatever bards, panegyrists, and heralds there were who were his favorites; || 14 ||
As well as washermen of clothes and likewise leather-workers.
Likewise, charcoal-burners, hunters, and those who are fishermen; || 15 ||
And those who wear skulls as ornaments, and those who carry wooden planks.
And those men who are intent on sewing clothes and those who are builders of houses; || 16 ||
And whoever are potters, and whoever are beard-groomers;
And those who are scribes, accountants, as well as rice-grinders; || 17 ||
And whoever are makers of roasted flour, as well as those who subsist on the trade of vegetables;
Oil-pressers, perfumers, and those who perform the purification of sacred bathing sites. ||16||
Those who are skilled in the art of painting, and those people who are tailors.
O Lakṣmaṇa, there were charioteers, cooks, and eunuch-attendants as well.
The cowherds, those who roam the forests, and those who frequent the riverbanks.
Let them follow at their pleasure with herds of cows and herds of buffaloes.
And those who are guild-masters, as well as village and hamlet headmen.
Likewise, those who were forest-dwellers and those who roamed the mountains. || 21 ||
O Saumitri, all of these have been well-supported and well-honored by me.
Let them follow my son Bharata, who is devoted to his brother.
Thus addressed, he, by the command of the king, gave orders to all of them.
Having addressed Rāma and bowed their heads to him, they all departed from the city filled with joy. ||23||
Thus ends the two hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of the Retinue," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra. || 203 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
At that very time, however, Rāma heard that great news.
The retinue of Bharata was accompanied by the sound of conch shells and musical instruments. || 1 ||
The highly illustrious Bharata also arrived at the palace gate.
Having dismounted from his horse, he went on foot to the king.
Then he beheld Rāma seated upon a jeweled lion-throne.
Anointed with the most excellent, fragrant sandalwood paste.
Wearing a fine garment and adorned with all kinds of ornaments.
In splendor he was like the sun, and in beauty he was comparable to the moon.
In patience, he is equal to the earth; in anger, he is like the fire of cosmic destruction.
Equal to Bṛhaspati in intelligence and like Viṣṇu in prowess.
O Raghava, you are incomparable in truth, generosity, self-restraint, and virtue.
Accompanied by his domestic priests, ministers, and likewise by the subjects.
Having seen him, the illustrious Bharata prostrated his head upon the earth.
[He appointed] Bharata as the crown prince for Rāma, who was self-realized.
The righteous-minded doorkeeper announced [the arrival] of him who was accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa.
Then Rāma also rose and embraced Bharata by the neck.
And having smelled the crown of his head, he issued him this command.
But to Bharata, who was seated comfortably, Rāma spoke these words.
Having slain those sons of the Gandharvas, the two cities must be constructed.
On both banks of the Sindhu, however, [he established cities] for the sake of both his sons.
Then, O child, having consecrated his two sons in those two cities.
Having entrusted [the matter] to Yudhājit, you ought to return quickly. ||11||
O tiger among men, I do not wish to live without you.
Placing the duty of a Kshatriya foremost, you were sent there by me.
Therefore, go, O highly fortunate one; let there be no delay for you.
May there be well-being for you from those of the atmosphere and those of the earth as you go. || 13 ||
And likewise, O sinless one, from the divine beings in the midst of battle.
The guardians of the quarters, possessing blazing splendor, each established themselves in their respective directions.
May those who bear radiant bodies protect you always. || 15 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts;
The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the two Aśvins, the best of physicians. || 16 ||
The Bhṛgus, the Aṅgirases, and likewise the divisions of time.
Rivers, oceans, mountains, seas, and lakes. || 17 ||
Daityas, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
Likewise, all the wives of the gods and the mothers of the gods as well. || 18 ||
May weapons, missiles, and sacred scriptures bring you auspiciousness.
May they grant you victory, long life, and other enjoyments as well. || 19 ||
Having heard this benediction uttered by the king, he—
The wielder of the bow, having saluted Rāma’s feet with his head, [stood there].
Having departed from the royal palace, he went to the world as commanded by Rāma.
Resembling a peak of the Himalaya mountains, with a face radiant with beautiful fangs.
And the courtyard of the royal palace was being drenched with rut-fluid, O King.
And its flanks were also overrun by bees greedy for the nectar.
With its large ears, both firm and beautiful, it was indeed moved by compassion for the bees.
With its long tips and its path made by the eyes, it has fashioned a crest-ornament of horns.
Svāsana, Vyūḍhakumbha, as well as Udagra and Mahābala.
Wearing a golden garland of stars upon his head.
Likewise, when the bell was resonant, beautiful to behold, and captivating to the mind.
A variegated and beautiful rug, and a great banner of the kovidāra tree. || 25 ||
And there were Vaijayantī banners adorned with garlands of networks of small bells.
It was mounted by a wise and sagacious chief minister who was skilled in statesmanship. || 26 ||
Holding a golden goad with a sharp tip and a handle made of beryl.
And by another [arm] held at his hip, bearing an excellent tomara-weapon. || 27 ||
Likewise, it was consecrated by a knower of the gods with mantras that ensure victory.
The one of great splendor ascended while those who were victorious welcomed him with shouts of joy.
It has the form of a full moon’s orb, with a beautiful golden shaft.
Taking the umbrella, Lakṣmaṇa affectionately ascended it. || 29 ||
Having taken up two chowries that possessed a luster equal to the rays of the moon.
A pair of women, peerless in beauty on earth, had mounted it.
Having mounted that king of elephants, who was approaching Madalekhā.
He departed together with Gārgya, who was mounted upon a chariot, O Yādava.
O highly fortunate one, he followed him with a great fourfold army.
He was making the earth crowded with banners and standards. || 32 ||
Hawks, crows, herons, piśācas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas;
The attendants of that high-souled Bharata went before him. || 33 ||
Greedily longing for the flesh of the Gandharva's son, those who subsist on meat [seized him].
With the great sound of musical instruments and the chanting of bards.
Being fanned by a fragrant, favorable breeze, his mind was gladdened by the sight of the foremost auspicious objects. || 39 ||
He went out by way of the royal road, which was crowded with people.
The splendors of the radiant and the hearts of women—these two are difficult to master. (36)
Taking [it], the one of great splendor departed from the city.
Having gone from there for the distance of one krośa, on level ground and near water; || 37 ||
The camp, previously occupied, was filled with excellent trees.
Then Bharata entered, accompanied by highly skilled army commanders.
Having entered his own camp, that one of great splendor went to his quarters.
Having performed the auspicious rites of commencement, the Lord sat upon an excellent seat.
O Yādava, he dispatched all the people of the city and the countryside.
Then, after embracing Lakṣmaṇa, who was endowed with auspicious marks.
And having thus smelled him on the head, the knower of dharma sent him forth.
"And on the morrow, let the drum for my departure be beaten."
Let the guides go before, as well as those who descend from the trees.
And having likewise issued commands to the entire camp in that manner.
But in regions where there are no trees, let people plant trees.
As well as thorny trees and those that obstruct the path. || 43 ||
Go and cut them down today with sharp axes swiftly!
Likewise, let them dig wells for me in regions devoid of water. || 44 ||
And likewise, may they make the uneven regions along my path level.
And let them create the banks and the sandbanks of the rivers as well. || 45 ||
So that there may be no jostling with people as one travels on the road.
Let those who increase the joy of victory go at the head of the army.
And Nīla, Nakradeva, Vasumān, and likewise the Munis.
In the middle of the expedition was Gāndhāra Jayanābha, fierce in battle. || 47 ||
Let Suśīla and Kāmapāla go forth, armored and accompanied by their army.
I shall protect the flank of the army as I see fit. || 48 ||
I shall go with my army for the sake of the king's victory.
Let the guides look for a place with abundant fodder and fuel. || 49 ||
And where there is water and level ground, there let my army encamp.
Having thus given his command, Bharata lived there according to his pleasure.
And there he slept through that enchanting night during the heat of the summer season.
While that descendant of Raghu slept there, that auspicious night passed away for him of undiminished spirit.
Adorned with the full moon as her ornament, she appeared radiant in the month of Jyeṣṭha, which was eager for battle.
Thus ends the two hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Bharata’s Departure," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When the night had turned to dawn, the drum was struck.
O Great King, there was a great clamor from the procession of Bharata. || 1 ||
By that great sound, the people in the camp were awakened.
Having performed their necessary duties, O King, they were filled with haste.
They called out to one another in haste for the purpose of departing.
They began to endure the beautiful palatial residences. || 3 ||
They were large, very pleasing, and fashioned from spun wool.
And they made them easy to carry, O king of kings, without any effort.
Then they caused them to be mounted upon young camels and donkeys.
Meanwhile, others hurriedly mounted the finest ox-carts as well as elephants.
Various kinds of vessels and soft beds as well.
And the principal seats, as well as whatever utensils were in the kitchen.
And drink, as well as fodder, and various kinds of weapons.
The armor for the horses and whatever implements of craftsmanship there were.
And various kinds of wealth, O King, as well as all necessary implements.
But while the vessel was being loaded, let the camels be led away.
A tumultuous noise was heard, along with the harsh cries of donkeys.
Of the elephants being yoked together with the horses and chariots.
The tumultuous sound of musical instruments being struck was heard.
O King, by the sound of the elephants' bells and their trumpeting cries.
From the neighing of the horses, a tumultuous sound arose.
Taking up his departure drum, he struck it right away.
He went at the head of the procession with great honor, accompanied by kettledrums.
And taking their wares, the merchants departed in haste.
And others, desiring to take [them], were likewise provided with water and level ground.
And the foremost men went to the places of the chief leaders. || 13 ||
But the chief officers of the kitchen and the swift messengers likewise departed in haste.
Likewise, upon comfortable vehicles and delightful mules.
Having placed the women upon it, the joyful people departed at dawn.
And other women were mounted [on elephants], like female elephants with their trunks raised and covered by sunshades. ||15||
She was guarded by chamberlains wearing cloaks and turbans, and likewise protected by eunuchs.
O king of kings, they departed with their armies, preceded by songs and instrumental music.
They gratified the wretched, the blind, the miserable, and the helpless with wealth.
The wives of the kings, adorned with divine ornaments, [were like] the consorts of the lords of men. || 17 ||
Likewise, other men with girded swords and quivers [stood ready].
Having set fire to the thatched huts, they departed with hurried minds.
Bharata also ascended a palanquin adorned with jewels.
The one of great splendor went forth, preceded by the sound of musical instruments. || 19 ||
The campsite was empty and crowded with circles of vultures.
In an instant, it became crowded with many flesh-eating demons.
It was joined with the bodily limbs of elephants, camels, donkeys, and horses.
It was strewn with broken vessels and covered with the limbs of bodies.
It was crowded with many flesh-eating demons and filled with heaps of dried cow dung.
With pits located in the kitchen area, filled with burnt earth.
It was filled with mud and lotus-buds, and swarming with flies.
Having abandoned him, all of Bharata’s soldiers departed.
As that army set forth, the oxen were overcome with fatigue.
They diligently caused the Nāgas, who were seated, to rise up. ||24||
Some, terrified by camels, were struck down by donkeys.
Those best of men once again loaded the goods onto the carts. || 25 ||
In the crossings of rivers, some [beheld] buffaloes scorched by the rays of the sun.
The people struck those who were already seated, along with their burdens.
Some [fled] on mules, terrified by the trumpeting sounds of the elephants.
O King, they carefully grasped the reins of the women who had mounted the chariots.
Some men were thrown to the ground by horses terrified of the elephants.
With their legs fashioned like the necks of horses for the purpose of resting their knees. || 28 ||
And then the horses became bewildered, and the riders' shields fell away.
O Yādava, some there, having attacked with speed, seized [them].
Likewise, some men took rest in the shade of trees.
Some performed their meal-taking on the banks of the rivers.
Some [were struck] by those who had risen up, closely following terrified horses.
With great effort, they seized those horses with swift movements like those of piñjala birds.
Some [beheld] herds of deer fleeing, terrified by the army camp.
Having assailed him with speed, they struck him with arrows, O scion of the Yadu lineage.
Some made fodder of it, and some made fuel.
Likewise, it was doubled by others, and similarly, there was the sound of kettledrums. || 33 ||
O scion of the Yadu clan, they quickly abandoned their fatigue from the journey.
Some [saw] a great bamboo pole raised high at the forefront of the market street. ||34||
Seeing it with its banner, the men thought, "We have arrived."
And some repeatedly composed Vedic meters for their companions. ||35||
O Indra among kings, for those who have gone before him, out of a desire to attain a stable position.
Some, seeing their own cloth tents, departed in haste. || 36 ||
Seeing that the grass had been rolled up, others departed quickly from their homes.
O best of kings, some of their houses there were flooded.
There, the men saw deeds already accomplished and those currently being performed.
And likewise, with drums being rested and mats being prepared; || 38 ||
And with houses being constructed, fashioned from cotton, wool, and straw;
That camp of the one of auspicious deeds shone brightly, O great king. || 39 ||
O lord of the earth, for those men who purify the ground with a weapon, [there is no sin].
The bodies of those whose forms were overcome by passion shone with a lack of luster.
And likewise, people standing nearby with leather bags filled with water.
They are seen running about, busily engaged in cleaning the house. || 41 ||
Others, O King, even sprinkle water upon their grass huts.
For those who were tormented and desired coolness, there was water emerging from the mouths of leather bags.
It was completely overwhelmed on all sides by the smoke of the incense.
His army became as if enveloped by mist. || 43 ||
O delighter of the Yadus, for those who have laid down their burdens and are self-controlled.
They sprinkled the backs [of the horses] with cow dung and water. || 44 ||
It emerged for the purpose of being stepped upon by donkeys, camels, and oxen. || 45 ||
Indeed, a multitude of many thousands was seen in Bharata's camp.
Others, skilled in the management of horses, unyoked the steeds from the chariots.
They gradually consoled those who had laid down their wares.
Dust from the earth was raised by the turning of the horses. || 47 ||
O Indra among kings, he ascended the mountain, which was pale and reddish-brown like a pigeon.
And others stationed the horses at a place near water. || 48 ||
Likewise, O King, others formed ranks in the shadows of the eaves.
Likewise, some stationed the horses beneath canopies.
Having given grass to the horses, some people partook of food.
And others by the thousands created the shadows of palm trees for the nāgas.
And excellent canopies for the purpose of alleviating the heat of the sun.
O Lord of Men, having obtained water, the Nāgas went to the bathing pool.
They carried the jars, covered and wrapped in their own garments, to their own abode.
At a distance from the camp, they tethered the royal elephants.
O Great King, men fasten their elephants to hitching posts made from great trees.
Having taken [them], the cowherds were there at a distance from the camp.
They separated the herds of cows and the herds of buffaloes as they pleased.
And likewise, O lord of men, they brought products of the cow to the camp.
And the marketplace street of the bazaar, adorned with all kinds of merchandise.
The men there beheld it as if it were another Ayodhyā. || 55 ||
O lord of men, these are the emblems of all physicians and their respective positions.
And the footprints of Bharata’s sandals were seen upon the mountain pass.
By the heroic and high-souled Vijaya, the commander-in-chief.
The encampment of the army has been established in accordance with the treatises.
The illustrious Bharata entered, accompanied by his fourfold army.
Followed by his two heroic sons, O delighter of the Yadus.
And by the hero Puṣkara, and by the high-souled Takṣaka.
Likewise, by the leaders of the army and others, such as the sūtas, māgadhas, and bards. || 59 ||
With the sound of conch trumpets and the resonance of kettledrums.
They arrived at the vicinity of the archway at the gate of Bharata’s house.
O delighter of the Yadus, those who were the foremost among the powerful became the guardians of the quarters.
Having abandoned the middle path, the high-minded one entered.
Those [princes] were being proclaimed by bards according to their names, deeds, and noble exploits.
With a nod of his head, Bharata sent them back to their own dwellings.
Then, having dismissed the leaders of the army, he entered his own home, which was endowed with every prosperity.
The soldiers of Bharata were exhausted from the two-yojana journey. || 63 ||
They entered their respective dwellings and took to their beds.
Bharata also, having entered his excellent residence, remained there according to his pleasure.
He dwelt there, O Great King, possessing a splendor equal to that of the king of the gods.
O protector of the earth, by this sequence, the righteous-souled one [practiced] day after day.

Even as he was traveling, he reached the river Gaṅgā, which flows through the three paths; she had acquired her splendor from the washing away of the fine sandalwood paste resting upon the full breasts of celestial women, and her upper garment of cool water was increased by the melting snow due to the heat of the summer sun.
Thus ends the two hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Departure," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. || 205 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, that descendant of Raghu established his camp on the bank of the Ganges.
Then they constructed water-pavilions on the Ganges for Bharata.
In the same way, O lord of men, [he honored] the leaders of the forces according to their preeminence.
And his soldier, having reached that celestial river, [remained there]. || 2 ||
He considered his birth to have achieved its purpose and likewise abandoned all weariness.
Filled with great joy, he bathed and drank milk to his heart's content.
There, those who were fond of horses caused the horses to be bathed.
And likewise, the mahāmātras caused the elephants to bathe.
The river Ganges was plunged into by many thousands of elephants as they bathed.
That very [region] shone with the Kirāta territories, just as it did with its stones.
Having seen the high ministers who had risen up, [he acted] under the pretext of a ritual sprinkling.
Some played with water-skins, while others entered [the water] using their arms alone.
Having reached the Gaṅgā, Bharata’s soldiers were filled with joy.
Bharata also, having likewise bathed and performed the worship of the deities, [proceeded].
The one of great splendor performed the ancestral rite (śrāddha) and likewise bestowed gifts.
Having bestowed great gifts there, O Yādava, he issues his command.
"Let the artisans build delightful gabled mansions for me."
And at night, for the purpose of lighting lamps, they were placed by the hundreds and thousands.
"Let boats be brought for my army to cross over."
Let hundreds of leather boats and rafts likewise be prepared.
Having reached the northern shore, let your encampment be established accordingly.
May people go to the further shore within the interval between sunrise and sunset.
Having understood this, Bharata lived according to his pleasure.
O King, the sun extends its rays everywhere.
He departed from that place out of sight, solely out of shame before Bharata.
And in an instant, the western direction became like the hue of the tip of a lotus petal. ||13||
When the sun had set, she was colored by the glow of twilight.
Then, however, when everything was pervaded by darkness, nothing at all could be discerned.
He saw the gabled houses, previously constructed by the command of Bharata, which were provided with lamps.
They cast [the offerings] into the waters of the Jahnavī, which were encircled by garlands of banners.
And likewise, by the soldiers and the principal officers of Bharata, thousands of lamp-trees were cast individually into the waters of the Ganges. ||16||
That Gaṅgā, garlanded with lamps, had her form illuminated by the riverbanks.
She laughed with a foam-like laugh, like the beloved of the sky [the lightning] with its tongue.
With beautiful lamp-trees, lamps emerged from within the water.
Likewise, the Gaṅgā appears as if blazing due to the reflections cast by the waves. || 18 ||
Thus did those men sport there on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
O King, they set out directly by various kinds of boats during the night itself.
Having beheld the lake of the sky with the moon as its royal swan, people [are filled with wonder].
Being thus attacked, they fell asleep at midnight, overcome by slumber.
The army, resembling a forest of lotuses, was fast asleep at the rising of the moon.
In that manner, he caused the mass of the sun's rays to be perceived.
Then they pulled the boats, just as helmsmen pull their own vessels.
And then they caused their entire army to cross to the further shore by means of Taraṇī. || 22 ||
The ship shone with networks of small bells and with banners.
Struck by the buttocks of the helmsmen, they carried the army to the further shore.
Some were filled with vessels, and others were filled with people.
Likewise, others were filled with horses, as well as with cattle, donkeys, and camels.
Then some boats, carrying elephants, went to the further shore.
Likewise, boats filled with women whose eyes were like lotus petals were provided. || 25 ||
O lord of men, celestial palaces are seen shining upon the waters of the Gaṅgā.
They were accompanied by excellent helmsmen and surrounded by staff-bearing men.
Others likewise went forth once more for the sake of delivering the world.
Some went by means of leather boats, and others by well-secured rafts. || 27 ||
They departed, taking with them their vessels and, in some cases, their water-skins.
The horses were being dragged by men mounted upon leather water-skins.
Some went to the further shore by means of their arms, O lord of men.
Others went to the further shore, held fast by the reins.
The horses were swiftly driven by others standing on boats, using the arms of the king as oars.
And there were herds of buffaloes and cows, O delighter of the Yadus.
Together with the cowherd boys, they went to the further shore by means of their arms.
Herds of camels and donkeys were being ferried across by means of their arms. || 31 ||
They returned again and again, and a great clamor arose there.
O best of the Yadus, for a man who has crossed over and is helping others cross over...
A terrible clamor arose on both banks as well.
The highly resplendent Bharata also bathed and offered oblations into the sacrificial fire.
O Yādava, having worshipped Viṣṇu in the form of a fish upon a cloth-painting, [one attains success].
Then he should cause the Brahmins to pronounce blessings with gifts of cows, garments, and wealth.
Having worshipped the goddess Jāhnavī with perfumes, garlands, and unguents.
Then he honored the best of the twice-born once again.
With cows, horses, as well as gold coins, garments, and likewise with fragrances;
Then he ascended the boat, which was covered with white woolen blankets.
It was spread with networks of tinkling bells and adorned with garlands of flags and banners.
But when Bharata had embarked, the boat was struck on its buttocks by the helmsman.
O King, that boat, resembling a celestial chariot, reached the further shore.
Then, having reached the further shore, he was accompanied by his entire army.
O King, he dwelt right there, just like the Lord of the Gods in heaven.
The Goddess, who dwells upon the slope of Mahādeva’s matted locks, her coolness increased by contact with the moon.
Having crossed over, King Bharata, whose splendor was equal to that of Śakra, led her to his residence. || 39 ||
Thus ends the two hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Descent of the Gaṅgā," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When Bharata had crossed the Gaṅgā, the girdle of the sky, [the people]...
Another Kuru king entered his camp. || 1 ||
Accompanied by a fourfold army resembling the ocean in its vastness.
And the lord of the Kirātas was a king named Damana. || 2 ||
He was seen accompanied by many thousands of forces belonging to the Gandharvas.
Having honored him as was fitting, Bharata, who is devoted to righteousness, [did so]. || 3 ||
He reached the Yamunā, the daughter of the Sun, which destroys all sins.
The meritorious sister of Yama, Nīlamālā, who is captivating to the mind.
For wherever one performs a śrāddha at a river, O lord of men, [it is efficacious].
One obtains inexhaustible fruit and rejoices in the vault of heaven. ||5||
Where, having bathed on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and having worshipped the daughter of the Sun, [one attains the fruit].
He is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of the gods. || 6 ||
At the time when the sun has not yet risen, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
Having bathed in that [tirtha] and worshipped Dharmarāja with water mixed with sesame seeds, one attains [the fruit].
One does not fall into an evil rebirth and indeed uplifts one's own family.
Indeed, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, at any river whatsoever.
Having bathed in all the waters of a river, one is liberated from sins.
But Yamunā, specifically, was the sister of Yama.
And having bathed in the waters of the Yamunā, he offered libations to the ancestors and the gods.
He does not fall into an evil rebirth, nor does he go to the world of the gods.
Having reached that Yamunā, it was just like the water of the Gaṅgā.
Having stayed there in that manner, Bharata likewise crossed the great river.
Of the high-souled Bharata, who had crossed over the Yamunā.
Then King Suratha entered the camp of the Matsyas.
Gorasena was the leader of the Śālvas, and Prabhadraka was the leader of the Śibis.
Together with those kings, he proceeded to Kurukṣetra.
For this purpose this ancient verse circulates in the world:
Even the dust particles of Kurukṣetra, when stirred by the wind, [attain liberation]. || 14 ||
Even those who have performed evil deeds are led to the supreme destination.
O lord of men, those who die in the meritorious Samantapañcaka [attain the highest state].
Having reached the celestial realm, they all shine in heaven like gods.
O Indra among kings, there is a holy ford (tīrtha) renowned throughout the three worlds where Sannīti resides. || 16 ||
It is renowned as "Sannīti" precisely because it brings together the various sacred fords (tīrthas).
Whatever sacred fords there are on earth, including the oceans and the lakes; || 17 ||

Having heard that, he then ascended the palace, which was as white as snow.
