Then, a certain soldier from Bharata's camp [spoke].
He struck his palm against his palm by chance for the sake of producing a sound.
Then all the soldiers raised a great clamor with the clapping of their palms.
O tiger among men, at that time they made him ascend to heaven. || 105 ||
And at that time, O bull among men, a wind blew from that direction.
At that very time, however, the radiant King of Madra [arrived].
Having ascended the excellent palace, he then learned of Bharata.
By the light of the lamps, by prosperity, and by the expansion of the palace. || 107 ||
Then that king went forth, laughing at the multitude of soldiers.
I shall show my strength to Bharata through a stratagem alone. || 108 ||
Having set fire to a handful of grass, every person in the camp [acted].
Taking it in his hand, let him indeed utter a joyful shout of triumph. || 109 ||
When the wise king had spoken thus, [the army] in his camp [was stirred].
In an instant, every person came to have a thunderbolt in their hand.
The camp of the King of Madra was like a second sky.
At that time, it became variegated with stars by means of the men holding torches in their hands.
That boundless flood of troops was surrounded by men with firebrands in their hands.
Having seen this, the righteous scion of Raghu’s lineage experienced supreme joy. || 112 ||
Hearing the war-cries and shouts of joy, he was filled with delight.
When that fire had been extinguished and its roar had subsided, || 113 ||
The drums were beaten separately in the camps of the various kings.
And then there were delightful musical instruments known by their names, as well as various types of cymbals.
O Great King, because of that, there was a great clamor.
It became a source of joy for the high-souled Bharata. || 115 ||
Then the illustrious one consulted with Yudhājit for just a moment.
Having eaten together with him, she slept upon an excellent bed.
With sweet and beautiful singing, and with the sound of the lute and the flute. || 116 ||
White as snow, variegated with excellent garlands, provided with a canopy below, and enchanting.
That one of great majesty slept through the night upon the coils of the lord of serpents, just as the conqueror of Madhu [Vāsudeva] does.
Thus ends the two hundred and ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Occurrence of Battle," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, having heard the drum of the summons, the daughters of Śailūṣa [approached].
They all approached that king, who was like a stage-player, having gathered together. || 1 ||
Namuci, Kāmapāla, Gaveṣaṇa, and Sudarśana.
Vīrabāhu, Subāhu, Vāyuvega, and Suvarcas. ||2||
Nikumbha, Kumbha by name, Balāka, and likewise Balaka;
Harikeśa, Mahojas, and Sūryaraśmiprabhaṃkara. || 3 ||
Vṛndāraka, Jyautiṣika, Dṛḍhasyu, and Aparājita.
Kumuda, Kumudāpīḍa, Vasunātha, and Sulocana. || 4 ||
Candrāpīḍa, Gadī, Maulī, Kinnara, Ajagara, and Ruha.
Kesarī, Varavāṇa, Bhānurāgāvaha, and Rayi. ||5||
Ekalavya, Viśāla, Kalaviṅka, and Kalāpriya.
Bhīmanāda, Mahānāda, Vāsuki, Panasa, and Gada. || 6 ||
Candravarmā, Mahāvarmā, Vasuṣeṇa, and Agrajāraka.
These and other Gandharvas were the sons of the lord Śailūṣa.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, they were adorned with celestial sandalwood paste.
Then they entered the assembly hall and took their seats upon costly thrones.
That assembly hall, adorned with jewels, was guarded by the sons of Śailūṣa.
O King, she shone like the autumnal night adorned with variegated stars.
When they had all sat down together, the actor then spoke to them.
All of Gārgya’s speech, as well as his own inference, was exactly so.
O lord of men, having then heard of that assault by humans, they...
With their minds filled with fury and rage, they performed various kinds of gestures.
Those sons of the Gandharva king, weeping out of anger, shed tears like rain.
Having the luster of a cloud at the end of the eon of dissolution, she is like a flash of lightning seen with the eyes.
Namuci bore a face colored with both anger and passion.
From the northwestern direction, there arose a sound indicating a great battle.
The three-pronged frown situated on the forehead of Kāmapāla shone forth.
Like the Gaṅgā falling upon the Himalayas, she descended by means of three cascades.
It is dark at the end of the bright fortnight, colored by the passion of anger.
But Kumuda and Āpīḍa had eyes that became copper-colored at twilight. || 15 ||
With a body overcome by anger, Kumuda was as radiant as a white water-lily.
In an instant, he assumed a form resembling a red lotus.
The beautiful face of Candrāpīḍa resembled something darkened by the smoke of his anger.
She bore the form of the moon when it is gathered by thin clouds at night.
Then the face of the Sun was covered by the smoke of his wrathful sighs.
O best of the Yadus, it became like the sun during an eclipse. || 18 ||
His face and limbs were turned smoky-grey by the smoke produced from the crushing of charcoal.
At that time, Sudarśana truly acquired a name that was consistent with his actual nature.
With the impetus of his search, his nature blazed like the interior of a fire.
The destruction of the king was indicated by that very shower of stars.
By the dust arising from the friction of jewels caused by the blows of the arms of heroic men.
Then it yawned in an inappropriate place, as if by wrath personified.
The clashing of Subāhu’s arms produced a sound like the roar of a thunderbolt.
Deep as a thunderclap, it foretold the death of kings. || 22 ||
The earth was scarred by his feet, which moved with a great speed like the force of the wind.
O protector of the earth, it split open, foreboding the fear of destruction.
Adorned with perspiration born of exertion and the bristling of hair.
Suvarcā held the forehead-plate upon the surface of her brow.
With his limbs perspiring, he was tawny like a golden pillar.
Kumbhanābha, however, became like Wrath personified.
[He was] adorned with a garland of whorls of hair like flames of fire well-issued forth.
The Sun-god imitated the form of Hari in his man-lion (nṛsiṃha) incarnation.
The entire circle of Gandharvas had transferred itself to his body through perspiration.
From his head, Viśvarūpadhara laughed at Janārdana.
Those sons of the Gandharva king had their minds carried away by fury.
Then, O protector of the earth, they all became especially distinguished. || 28 ||
Thus, having observed the anger of his sons and recalled the words of the family priest, [he reflected].
That king, his face terrifying with his bitten lips, became exceedingly filled with wrath. || 29 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Disturbance in the Assembly of the Gandharvas," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. || 210 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having seen that the mind of the Gandharva king was agitated by anger.
The Gandharvas, proud of the strength of their own arms, said to that king: || 1 ||
Aparājita said:
O King, Aśoka offers everything at the hands of the heroic warriors.
Therefore, death by valor is what pleases me for the descendants of Raghu. || 2 ||
Nikumbha said:
O Lord, this wrath that has arisen within me toward the descendants of Kakutstha—
The entire world, though indestructible, will undergo destruction. || 3 ||
The Kinnara said:
That Lakṣmī whose limbs were smeared with the saffron of the blood of enemies.
Even though she is beloved, she does not inspire affection in the minds of the wise.
Vasunābha said:
Arising from the destruction of the hosts of enemies by the edge of the sword.
O King, what need have men of virtuous character for that prosperity which does not [benefit them]? (5)
The python said:
The adornment consists in the attainment of prosperity that remains close to the hosts of unconquered enemies.
Among those [forms of adversity], that which is not adorned by prosperity is the most excellent.
R̥bhu said:
The harsh and brave shine like uplifted breasts.
And for heroes and for breasts, delight consists in being held in contempt by others.
Keśa said:
The exaltation of the radiant ones is worthy of homage throughout the three worlds.
Just as every person rejoices when the sun rises. || 8 ||
Paravāraṇa said:
The trees were playfully uprooted by the lion, who was preeminent in strength.
Elephants, though resembling mountain peaks, were unable to stand before him. || 9 ||
Ābhāvaha said:
There is never any quelling of that splendor which [overpowers] the splendor of all splendors.
Of what use is he who is born in vain, causing only old age for his mother?
Ekalavya said:
When his name is proclaimed, enemies do not remain because of fear.
With the complexion of their faces turned pale, what compassion can there be for his life?
Viśāla said:
For those greedy for union with Lakṣmī and for heroes, [the desire] arises from battle.
That very Fame quickly becomes her friend, bringing about union.
Kalipriya said:
Sprinkled with the blood of enemies and with the tears from the eyes of enemy women.
For one whose fame has not been sprinkled abroad, what desire can there be for life?
Bhīmanāda said:
The sun has indeed pervaded the entire world with its very radiance.
He places his footstep upon the heads of all.
Mahādharma said:
She who sports by placing her footstep upon the head of the enemy.
May your fame, grasping the hand offered by the poet, ascend to heaven.
Vāsuki said:
[She who] has split open the island in the midst [of the ocean] where the elephant slain by Māyā was located.
Having pierced the earth, the maiden entered the surface of the ground, known as Vasudhātala.
Panasa said:
Of you, whose face blossoms with the union of the Goddess of Fortune who has destroyed all enemies.
Let my fame spread swiftly through the ten directions like a flash of lightning. ||17||
Gada said:
By the nāgas, who had the appearance of water-laden clouds and were raining down gifts.
In this battle that has pervaded the quarters of the sky, may my sword act as lightning. || 18 ||
Mahānāda said:
The multitude of elephants was terrified by my lion’s roar.
Strike down the strength of the enemies with your straight-jointed arrows.
Vasu said:
The dust kicked up by the feet of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
You shall see [the battlefield] turned to tranquility on all sides by the blood of your enemies.
Vṛndāraka said:
In those [teeth] which shone like pearls situated within the ocean of an elephant's frontal globes.
O King, while swords are still at hand, who could endure defeat? (21)
The astrologer said:
Upon the two curved tips of her creeper-like eyebrows, which were arched like the bow of Kāma.
And while bows are at hand, who could endure defeat? || 22 ||
Dṛḍhasyu said:
O King, he whose five arrows are sharp is truly one who possesses honor.
What else need be done for him by his partisans in battle? (23)
Candrāpīḍa said:
Of what use are weapons to those endowed with strength, who possess beautiful, staff-like arms?
By those who cause the interruption of battle for those whose anger has been instantly aroused. || 24 ||
Gadhi said:
Let my swords remain useless, laughing loudly at the ruin of those who have already been consumed.
Who, even if reduced to a single staff-like arm, would endure such humiliation? || 25 ||
The kalaviṅka said:
From the great ocean of the enemy host, agitated by Mount Mandara in the form of my arm.
O Lord of the World, enjoy the prosperity that has arisen for you for a long time.
The elephant said:
Of what use are weapons to the virtuous, and of what use are weapons to wicked men?
For the weapons of some are indeed ineffective against others. || 27 ||
Bālaka said:
When Hari was struck by the tusks of Indra’s elephant, which had been uprooted by one who was weak;
"By my [grace], may you today become the king of the gods and the lord of the three worlds."
The worship of the deities had been lost, the ritual offerings were absent, and it was in a state of extreme decay.
O Lord of great splendor, today even the three worlds have been created by me.
Harika said:
Today, however, by means of Hara’s bull, [the earth] has been seized from the buffalo of Kīnāśa.
And with the tail of the serpent Śeṣa, I shall cause Ayodhyā to be carried away.
Mahodara said:
In this world of moving and unmoving beings, the sun of Māra has been cast down by me.
Behold Yama’s buffalo treading upon the horses of the sun. || 31 ||
Sūrya said:
By me, the entire assembly of deities throughout the three worlds has been established.
Behold today the elephant of Maghavan, torn apart by the lion of Durgā.
Prabhāsa said:
Having cast off the thirst for water, they have drawn forth the lords of wealth.
Let the hosts of gods, their luster destroyed, bow down to you this very day.
Bhadraka said:
When this triple world has been rendered empty of Skanda and Śaṅkara by me, [what will you do?]
May Śikhin consume today the serpents that serve as ornaments for Śarva.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
He gazed upon the sons of the Gandharva king, whose beautiful faces were clouded by the darkness of anger.
Then the priest named Nāḍāyana, being of undaunted spirit, spoke to the king.
Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Thundering of the Gandharvas," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra. 211.
Nādāyana said:
Having ascertained two by means of one, bring the three under control by means of four.
Having conquered the five and mastered the six, having abandoned the seven, be happy. || 1 ||
O King, by means of a single wisdom, a person [discerns] the duality of what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
But he who, having reached a firm decision, carries out his task therein—he is a wise man.
Whether it be a neutral party, a friend, or even an enemy, one should act out of the gravity of the task at hand.
Having understood both the place and the time, one should indeed proceed with skillful means.
And the means are proclaimed to be conciliation, sowing dissension, and bribery.
And here, the fourth means is punishment; it is a resort only when there is no other way.
By him who, desiring victory, first achieved mastery over the five senses.
To me, his victory over the three worlds does not seem far off.
Having conquered the five senses, one should take refuge in the six virtues.
Having correctly understood the relative strength and weakness of both oneself and the other.
O lord of men, he by whom the seven royal faults have been abandoned.
O King, his accomplishments and virtues come to fruition in due time.
Hunting, vehicles, excellent women, men, and speech.
The corruption of wealth and likewise violence by means of punishment. || 8 ||
O King, the descendants of Raghu were abandoned there by the faults of the monarch.
Those who know the distinction between qualities and their substratum do not find delight in such a physical form. || 9 ||
We have been addressed with conciliatory words by Bharata, even though he stands at the head of a great army.
May that very thing which was first undertaken be pleasing to you.
If we were to go to the mountain by conciliating Bharata with gentle words.
O highly fortunate one, O sinless one, that would be for the welfare of you and your entire lineage.
Having brought about the total extermination of the kings who dwell among the people, by you—
Without cause, a great enmity was created with the kings.
By dwelling among people, we would suffer only insignificance.
And there is repeated association with humans as well as conflict with them again and again. || 13 ||
Neither agriculture nor trade is of any use to us people.
Therefore, leaving this land along with our people, we shall go to the mountain peak.
And having regard for place and time, as well as for peace and war.
And he who acts after having understood the result, O King, is a wise man. || 15 ||
Land, gold, and allies—these three are the bases for war.
It was our own assumption that Mount Meru is a mountain of gold. || 16 ||
"O destroyer of enemies, we have no need for gold at this time."
Since we have no agriculture, the earth is therefore useless to us. (17)
Therefore, O lord of men, seek to win over Bharata as a friend through conciliation.
Having made the Raghu dynasty his friend, he took up residence on the Himalaya mountain.
Invisible to the armies of the gods, may you enjoy happiness for a long time.
"You ought not to consider Bharata as merely a human being. (19)
For the sake of subduing the wicked, Janārdana manifested in four forms.
O King, he was born in the lineage of Raghu as the son of Daśaratha.
The highly illustrious Rāma was born as a partial incarnation of Vāsudeva.
And Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, was born from a portion of Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Likewise, Bharata, who was devoted to righteousness, was born from a portion of Pradyumna.
And from a portion of Aniruddha was born Śatrughna, who possessed exceedingly great strength.
There, by Rāma, the lion among the descendants of Raghu, whose deeds are performed without effort, [the world was protected].
Rāvaṇa, the terror of all living beings, was slain in battle.
And Meghanāda was repelled in battle by Lakṣmaṇa.
And the wicked Rākṣasa Lavaṇa was slain by Śatrughna. || 24 ||
I consider the high-souled Bharata to possess a truly distinguished nature.
By him that Rākṣasa dwelling in Laṅkā, Mālin, was formerly slain.
This very Bharata is Viṣṇu, who has come to the field of battle for you.
He who is ever established in the welfare of the gods, with his intellect intent upon the destruction of the lords of the Daityas.
Go quickly with that immeasurable Janārdana, O noble-souled one! 27.

Thus ends the two hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of Nādāyana’s Instruction to Śailūṣa," within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara, in the words of Nādāyana. 212.
The actor said:
How was Sumālī formerly struck down in battle by Viṣṇu?
Cut through this doubt of mine; it is heard that he is possessed of great strength.
Nāḍāyana said:
O tiger among kings, this story was told in the past by the wise Agastya.
O hero, it was told to Rāma; listen as I recite it to you. ||2||
Long ago, when Vṛtra had been slain, the Daityas were left without a leader.
Having made the ocean their fortress, they indeed slaughter the people at night.
Having assembled with all the gods, he likewise could not be slain by others.
Then Agastya was urged to drink the waters of the ocean.
O King, the sage Agastya was then greatly delighted by the performance of the divine rites.
Having drunk it, O Indra among kings, he rendered that reservoir of water devoid of water. || 5 ||
And the Daityas were slain by the gods in a waterless reservoir.
Then, on one occasion, Vindhya spoke to the sun and the moon.
O illustrious ones, leaving Meru, come and circumambulate me.
Then those two said to Vindhya: "O Mountain, come under our control."
By him the path has been made for us, by whom this world was created.
Having heard this, Vidhni performed austerities before the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Then, day by day, he attained a height equal to the flight of an arrow.
Then, after a few days, having covered the southern direction.
He stood blocking the path of both the sun and the moon.
Thereupon, O best of kings, the entire world of mortals became blind.
Then, impelled by the words of the god, Agastya of great asceticism [set forth].
Having gone, he then said to Vindhya: "I am going on a pilgrimage."
Become short for my sake, so that I may go forth in happiness.
Then, having understood the power of Agastya, that great mountain...
Agastya also then quickly went to a short stature and departed.
"Having abandoned the southern region, I have not yet returned. (13)
O Acala, you shall remain short in stature along with your sons and wife for that long.
Having spoken thus, he [addressed] the Vindhya mountain along with its wives, offspring, and kinsmen.
He went toward the southern direction, and the Grandfather spoke to him.
O Great Brahmin, this auspicious and great task for the sake of the gods has been accomplished by you.
Therefore, I grant you a place outside the path of Vaiśvānara.
There, you shall possess a divine body, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot.
Adorn the southern direction, accompanied by both sunrise and sunset.
Upon your rising, there is clarity, coolness, and freedom from poison in the waters.
O you of stainless wisdom, it shall indeed belong to you alone through my grace.
Rejoicing in the autumn, go to your rest in the spring.
Endowed with the power of irresistible will, wander thus over the entire earth.
As long as you remain in the form of Pradhāna, together with your wife, children, and kinsmen. || 19 ||
The Vindhya mountain shall remain standing as long as it has not been traversed.
But when he is endowed with a body of irresistible power (prākāmya) and established anywhere at all— || 1.213.20 ||
The great mountain Vindhya will no longer increase in height while you are present.
And the evil-minded Ilvala was likewise [killed] by his brother who had assumed the form of a ram. || 21 ||
When he feeds the Brahmins after the twice-born have already eaten;
But Vātāpi, having split open the belly, would emerge once again. || 22 ||
While he was thus slaughtering them, what was done by you, O Brāhmaṇa?
I am pleased by that refuge and by the paralyzing of the Vindhya mountains.
O Brahmin, because you have reached the autumn season at the time of your new emergence.
O best of the twice-born, by my grace you shall receive worship in the world.
And those who shall worship you with perfumes, garlands, fruits, and unbroken grains;
And with curd, gold, jewels, and abundant supreme food. || 25 ||
With full jars, along with kūṣmāṇḍa gourds, umbrellas, sandals, and staffs.
With a cow, a bull, edible offerings, garments, and gold. || 26 ||
And for one year, he may also [subsist] by the renunciation of even a single fruit.
By means of worshiping the foremost of Brahmins and by proclaiming your deeds. || 27 ||
They shall always obtain sons, wealth, and indeed good health.
As well as supreme longevity in this world and invincibility against enemies.
Good fortune, abundant desires, and likewise the increase of dharma.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished right there. || 29 ||
Likewise, the great ascetic Agastya also reached that place.
By whom hundreds of sacrifices were performed and likewise great austerity was practiced.
By means of that very ascetic power, he created Lopāmudrā, who was sweet-spoken.
Likewise, he [spoke] of the daughter of the King of Vidarbha as his lawful wife.
Dṛḍhasyu was his son, and he was an ascetic of great austerity.
Pramucu, Mumucu, and Tanmucu were also there, O one of great asceticism. || 32 ||
Likewise, the learned Svastyātreya was the disciple of that high-souled one.
An impenetrable armor was given, as well as two inexhaustible quivers.
And he gave those two exceedingly powerful bows to Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
And he was indeed joined with a terrible splendor belonging to Viṣṇu.
Even in hundreds of years, a person cannot fully recount his deeds by means of their actions.
He is unable to act, even when Rāvaṇa possesses the power of irresistible will.
The sage went quickly to Ayodhyā to see Rāghava.
Beholding him arrived, Rāghava honored him.
With water for the feet, the respectful offering, water for sipping, and all other presentations of royal honors.
Having been thus honored by him, he then engaged in auspicious conversations there.
Then, at the conclusion of a certain conversation, Rāghava asked him a question.
Listen to that which was said by Viṣṇu regarding the slaying of Mālinī. || 38 ||
That which was spoken by the delighter of the Raghus, whose power is like that of the moon, the sun, and fire.
O sage, understand this very account of the most terrible slaying of the lord of the hosts of Rākṣasas.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Agastya as Spoken by Nādāyana to Śailūṣa," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Agastya said:
O Indra among kings, there were Māli, Sumāli, and Mālyavat, who was fierce in battle.
Having reached the fortress of Laṅkā, they dwelt there, striking one another with various weapons.
Māli and Sumāli, both of wicked conduct, were afflicting the gods.
O King, although they were constantly being restrained by that Mālyavat, [they did not desist].
The gods, terrified by them, informed Brahmā of the matter along with its purpose.
Accompanied by Brahmā, they went and informed the Destroyer of Tripura.
The gods, accompanied by Brahmā and Śiva, went to Viṣṇu for refuge.
They went to the one situated in the salt waters in order to inform Acyuta.
And they beheld, O best of the Raghus, the ocean whose waters had been drunk up.
It seemed to be leaping with the wind as its waves danced in multitudes. || 5 ||
It seemed to laugh with its masses of foam as it tumbled through the mountain caves.
It was roaring as if toward the shoreless ocean, surrounded by various hosts of aquatic creatures.
With its moving waves acting as hands, it seemed to beckon him away from the gods.
They are foamy, scattered, gathered together, and raised up high. ||7||
And its waves are seen like moving mountains.
Timiṅgilas, tortoises, as well as timis and timiṅgilas.
And even sea-monsters are seen, appearing like mountains submerged in water.
And thousands of conch shells were submerged in the waters on all sides.
They appeared just like stars at night, partially veiled by thin clouds.
In one place sleeping, in another roaring, in another reeling, and in another stumbling.
The lords of the thirty-three gods beheld that ocean resembling one who is intoxicated.
In some places it was inhabited by Daityas, and likewise in others by the enemy of the Daityas.
And in some places it was filled with terrifying serpents and possessed great depth.
Its waters were turbid, having been agitated by Viṣṇu in his form as a boar.
And [he was] unassailed by the hundred-petaled lotus for a hundred years.
By that Viṣṇu, the god beyond gods, the all-powerful lord.
His form was rendered stainless by that which eternally dwells within.
A multitude of hundreds of mountains, terrified by the fear of Śakra’s vajra. || 14 ||
The coral-like garment, whose form resembles that which has been scorched by fire.
As if desiring to wash away the stain upon the full moon with their surging waves. || 15 ||
He who always assails the sky with his waves on full moon nights.
Countless, with its mass of waves reflecting the orb of the moon.
Or laughing, he possessed the splendor of the sky itself as it bears the moon.
At the times of giving portions of the directions, one should be prepared with sandalwood water.
And it sleeps constantly wherever there is the water of the gift.
It was like the mid-air, its quarters filled with garlands of vast and restless waves.
Having reached the ocean, those dwellers of heaven, fierce in their power and devoted to austerity, stood there.

Thus ends the two hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ocean," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, in the speech of Nāḍāyana to Śailūṣa. ||214||
Agastya said:
The God of gods, Janārdana, was gratified by the gods through their ascetic penance.
Having abandoned his residence in Mahodaya, he granted an audience to the gods. ||1||
And they [honored] that slayer of the enemies of the gods with dust raised from falling to the earth.
With their knees, hands, and foreheads touching the ground, they bowed joyfully to Hari.
They praised him with such words and then stated their own purpose.
For the purpose of slaying the sons of Sukeśa on behalf of the God of gods.
Then the Lord Hari promised them the slaying of Māli.
O best of gods, you are capable of slaying Sumālī.
Moreover, this Mālyavat, who is ever devoted to righteousness, is also incapable of being slain.
Having spoken thus, Keśava then summoned Tārkṣya.
The Soul of All ascended that golden bird, the son of Vinatā.
Madhusūdana is marked with the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.

May the blessed Hiraṇyagarbha grant me gold.
May Kapila, the teacher of Sāṃkhya, bring equilibrium to my bodily constituents. || 9 ||
And may the unborn one, who dwells in Śvetadvīpa, lead me to Śvetadvīpa.
May the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha destroy all enemies.
May Viṣṇu forever draw away my sin from my body.
May Haṃsa, Matsya, and likewise Kūrma protect me in every direction. || 11 ||
May the Lord Trivikrama sever all my bonds.
May the divine Nara-Nārāyaṇa protect my intellect. || 12 ||
May Śeṣa, whose knowledge is entirely stainless, effect the destruction of ignorance.
May Vaḍavāmukha destroy the defilement that has been committed by me. || 13 ||
May my Lord Aśvamūrdhan grant me supreme knowledge.
May Dattātreya protect [us], along with our children, cattle, and kinsmen.
May Rāma destroy all my diseases with his axe.
May the mighty-armed son of Daśaratha, the slayer of Rākṣasas, protect me always. || 15 ||
May Rāma, the joy of the Yādavas, slay my enemies with his bow.
The destroyer of Pralamba, Keśin, Cāṇūra, Pūtanā, and Kaṃsa.
May that Kṛṣṇa, who [was so] in his childhood state, grant me my desires.
[He saw] darkness, a terrible gloom, and a man who was blackish-brown.
Tormented by fear, I see him like Death himself with a noose in his hand.
Then I went for refuge to the lotus-eyed Acyuta. || 18 ||
It resides within the form of the mind of the Lord of Yogis, stainless like the auspicious and cool-rayed moon.
I am blessed and eternally victorious, for the Blessed Lord Hari belongs to me.
Having recollected the god Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of all calamities.
Having donned the Vaiṣṇava armor, I wander upon the surface of the earth.
I am invincible to all beings, for I am entirely composed of Viṣṇu.
By remembering Viṣṇu, the god of gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
"May there be constant success for me; thus is the mantra proclaimed."
He who sees me with his eyes, and whom I see with my eye; || 22 ||
May Viṣṇu bind with his eye all those who possess equal vision.
Of that discus which belongs to Vāsudeva, there are spokes.
May they sever my evil; may those who would harm me not cause me injury.
Among the Rākṣasas and Piśācas, and in wildernesses and forests. || 24 ||
In disputes on royal roads, at gambling matches, and in quarrels.
When the crossing of a river was imminent and terrible, and a danger to life had arrived. || 25 ||
And in the event of fire, thieves, or falling [from a height], and for the warding off of all planetary influences;
In the event of lightning, snakes, or the administration of poison; in a pit, a well, or a perilous situation involving enemies. ||26||
One should constantly recite this truth whenever fear arises within the body.
This mantra of the Blessed One is the supreme among mantras. ||27||
This celebrated and secret armor is the destroyer of all sins.
He creates emanations through his own māyā and brings about the destruction of the world at the end of the aeon.
O Padmanābha, salutations to you, the beginningless seed of that world.
Oṃ, to Kāla, svāhā!
Oṃ, to the Kālapuruṣa, svāhā!
Oṃ, svāhā to the Fierce One!
Oṃ, to the fierce man, svāhā!
Oṃ, svāhā to all!
Oṃ, to the All-of-all, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Bhuvaneśa, the abode of the three worlds; iti ṭipi riṭi svāhā.

Oṃ! By this supreme [mantra], may there be no harm for me, nor for the wind, nor for those beings who follow evil paths—namely, the *daityas*, *dānavas*, *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, *kūṣmāṇḍas*, *apasmāras*, *unmādas*, and those afflicted by fevers: the quotidian, the tertian, the quartan, the hourly, the daily fever, the nightly fever, the constant fever, the fever at twilight, and all other such fevers. May this body of mine be invincible against spiders, insects, thorns, *kaṭapūtanas*, serpents, and the poisons of both mobile and immobile creatures.
So be it! Oṃ! At the syllable *sukāra*, you who possess fierce, formidable, and terrifying tusks, protect [me] from the east!
Oṃ haiṃ haiṃ haiṃ haiṃ! O you whose fierce splendor is equal to a thousand suns, protect, protect from the west!
Oṃ, O you who are ablaze with the *niri-niri* [mantra], O flaming fire, O you whose matted locks are dark brown like the great fire at the end of time, protect me from the north!
Oṃ cilicili milimili cekaḍi gaurī gāndhārī viṣohani, let poison not delude me, svāhā! From the south, protect me, [name], from all fears and calamities caused by spirits, svāhā!
Victorious is Vijayadāna; may he arise, the destroyer of the cities of his enemies; may this noble Acyuta grant me freedom from fear—the fear that arises from both internal and external dangers.
Into whose entire belly the rays of light enter.
The ancient seers, who possess a beginning and an end, are subtle, vast, and indeed the instructors.
May Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Vāsudeva destroy all my fevers. ||29||

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Armor of Viṣṇu," in the dialogue between Nāḍāyana and Śailūṣa within the Māgha-māsa section of the first book of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. ||237||
Vajra said:
Having heard the burning of Kālāṅgada as uttered by the Brahmin, [he was filled with grief].
O Brahmin, what did that actor, impelled by Death, ask at that time?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard the words spoken by the Brahmin regarding the burning of Kālāṅgada.
Then he questioned him further regarding the life and deeds of Rāvaṇa alone.
The actor said: "Whatever remains of the life-story of the ten-necked Rākṣasa..."
Therefore, I wish to hear that, for I have a great doubt in this matter. ||3||
Nāḍāyana said:
Then Rāvaṇa once again wandered through his city.
Then he saw there a palace made entirely of gold.
It was encircled by nets of pearls and likewise featured crossings made of coral.
And with red *gāruḍa* [sandalwood], let a sacrificial altar (*vedikā*) be made all around. || 5 ||
It had pillars radiant with lapis lazuli and was blazing with the luster of rubies.
It was covered with the luster of sapphires and adorned with hundreds of turrets.
It was crowded with great worlds and adorned with magnificent gardens.
It had stairs that were easy to ascend and was filled with hundreds of oblong ponds.
It was adorned on all sides by trees bearing flowers of every season.
It was delightful, furnished with every kind of seat, and superior even to the abode of Mahendra.
Having seen that thread in the house, O King, he spoke these words to Prahasta:
"O Prahasta, go quickly and find out whose excellent mansion this is."
Thus addressed, Prahasta entered his excellent residence.
And when that stage was reached, it resembled a heap of crushed collyrium.
Adorned with all ornaments and endowed with all the primary marks.
Having taken up an iron pestle, he stood at the entrance.
He beheld a terrifying man, difficult to look upon because of his circle of flames.
But seeing him in such a state, the Ten-faced One entered.
And when the round of matches was concluded, he beheld that very same person.
The lord of the hosts of night-stalkers, possessed of great splendor, spoke to him.
I have arrived seeking battle; grant me the hospitality of war.
Or rather, praise him who resides in his house. || 14 ||
Then a man spoke these words to the king of the rākṣasas.
"In this house dwells the mighty King Bali, the lord of the Dānavas. (15)
If you will illuminate it, O hero, then enter this most excellent house.
You ought not to fight with him; he is a great-souled one of immense strength.
Devoted to Brahmanas, a refuge for all, a hero whose valor is truth.
A hero endowed with many virtues, powerful, and of firm prowess.
Resplendent like the rising sun, he never retreats in battles. || 17 ||
He is pleasant-spoken, shares his wealth, and is devoted to giving secret testimony.
Thus addressed, the Ten-necked One entered his excellent palace.
Then, by the mere sight of him, the high-souled Bali [was moved].
Having quickly placed him on his lap, he was then asked about his arrival.
To him spoke Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, endowed with great splendor.
"O illustrious one, I have heard that you were indeed bound by Viṣṇu."
Thus, I am certainly capable of releasing you from bondage; of this there is no doubt.
Having been addressed thus, Bali then let out a laugh and spoke as follows.
"These two divine earrings of mine are adorned with great jewels."
"Bring one of these two and sit here; do not delay."
And while you are seated here, I shall explain to you the strides of Viṣṇu.
Thus addressed, Daśagrīva then set out for the retrieval of the earrings.
The slayer of enemies made a supreme effort, yet he was not able [to prevail].
And when he was unable to move Kuṇḍala from its place, [he spoke].
With all his limbs perspiring, he bit his lip.
With his face contorted by a frown, he was struck with supreme astonishment. || 25 ||
Having placed him in that state upon his lap, Bali spoke as follows.
My great-grandfather was named Hiraṇyakaśipu.
When he was born, these two earrings indeed came into being for him.
By means of these two earrings, he had previously been adorned.
Having been placed upon his thighs, he was torn apart by him with his claws and hands.
How can you resolve today to conquer that highly fortunate one? || 28 ||
That very same man, dark-complexioned, stands constantly at the door.
By this [means], the lords of the Dānavas and others who were arrogant in their strength [were likewise subdued]. || 29 ||
And those who were even earlier than the earliest have been brought under control by the powerful one.
And I am bound by this very [time]; time is difficult to overcome.
O Rākṣasa, who in this world will deceive this man?
He is likewise the creator and the destroyer of the entire triple world. || 31 ||
He withdraws all beings, both the stationary and the moving.
Furthermore, the Great Lord, who is without beginning or end, creates everything once again.
Whatever has been sacrificed, whatever has been offered in oblation, and likewise whatever austerity has been practiced;
For the Lord of the World is undoubtedly the creator and protector of everyone. || 33 ||
He is indeed composed of all the gods, and likewise composed of all living beings.
He consists of all the worlds and likewise consists of all knowledge. || 34 ||
He who possesses all forms, the great-formed one, the great child, and the great-armed one.
By remembering, praising, and likewise worshipping [him], one shall obtain everything from him. || 35 ||
Having heard these words, Rāvaṇa then went forth.
And the night-stalker did not see that man there.
Having gathered his allies, the lord of the Rākṣasas once again traversed the entire earth.
And that foremost of the enemies of the gods did not see any other steadfast person in the worlds.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Meeting of Bali and Rāvaṇa," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara, in the words of Nāḍāyana addressed to Śailūṣa.
Nāḍāyana said:
Once, that younger brother of Dhanada was wandering over the entire earth.
On an island in the western ocean, he beheld a beautiful man.
Resembling pure Jāmbūnada gold, it possesses the brilliant luster of a blazing fire.
To the god who assumes universal forms, the giver of boons, who can take any form at will.
Both his dharma and his austerity are the causes for the perfection of the world.
They stood leaning against her thighs, while Manmatha took hold of her phallus.
The Viśvedevas reside in the region of the hips, and the Maruts in the head of the bladder.
And in his two feet is the goddess Earth, and the Piśācas reside in his nails.
In his middle there were eight Vasus, and the oceans took refuge within his belly.
And in the flanks, all the directions; and in all the joints, the vital air.
The ancestors are situated on his back, and the grandfather (Brahmā) is in his heart.
The gifts of cows are purifying, as are the gifts of land.
And gifts of gold, as well as the spaces between the liver and the skin.
In the portions of his bones are the mountains, and likewise, in his veins are the rivers.
His chest was adorned with jewels, and it appeared as if the very heavens were situated upon his body.
At the nape of the neck are the Sandhyās and those thick vessels known as the Talavāhas.
Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ are the two arms, while Bhaga and Pūṣan are the two hands.
All the snakes with terrible venom were stationed upon his fingernails.
Agni became his mouth, and his two shoulders were presided over by the Rudras.
His teeth are the months and seasons, and his fangs are the year.
The new moon day (amāvāsyā) is also in the nose, and the days [of the lunar fortnight] are in its nostrils.
His neck became the sacrificial altar, and his speech became Sarasvatī.
Both his ears were the Nāsatyas, and his eyes were the moon and the sun.
The Vedāṅgas, the sacrifices, and those forms which are the stars; || 12 ||
These indeed reside within the body of that one who possesses a human form.
Then, by that massive body, the rākṣasa was crushed by the hand. ||13||
His ministers fainted and fled in the ten directions.
Resembling the Rigveda, he is the most excellent, adorned with a garland of lotuses.
And then, resembling a mountain, he gradually entered Pātāla.
And having risen, the Ten-necked One summoned his three ministers.
"Where has he suddenly gone? Tell me, Prahasta, Śuka, and Sāraṇa!"
When the lord of the Rākṣasas had spoken thus, the Rākṣasas then said to him: ||| 16 ||
Having entered right here, that man, the destroyer of the pride of gods and dānavas, [remains].
Then, by that very same path, the night-stalker entered.
He alone was possessed of great splendor by virtue of a boon from the Self-Existent One.
Having entered, he beheld there those adorned with all kinds of ornaments.
Eternal, free from fear due to tranquility, partless, and radiant as fire.
They had four arms, possessed of magnificent forms, and were marked with the Śrīvatsa.
They all assumed a single form, wearing red garlands and unguents.
[He saw] those who are completely free from passion and hatred, possessing all powers, and lords of the world.
They were serving Janārdana with dance, song, and instrumental music.
Having performed human worship of the God of gods, the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu). || 21 ||
They arrived in the presence of that very Parameṣṭhin.
Thousands of crores were seen, and having seen them, the night-stalker [was struck with wonder].
Then, with his hair standing on end, he moved from that place to another place.
He went there and beheld a residence of incomparable excellence.
And then he saw there a man lying upon a bed.
With a white, highly precious cloth for his bedding and seat. || 24 ||
That tiger among men lies there, enveloped by fire.
His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes, and he was adorned with celestial ornaments.
Clad in divine garments, that virtuous woman is the sole ornament of the three worlds.
Holding a yak-tail fan in her hand, she was indeed peerless in beauty upon the earth. || 26 ||
Having placed his feet upon the lap of that god who wields the discus.
Desiring to seize the virtuous woman by force, he suddenly fell down due to his own power. || 27 ||
Only the mere veil [of his face] was seen by that great-souled one.
Then the god, seeing that lord of the rākṣasas, laughed aloud. || 28 ||
Yet by the power of destiny, that Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the worlds cry out, [prevailed].
Like a tree whose roots have been severed, he fell upon the surface of the earth.
To that lord of the Rākṣasas who had fallen, the god spoke these words:
Arise, O night-stalker; there is no death for you at this time.
The Rakshasa Prajāpativara, by whom you now live.
Then the king, overwhelmed with agitation, spoke to that leader of the rākṣasas.
Who are you that lies upon this bed, resembling the fire at the end of an eon?
Thus addressed by him, he then replied to the night-stalker.
O Ten-necked One, you are to be slain by me; it will not be long before you fall into my hands.
And in this very way, O Ten-faced One, death shall come to you.
Because you desire to seize her out of delusion, you shall take her back once more.
Having attained this human state, O Rāvaṇa, I shall slay you.
"For the sake of this large-eyed woman, go now, O Rākṣasa."
Having heard these words from the god, Rāvaṇa spoke this speech: || 35 ||
In this world, including the three realms, there is no one more fortunate than I, excluding myself.
O Lord of the World, he whose death shall come at your hands— || 36 ||
Death at your hands would be both glorious and praiseworthy for me.
Then Rāvaṇa, of terrifying prowess, beheld [the marks] upon his body.
O King, the entire triple world belongs to him who bears the universal form.
O King, having seen this, Rāvaṇa’s eyes blossomed wide with wonder. || 38 ||
He held himself in high esteem and likewise departed.
Permitted by the God of gods, he then went to his home.
For the purpose of slaying him, Janārdana assumed four forms as a god.
O King, he has come to the human state; therefore, do not engage in conflict with him.
Rāma is Janārdana himself, and Sītā is likewise Lakṣmī.
Likewise, Bharata, Śatrughna, and the highly illustrious Lakṣmaṇa also [departed]. || 41 ||
The portions of Viṣṇu, whose prowess is equal to that of Viṣṇu, must be recognized by you.
A great deed was performed by Śatrughna in the slaying of Lavaṇa.
Therefore, I consider Bharata, who is devoted to dharma, to be even more distinguished.
Neither by hosts of gods, nor by humans, nor by yakṣas, nor by rākṣasas, nor by the best of nāgas, nor by daityas [can it be overcome].
But those for whom that immeasurable Hari is their protector can be conquered in battle by the descendant of Raghu. || 43 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Rāvaṇa’s Vision of the Mahāpuruṣa," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*, specifically in the speech of Nāḍāyana addressed to Śailūṣa.
The actor said:
O Brahmin, I wish to hear in truth about the slaying of Lavaṇa.
How was Lavaṇa struck down in battle by Śatrughna? ||1||
Nāḍāyana said:
O King, while Daśaratha was still present in Ayodhyā, in the city of Ayodhyā.
Once, however, when spring had not yet passed, that season which increases delight, ||2||
Neither too hot nor too cold, pleasant and enchanting to all living beings.
In which the bees, possessing beautiful sounds, were nestled within the branches of the blossoming trees.
Abounding with the cries of cuckoos and possessing trees covered in young shoots.
At a time when the rays of the sun were pleasant and the surface of the earth was adorned.
Resounding with the songs of cuckoos perched upon the tips of branches from which leaves have fallen.
Desirous of going forth, they set out on their journey, but were turned back once more. || 5 ||
Where the flower-clusters of the mango trees have bees clinging to them.
The arrows marked with the name of Kāma were like those of the embodied Kāma himself.
Wherein beautiful women firmly cause those full of desire to renounce their passion.
By means of the wind, courtesy has been manifested everywhere.
Abounding with young barley-grass and flowers stirred by a gentle breeze.
The row of hissing sounds shone like a river flowing along.
The forest groves have been embraced on all sides by the spring.
Then the Palāśa trees themselves clearly displayed their passion through their blossoming flowers. || 9 ||
The earth was strewn with flowers and leaves by a gentle breeze.
At night, the earth, covered with young grass, bore the beauty of a cloudless sky.
By those who have deceived the newly born calves that speak so softly.
In that place, O best of Gandharvas, there is great splendor in the cow-pens.
Resounding with lowing sounds, they moved with swift and rhythmic steps.
Into which the cows, longing for their calves, enter at the close of day. ||12||
With their tails raised high, the calves were drinking from the udders of their mothers.
Where the cowherd women repeatedly experience supreme bliss from being licked by their mothers.
There, the sprout-like hands of the amorous women gathered heaps of flowers.
But because of their similarity to young shoots, they were not recognized at all by those filled with desire. ||14||
The song of the cuckoos in springtime is her lute, and the humming of bees is its accompaniment.
Upon merely hearing it, the creepers there danced as if struck by a gentle breeze.
When that spring had passed, O lord of men, he caused the entire world to suffer.
The summer season is like salt—its path obstructed and its foliage exceedingly vast. || 16 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of Ayodhyā as it Appears to the Actor," within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra concerning the words of Nāḍāyana addressed to Śailūṣa, in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. ||240||
Nāḍāyana said:
At that time, during the summer season, when the jasmine flowers were in full bloom.
Where the movement of travelers had ceased, amidst heaps of scorching sand.
It was filled with blossoming pomegranate trees and the interiors of blazing houses.
It was resplendent with rows of forests rich in beautiful campaka flowers.
Adorned by swarms of bees settled upon *pāṭala* flowers.
Upon which the lotus ornaments were rolling in the lap of the scorched buffalo-cow.
In a lake whose waters were churned by mountain-high elephants,
In sweet-sounding waters and on mountains shrouded in mist. ||4||
Their limbs are moist with camphor and sandalwood paste, and their beloveds wear bracelets of lotus stalks.
There, having fashioned garlands from forest blossoms, they delight their beloveds.
Where the rays of the moon, which increase the passion of lovers, are to be enjoyed.
And where the nights are exceedingly beautiful at their onset.
At the end of the night, there were cool breezes, fragrant with the scent of flower-beds.
Having smelled it, those who possess desire and seek sexual pleasure are born. || 7 ||
The nights pass swiftly, while the days pass slowly.
Due to the sun's approach toward the zodiac sign of Gemini, its rays became intensely scorching.
They were filled with masses of foam from the streams of water as the snow melted away.
The rivers are exceedingly cold, as are the mountains of snow.
Likewise, with sandalwoods made fragrant by abundant resinous exudations.
In that same way, lovers increase the passion of those who desire them.
The water produced from the exhaustion and fatigue arising during the intervals between sexual unions.
Where lovers used camphor powder to destroy [their passion]. || 11 ||
O King, in that summer season when the mango trees were laden with fruit, you were richly adorned throughout the year.
Desiring to see that foremost of the Raghu clan, they then set out once more for Ayodhyā.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Summer during the Vision of Ayodhyā," within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra concerning the words of Nāḍāyana addressed to Śailūṣa, in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 241 ||
Nāḍāyana said:
Then the doorkeeper spoke these words to Rāma, who had arrived at the assembly hall:
The sages dwelling on the banks of the Yamunā stand at the gate. ||1||
Placing the descendant of Bhṛgu, Cyavana, who was blazing with splendor, at their head.
They are of great majesty, bestowers of boons, and have burnt away all impurities through their ascetic penance.
Then, having heard the words from the gatekeeper, Rāma [spoke] with his domestic priest.
Accompanied [by them], he went out in haste to see those ascetics.
Having approached the hosts of ascetic seers, that one of great splendor—
Having saluted and bowed down to them, and having placed them at his head, he then went home.
Then he caused them to enter and offered them water for their feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, and so forth.
He offered him a seat, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and likewise the kingdom.
Having accepted it, they all gave the kingdom back to him once again.
And likewise, the waters of sacred fords and various kinds of fruits [should be offered]. || 6 ||
And having accepted them, Rāma inquired after their welfare and well-being.
Then that illustrious one questioned them regarding the purpose of their arrival.
Having heard Rāma's words, Cyavana spoke these words.
O King, there was a Rākṣasa named Lavaṇa who dwelt in Madhuvana.
He torments all the worlds; exert yourself to slay him.
And ten thousand living beings were his daily provision of food. || 9 ||
For the purpose of killing him, he [sent] Bharata, Śatrughna, and Lakṣmaṇa.
O fortunate one, let the quarters be peaceful; may all the worlds be free from affliction.
Likewise, O Rāma, establish a settlement in the prosperous Madhuvana.
And [he established] a meritorious city, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. ||11||
O high-minded one, you must honor and protect those assemblies of sages.
Having been addressed thus, Rāma, the knower of dharma, then reflected.
While dwelling in the forest, Lakṣmaṇa performed a great deed.
While protecting the kingdom, Bharata performed a great deed.
Today I shall dispatch Śatrughna with the desire for the slaughter of Lavaṇa.
Having reflected thus, Rāma spoke to Śatrughna.
Placing these sages at your head, O Śatrughna, go without delay.
"Have the evil-doing Lavaṇa, who is of wicked conduct, put to death. || 15 ||
And having caused Lavaṇa to be slain, settle the people there.
And likewise, a delightful city must be constructed by you there. || 16 ||
Dwell there, O highly fortunate one, while you protect the earth.
There, together with the sages, I shall consecrate you in the kingdom.
Having spoken these words, Rāma addressed that speech to the assembly of sages.
Then he endowed him with the divine consecration.
And the one of great splendor spoke to his brother of blazing splendor.
O sinless one, here are these four thousand horses for you.
And two thousand chariots, as well as one hundred of the best of elephants.
And ten thousand foot soldiers, as well as a hoard of gold.
And the market streets were adorned with various kinds of merchandise.
"Take [them] and go, Śatrughna, with sufficient troops and vehicles."
And your army, O hero, is well-maintained, contented, well-nourished, and free from arrogance.
And bring them under your control through conciliation and gifts, O delight of the Raghus.
For neither wealth, nor friends, nor kinsmen remain there.
O Rāghava, wherever a group of servants remains well-pleased, [there prosperity dwells].
Therefore, having stationed that great army amidst a multitude of wicked people, you [should proceed].
"Armed with a single bow alone, you should fight the son of Madhu."
And so that he may not recognize you, go toward him who longs for battle.
Lavaṇa is that son of Madhu; go to him without hesitation.
And it has been declared that there is no one possessed by the fear of death for him.
Whoever should come into his sight is destroyed by salt.
He was separated from his trident of Maheśvara while out on a hunt.
Block the gateway with salt and fight, O descendant of Raghu! (27)
The spear of Maheśvara is indeed unfailing, yet it has been avoided.
"Accept this arrow, my child, which destroys all weapons. || 28 ||
By means of this, you will undoubtedly cause Lavaṇa to be slain in battle.
Go now with the remainder of the summer, with the intent to slay Lavaṇa.
When the rainy season had thus set in, the best of rivers swelled with increased waters.
With an arrow given by me, cast down the lifeless body of that night-stalker.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "Rāma’s Instruction to Śatrughna Regarding the Slaying of Lavaṇa," within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra concerning the actor, found in the Nāḍāyana-utterances in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
