Eager for battle at dawn, he found no sleep upon his bed.
Someone, intensely tormented by the touch of the moonbeams, [cries out].
And he beheld the moon, surpassed by the face of her whose eyes were divine and lovely.
And someone else was thinking only of his beloved, the mistress of his life and wealth.
He made the multitude of stars his bed, spread out across the sky.
He beheld the directional leaf-cutting, which had been performed and released without being completed.
A certain man joyfully spends the night with his beloved, whom he himself won over.
One whose mind is weary of the world is tormented by the rays of the moon.
Someone deprived of a slender-limbed woman suffers even upon his own bed. || 7 ||
His heart's desire was for union with a slender-limbed woman encountered in a dream.
Someone asleep was inferred by the Gandharvas from the occurrence of horripilation. (8)
Having sent his beloved away by means of a female messenger, he remained intent on conversing with her.
No one, O Indra among kings, knew that even the night had passed away.
Someone [carries] the fire of separation, burning incessantly within the body.
Meditating upon his beloved, moon-faced wife, he suddenly brought [the fire] to rest.
Dark-complexioned, free from her bodice, slender, and the life-taker of young men.
And someone, filled with intense longing, remembers his beloved and his sword-blade.
She possessed auspicious marks, a slender waist, and was adorned with ornaments of fresh gold.
Someone remembered his beloved, and likewise, his bow-staff.
The Gandharvas and the soldiers of Bharata were filled with anxiety.
They were unable to overcome him because of his reliance upon Bharata.
Others as well who constantly remember the feet of Viṣṇu, the best of gods and Lord of the Yadus, [attain liberation].
For them, there shall be no fear whatsoever here from Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, or Rākṣasas. || 14 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Separated Lover," in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, as for those who were dispatched to the city named Rājagṛha:
There, the Gandharvas beheld the unsurpassed splendor of the city.
The principal houses in every respect have become co-wives to the moon.
They beheld many jewels, as well as abundant grain and wealth.
And they beheld beautiful city gardens on every side.
O Yādava, they were adorned with ponds and groves of trees.
In various gardens, [they dwell] followed by the foremost of men.
There, the Gandharvas who drink wine behold multitudes.
With the sound of lutes and with sweet singing.
The beautiful humming of the bees seemed to have attained oneness [with it]. || 5 ||
And in some places there, courtesans dance before the lustful men.
In some places, women intoxicated with passion slept together with their lovers, adorned with ornaments.
There, while the men and women were asleep, the Gandharvas carried out their activity.
With their forms concealed by illusion, they were seen among many wives.
Some sing, others weep, and others likewise laugh.
Likewise, others, intoxicated with passion, embrace one another.
Some, distressed and overwhelmed, speak indistinctly at every step.
And wandering about on their couches, they had their gaze fixed here and there.
And others likewise had their arms thrown around the shoulders of their beloved women.
Others engaged in quarreling, while others offered meaningless praise.
With faltering steps, they go to a place where the heart finds no rest.
Some call out to their groups, while others likewise offer salutations.
Thus, in that city crowded with virtuous people and resounding with the sound of song,
They beheld the activities of men and women within the principal houses.
Urged on by female messengers, their minds performed their grooming with haste.
Eager for the drinking of intoxicants, they go toward their beloveds in a state of agitation. || 13 ||
Some drank wine, which stirs intoxication, together with their beloveds.
Others were making their lovers drink, while others were feeding their beloveds.
In various palaces as well as in the windows.
Likewise, some women, exhausted from lovemaking, were sleeping together with their lovers. || 15 ||
A certain fair-complexioned woman, reclining on a bed, embraced her dark-hued beloved.
It shines like a garland of blue lotuses joined together with a garland of jasmine.
A certain beautiful woman, closely embraced by one as fair as Gaurī, shines forth.
Just as a moonstone is embraced by the rays of the moon. || 17 ||
O King, a certain dark-complexioned woman, closely embraced by a dark man, shines forth.
O King, just as a row of clouds in the sky is filled with water.
A certain young woman kisses her lover while he feigns sleep.
Tightly embraced by her beloved, she became both embarrassed and joyful. || 19 ||
And a certain mature woman herself [applied] camphor powder.
He sprinkles the beloved’s body, which is drenched with the sweat of passion.
Behold this star; indeed, the moon stands embracing it with his lap.
Thus spoke a certain mature woman, desiring the pleasure of love, to her beloved. || 21 ||
A certain woman, having recognized [her lover] by touching his thighs, desired sexual union.
She was embraced firmly by her husband, who was joyful and desirous of dalliance.
A certain woman, her lip bitten by her lover, had her face pressed for a kiss.
I shall not place my trust in you again if you act otherwise once more.
A certain woman, desiring sexual union, was embraced by her lover while she was fast asleep.
Having abandoned her sleep, she embraced her beloved intensely with great agitation.
Thus did Yudhājit address those soldiers who were likewise full of confidence.
The Gandharvas were unable to seize it because of their reliance on Bharata. || 25 ||
In their city dwells that Viṣṇu of great majesty, the protector of the Raghu dynasty.
O lord of men, in their city there is no fear from gandharvas, yakṣas, asuras, or serpents.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Enjoyment of the Night," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, having come from Ayodhyā as well as from the camp, the Gandharvas likewise [arrived].
In that manner, they all reported [the matter] to Śailūṣa from Rājagṛha. || 1 ||
There is no contentious speech there, nor is there any such need for protection.
But it was solely through the power of Rāma and Bharata.
"O King, what have we ever done to deserve being struck anywhere?"
Let the lord of the earth perform whatever remains to be done there.
Thus addressed by the Gandharvas at the end of that night, he then...
Quickly command the yogas and the yoga-mind with all haste. ||4||
Then, the war-drum was quickly struck.
By whose sound the Gandharvas arrived at the king's gate. || 5 ||
With a great multitude of elephants and a force of horses.
And with chariots rumbling like clouds, and with foot-soldiers fierce with intoxication.
With the sounds of shouting and the slapping of arms, and with the blaring of conchs and kettledrums.
With the ringing of the elephants' bells and the trumpeting of the elephants themselves. || 7 ||
From the neighing of the horses, however, there arose a great and tumultuous noise.
Then the actor, having bathed and offered oblations into the fire, performed the worship of the twice-born.
Having done so, the illustrious one, adorned with excellent sandalwood paste, went forth.
Wearing a crown, possessed of a beautiful body, armored, garlanded, and adorned with radiant ornaments. || 9 ||
A chariot yoked with horses resembling unbaked clay pots.
The one of great splendor ascended like a man of meritorious deeds ascending a celestial chariot.
In front of that chariot as described was one skilled in battle.
He was renowned as Naraketu, famous throughout the three worlds.
Upon his chariot, Ketu shone like the spring season personified.
Then he went out from the city with his army.
And having likewise arrayed his forces in the "Auspicious on All Sides" (Sarvatobhadra) formation.
Having done so, he then awaited the arrival of Bharata with indignation.
O King, with a vast army, [he went] toward the rising of the sun.
With weapons grasped in hand, they gladdened the hearts of their friends with the sounds of their war-cries and conchs.
The chiefs of the Gandharvas, fierce in battle and impetuous in speed, stood waiting for Bharata. || 15 ||
Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gandharva Army," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
At the end of the night, all the kings indeed awoke.
Eager for battle, they went forth on chariots that resembled fortified cities.
With a fourfold army accompanied by the sounding of various musical instruments.
They were being praised by bards and honored by the soldiers. || 2 ||
Each fully armored, they arrived separately at the city gates.
And having performed all his necessary duties, the highly illustrious Bharata also [did so].
He went out from the city on a chariot with golden parts.
The charioteer of that chariot was his maternal uncle himself, Yudhājit.
His banner, featuring a great kovidāra tree, shone resplendently.
Having gone outside in that excellent chariot, the king— || 5 ||
Having assembled with all the kings and having honored those monarchs, he [departed].
Having formed the great array called Vajra, he of swift prowess advanced.
As that army set forth, the earth itself seemed to tremble.
And by his great roar, the vault of the sky was rent asunder.
Another most dreadful night-time arose, filled with nothing but dust.
The earth shone with the brilliance of the rubies set in the crowns of kings.
Even in the darkness of night, that army proceeds at its ease.
Having traveled a long distance toward the rising of the sun, he proceeded.
He encountered the great army of the Gandharvas, which was difficult to overcome.
Those two, difficult to withstand like a vast torrent of troops, were equal in form to the two serpents of universal destruction.
Then those two oceans of strength, driven by the power of their wrath, struck each other with fierce blows.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Departure of Bharata’s Army," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. ||259||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then there commenced a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end.
It produces joy for the brave and increases the fear of the timid. ||1||
As the army marched forth from there, the world was shrouded in dust.
Nothing at all could be discerned in any direction, O Indra among kings. || 2 ||
The great and tumultuous sound of twanging bows is heard.
And the sound of conchs and kettledrums, and the trumpeting of elephants. ||3||
Of the neighing horses and of the warriors indeed roaring.
As weapons were being hurled down, even upon the armor of the warriors.
Stay, stay! You shall not escape from me alive at the head of the battle.
"I stand here; strike me! Do you not know who I am? (6)
Strike! Cut! Pierce! Slay! Do not delay.
Such words as these were heard at the forefront of the battle.
Likewise, while that most terrible and tumultuous battle was raging,
The dust of the earth that had arisen was laid to rest by the blood of the battlefield.
Like the surface of the sky covered by a cloud of dust rising from the east.
O King, at that time, the battlefield was pervaded by that dustless [state].
Then the heroes fought, gazing at one another.
Repeatedly proclaiming the names of their lineages and the gifts they had bestowed.
Of the armies being broken by the divisions of more powerful forces.
Furthermore, he heard a tumultuous sound from those who were returning. ||11||
And of the variegated banners and flags of the kings.
Blood was seen flowing profusely at the front of the battlefield.
Then, O great king, when that cloud of dust had subsided in the deep abyss.
Then, in the stainless quarters of the sky, a great battle commenced.
Thus did the battle proceed between the gods, gandharvas, and dānavas.
[It was surrounded] on all sides by Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and throngs of sages. ||34||
The sky was suddenly covered by the eagerness for battle with thunderbolts.
Their celestial chariots, though spotless, were seen in the sky.
Resounding with the tinkling of hundreds of small bells and adorned with banners.
Then, taking up a pleasant fragrance, the fragrant wind blew.
And a rain of flowers fell there upon the heads of the warriors.
Thus, when that tumultuous conflict had commenced, filled with the sounds of war-cries and shouts of triumph.
Then, in that battle, the foot soldiers struck down the foot soldiers.
Of foot soldiers who had been cut down by the edges of swords, [the heads were carried] by other foot soldiers. || 18 ||
Their limbs, severed in two, fell upon the surface of the earth.
Having taken up sword-strokes, some, clad in armor, shone resplendent.
O King, as they were drawing their swords, [the enemies] cut off their bodies.
Some had their heads shattered by maces wielded by mace-wielders as they lay upon the earth.
They were seen fallen there on the battlefield by the hundreds of thousands.
The remaining broken sword blades were cast aside, and likewise the enemies were slain.
They let out lion-like roars, rending the enemy host.
Some, having seized one another by the hair, struck each other with swords.
Others likewise reached the earth, having lost their lives.
With armor fastened upon their backs, they likewise equipped their horses for battle.
Having performed this in battle, they struck down the host of horsemen.
Some, clad in armor, impetuously leaped onto the enemy chariots in the battle.
Those experts in battle rendered the charioteers lifeless.
Some foot soldiers lopped off the trunks of the lordly elephants.
Some, placing their feet upon the tusks, mounted the elephants.
And likewise, some horsemen on the field of battle were seen without their heads.
The foot soldiers, having blown their trumpets, struck with swords as bright as the sky.
And some horsemen [struck] with spears five or seven arrows.
Skilled in battle and trained in their art, they pierced those who were indeed drawn up in ranks.
Some were overwhelmed by the multitude of arrows fixed upon the Śārṅga bow.
They drove the foot soldiers away in battle with horses possessing the speed of the wind.
And likewise, other horsemen joined together with horsemen. || 29 ||
Displaying their prowess in battle, they waged war in many ways as if begging for alms.
Some had their charioteers and leaders struck down, pierced by the tips of nooses.
Suddenly, the forests resounded loudly with the sounds of lion-roars.
Having thrown the area into confusion with elephants, those skilled in the management of horses and vehicles [acted]. || 31 ||
In the battle, they rendered the hosts of horsemen handless with their lances.
Or the foot-soldiers were slain in many ways by showers of arrows in the battle.
O protector of the earth, it shines with charioteers, resembling a cluster of lotuses.
Horses and horsemen were struck down by the chariot-warriors. || 33 ||
There, by the hundreds and thousands, they covered the earth.
A most terrible battle took place between chariot-warriors and chariot-warriors. ||34||
And with the discharge of arrows and tomara-spears, as well as maces, kampanas, and clubs.
And there was a great battle between the chariot-warriors and those mounted upon the backs of elephants.
It was difficult to look upon from any direction due to the great falling of arrows discharged with force.
A great many foot soldiers were seen there slain by elephants. ||36||
O tiger among kings, it was scattered in a thousand pieces upon the battlefield.
A very great slaughter was wrought among the horsemen together with their horses. || 37 ||
With elephants exulting under their mahouts and proud of their strength.
Having trampled upon the multitudes of chariots, they were crushed by the horses. ||38||
They were seen scattered upon the surface of the earth, O great king.
Thus, at the time of midday, when the sun blazes fiercely. || 39 ||
A fierce and tumultuous battle took place, a mire of blood.
The infantrymen also assembled together with chariots, horses, and elephants.
And there were elephants of massive body, as well as infantry, horses, and chariots.
And with foot soldiers, as well as horsemen together with their horses. || 41 ||
Chariot-warriors fought with chariot-warriors, and elephants with elephants.
In that tumultuous battle, where blood was the water, there arose a roar like that of the ocean.
Of those heroes, greedy for battle, whose minds were overcome by indignation.
A horseman was slain by a foot soldier, and a man was slain by an elephant.
In some instances, an elephant slain by a chariot-warrior remained unslain [by others].
And others were seen slain by foot-soldiers on the field of battle. || 44 ||
And the foot-soldiers, chariots, and elephants were struck down by the horsemen.
Chariots, elephants, and horses were also slain in battle by the foot soldiers. || 45 ||
And an elephant was slain by a man who was a hero of resolute mind.
An elephant was killed by a rider, and a rider likewise by a foot soldier. (46)
A chariot-warrior was slain by a foot-soldier, and a chariot-warrior was slain by a foot-soldier.
In that hair-raising battle, a horseman was slain by a chariot-warrior.
And in that tumultuous, intense confusion, the quarters were pervaded by dust.
O great king, though their lives had departed, they shone resplendently on the battlefield. || 48 ||
Of the nets of arrows falling and of the bows twanging.
And likewise of mallets, bhushundis, and javelins. ||49||
And of spears, double-edged swords, and slings, O Yādava.
Of iron balls, spears, shields, and then of armor; || 1.260.50 ||
A terrible sound is heard incessantly on that field of battle.
And by swift horses, free from weariness, galloping here and there. || 51 ||
And with chariots whose poles, axle-trees, and axles were broken, and which were deprived of their drivers;
And by elephants with broken tusks, their frontal globes and temples shattered. 52.
The battlefield attains splendor through those who resemble trees entwined by creepers.
With elephants whose riders had departed, which were terrified, and [accompanied by] men with firm bows. || 53 ||
The armies, by the hundreds and thousands, were being crushed.
Likewise, elephants tore apart men with their sharp tusks, while others had their tusks stuck in them.
Being fanned with ear-whisks, they shone as they were carried along.
The elephants, resembling mountains, with their tusks like nets of entrails clinging to them, [fell]. ||55||
Resembling trees entwined by creepers, they beautify the field of battle.
In that such kind of fierce battle, terrible to behold.
Rivers of blood flowed forth from the gore of men, horses, and elephants.
Adorned with swords, fish, great umbrellas, and royal swans.
Their heads were like stones, and their hair was their only ornament—resembling moss. ||57||
They were filled with great surges of foam and increased the fear of those who were already terrified.
Then those brave warriors, seeking the wealth of victory, cross over it. ||58||
O King, with their mounts and boats, they were intent upon one another through their resolve.
Their own limbs, severed by enemies in battle, do not even feel it. || 59 ||
There, those heroes of great fortune had their minds overcome by indignation.
Having reached the exhaustion of their weapons, they engaged in hand-to-hand combat.
Some fought hair-to-hair, while others fought tooth-to-tooth and nail-to-nail.
O great king, desiring to conquer the world of Brahmā, they waged war.
Others were crying out for their fathers and sons, while others were crying for their brothers and grandfathers.
Maternal uncles, nephews, brothers-in-law, and likewise other relatives.
Others [worship] paternal uncles and maternal uncles, while still others worship their daughters' sons.
Some run, others fall, and others roar out of a desire for victory.
Some cry out, others fall, and likewise others die.
Some grieve for their kinsmen, while others, being themselves objects of grief, are mourned by their kinsmen.
Others, O Great King, afflicted by thirst, likewise beg for water.
Others are led away by their kinsmen after being placed upon vehicles. || 65 ||
O great king, [they went] to the camp by the hundreds and by the thousands.
Others, concealing themselves out of fear, went into hiding.
And other men, urged by their kinsmen, went for the sake of water.
Having arrived and seen that the vessel was broken, they wept aloud.
Disregarding their own kinsmen, they were solely intent upon the business of their master.
There, the men fought only while facing their enemies.
While they were thus fighting by the hundreds and thousands, however—
O lord of the earth, those headless trunks that had arisen in the host—
A certain headless torso (kabandha), wielding a bow, danced in the midst of the battle.
Another likewise had a mace in his hand, and yet another bore a sword and shield.
One was bearing an axe, while another had a spear in his hand.
Abounding with dancing headless trunks and resounded by the beating of celestial drums. || 71 ||
While the battle was raging, which bestows the heavenly realm upon heroes.
O great king, piśācas of terrifying appearance were seen. ||72||
And there were Rākṣasas of massive body, as well as other flesh-eaters.
And then the sun, assuming a crimson form, went to its setting.
It was as if it had drunk the blood of all the warriors from the battlefield with its hands.
Then, when the Blessed Sun had set upon the Mountain of Sunset, possessing the hue of a cluster of hibiscus flowers;
Having made both armies descend from their vehicles to reach the camp, they were tormented by the arrows of the enemy.
Thus ends the two hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The General Battle," in the first section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra. || 260 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
At the end of the night, the Gandharvas formed an array that was very difficult to conquer.
They awaited Bharata, who was skilled in battle, as he approached.
And Bharata also, at the end of the night, was armored in the Vajra formation.
He encountered the great army of the Gandharvas, which was exceedingly difficult to conquer.
Then the battle commenced, increasing the population of Yama’s kingdom.
Resembling the battle between the gods and the asuras, it caused terror to the three worlds.
Foot soldiers with foot soldiers, and horsemen with horsemen.
Chariot-warriors against chariot-warriors, and elephants against elephants.
Let them proclaim their names and lineages, as well as those heroes who are roaring.
At that time, there arose the sound of twanging bows.
Then, when the battle had commenced, Puṣkara, the son of Bharata, [fought] in the fray.
He encountered the large-eyed Gandharva, who was arrogant in battle.
And the illustrious Takṣaka Bhārata fought with Vīrabāhu.
The illustrious Vijaya, the commander-in-chief, and Namuci also arrived there.
The illustrious Bhūmanyu, the Kaurava, was joined by Kāmapāla.
The Kirāta king Damana was united with Candrāpīḍa.
Likewise, Śibi Prabhadraka [fought] Ajīkara in battle.
The sage Mahodaya was joined by Harikeśa in that region.
Traigarta, Vasudāna, and Sūryaraśmi were united together.
The Gandharva Kumudāpīḍa and Jaya, the lord of Kulūta.
Then they waged a tumultuous battle, equal to that between the gods and the asuras.
Likewise, King Dāśeraka, and the Yavana Vāsana, the supreme. || 11 ||
And Ekalavya was [conquered] in battle by that great-souled one.
Kumuda, Śoṇimā, Śūra, Balabandhu, and Suyodhana. || 12 ||
Five Gandharvas from the mountains arrived together with five others.
And likewise by Balāka and Balakā, by Gadin, and by Maulin.
But by the heroic Kumuda, who never retreats from the field of battle in the assembly.
The King of Madra, named Aṃśumat, was engaged in battle with four [of them].
With Bhīmanāda, Mahānāda, Vasuṣeṇa, and Gajākara;
Dārva, Śrutañjana, the illustrious Abhimāna, and Kṛtañjaya. || 15 ||
Together with Candravarman, those two engaged in a terrible battle.
Kāśmīraka and Subāhu were slain by the Gandharva Subāhu.
He waged a tumultuous battle that increased the fear of cowards.
Furthermore, Bharata’s warriors were [attacked] by Gandharvas of terrifying prowess. || 17 ||
Then, they assembled in battle by the hundreds and by the thousands.
And the highly resplendent Bharata met with Śailūṣa. || 18 ||
He waged a tumultuous battle that struck fear into all living beings.
By the elephant Parvatābha, who was shedding ichor in three streams.
He oppressed his enemies in battle, like Mahendra against the Dānavas.
Viśāla approached Puṣkara on his chariot and chose him as his bridegroom.
Having pierced the force of the elephant Puṣkara with a torrent of arrows in battle, he checked its momentum.
Then he struck Puṣkara with many iron arrows.
But being struck by his enemies, the son of Bhārata, who possessed terrible prowess, [remained steadfast].
He rained down volleys of arrows upon Viśāla along with his army.
Then, Viśāla cut through Puṣkara’s bow at its middle.
With his bow broken, he then slew the charioteer of Viśāla. || 23 ||
Having attacked, he fought with the great chariot-warrior of Viśāla.
When, O great king, [he encountered] Puṣkara’s excellent chariot in battle... (24)
Even Viśāla abandoned the king’s chariot in order to slay him.
He fought Puṣkara's elephant with his mace.
Puṣkara also, mace in hand, went toward Viśālā.
Then those two heroes, desiring to conquer one another, [attacked] with maces.
There, they moved about in mandalas to the left and to the right.
Thus, seeking each other's death, they both struck one another.
In battle, by means of a stratagem, Puṣkara struck down Viśāla’s mace.
O lord of the earth, he released a sharp fire accompanied by sparks.
Then, in that battle, Puṣkara was struck down by Viśāla with his mace.
But he, resembling the Himalayas, did not move even a single step from his place. ||29||
O great king, Viśāla was struck down by Puṣkara with a mace.
Then, at the word of the actor, he was urged on by the mahāmātra.
Viśāla, arrogant in battle, mounted the great elephant.
And the illustrious Puṣkara ascended the chariot of the Gandharva. || 31 ||
Then those two, Rājendra and Puṣkara, mounted upon a single chariot.
In that battle, they both struck down Viśāla’s excellent elephant.
He whose [hand] was extended as he was about to fall from his elephant.
Then he cut off the head of Viśāla, which was adorned with flaming earrings.
Having slain Viśāla in battle, he mounted another chariot.
He covered that army of Gandharvas with volleys of arrows.
Seeing Viśāla slain, Ruha became exceedingly enraged.
Sādī struck the battle-proud Gāndhāra with a lance.
Gāndhāra, however, severed both his arms along with the javelins.
And his head, along with its helmet, [was severed] by a razor-edged arrow, O lord of the earth.
Takṣaka [departed] on a splendid chariot adorned with garlands of networks of tinkling bells.
He encountered the mighty-armed Vīrabāhu on the field of battle.
The sky became, as it were, of a single hue due to the multitudes of arrows from those two.
The wind does not blow there, nor does the sun shine. || 38 ||
The carpenter drew forth an arrow, complete with its feathers and radiant as the sun.
He severed the head of that charioteer, which was adorned with flaming earrings.
He was carried away from the battle by his charioteer in the chariot.
When he had been led away from the field of battle, Takṣaka mounted the back of an elephant.
O great king, the Gandharva Sudarśana arrived.
As soon as he had fallen, by means of that straight-knotted arrow, || 41 ||
Bhāratī, of terrible prowess, severed the head of the serpent.
The glorious Senānī Vijaya and Namuci both arrived.
With their arrows, they rendered the charioteer, the horses, and the standard invisible.
O Great King, those two of terrible prowess [fought] against one another in battle.
Having slain Namuci’s horses with four arrows, he...
With the fifth [arrow], he severed the head of the chariot-driver from his body.
Namuci, the slayer of enemy heroes, being deprived of his chariot, took up a sword.
The subduer of enemies quickly went toward the commander-in-chief.
Seizing the radiant discus as it was rushing toward him with great speed.
With eyes rolling back, he swiftly severed his head.
Bhūmanyu and Kāmapāla engaged in a most excellent battle.
Just as in the war between the gods and the asuras, Bala and Śakra were possessed of great strength. || 47 ||
Both of them, mounted upon elephants, were intent on slaying one another.
They engaged in battle with arrows possessing a radiance like the rays of the sun.
While they were still fighting, Bhūmanyu’s excellent elephant [was struck].
He struck the elephant of Kāmapāla on its side with his two tusks. ||49||
Accompanied by that serpent, he let out a terrifying roar.
While the battle was underway, he turned his back upon his own army.

He suddenly struck down the Gandharva army with sharpened arrows.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle on the Fourth Day," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 263 ||

The Gandharva covered him with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
When the horse sacrifice had commenced, it was as terrible as a shower of arrows.
O Great King, both Śailūṣa and Bharata should maintain [this].
In the sky, those two subduers of enemies cut down the volleys of arrows.
And thus they wrought a slaughter of terrible appearance between the two armies.
And by the two of them, with arrows that had not yet fallen away, horses and elephants were struck down.
O protector of the earth, rivers of blood flowed forth in the battle.
Carrying human bodies, they are frequented by yakṣas and rākṣasas.
By the showers of arrows released by those two, the rays of the sun were obscured in the sky.
They did not shine, O Indra among kings, as the sky became a single expanse of shadow.
Those two were slaying the soldiers while protecting their charioteers.
The two heroes, cutting down the excellent missiles and weapons [hurled] in battle, likewise [cut down those of the enemy].
Those two heroes produced wonder even among the gods.
Vāsava honored that battle with a shower of flowers.
Those two, the excellent wielders of arrows and bows, remained awake throughout the entire day.
In that battle, neither of the two suffered defeat.
Then, O Lord of the Earth, when the Blessed Sun had set, [the following occurred].
With each other's consent, they both went back to their respective camps. || 13 ||
Then, having spent the night and entered their respective homes, they reached the end of the night for the sake of battle.
Once more, those two heroes, resembling Mahendra, set forth, gladdening their own armies.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle on the Fifth Day in the Conflict between Bharata and Śailūṣa," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 264 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, when the sixth day, characterized by abundant sacrificial fees, had arrived.
Both heroes, like Śailūṣa and Bharata, engaged in battle. || 1 ||
O protector of the earth, the two of them, along with their armies, [struck] with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Bharata, the commander of the army, was joined by Śailūṣa. ||2||
In battle, the slayer of enemies severed the head of Sūryaraśmi with an arrow.
Having slain Sūryaraśmi and the great chariot-warrior Ekalavya in battle.
With an arrow, he struck down the subduer of enemies from the seat of his chariot.
The king of the Gandharvas, seeing those two principal sons slain, [was overcome with grief]. || 4 ||
With his spear he pierced Vijaya, and likewise with his discus he struck Puṣkara.
Likewise, he struck Takṣaka with a lance and Suyodhana with a mace.
They all entered the interior of the chariot, completely unconscious.
And by the controllers, they were all driven away from the battle.
Then Bharata, enraged, [struck him] with four arrows.
O Yādava, he rendered the horses lifeless in battle.
And with volleys of arrows, he rendered his prowess powerless.
Then, having steadied himself with fortitude against the force of the high-souled one's arrow, [he stood firm].
The mighty one, being well-armored, quickly mounted his chariot.
Having mounted his chariot, he pierced him with a straight-knotted arrow.
And Bharata, being struck, fainted deeply in his heart.
In the meantime, a cry of "Alas! Alas! was uttered by the gods and the asuras.
While the joy of the Raghus was neither elated nor dejected, but remained utterly bewildered.
Regaining consciousness through that great cry of "Alas! Alas!", that descendant of Raghu [arose].
Having forcibly drawn the great bow of the actor, his powerful bow.
O Indra among kings, he split him in two and struck the actor (Śailūṣa) violently.
With his bow severed, he swiftly took up a mace with great speed.
O knower of dharma, he dispatched [them] to the high-souled Bharata. || 13 ||
Seeing the mace falling upon him at the forefront of the battle, Bharata—
He split it in two with his discus while the entire army looked on.
Then he quickly hurled a heavy iron club at Bharata.
He firmly cut down that approaching [missile] with four arrows. || 15 ||
Then, taking up another bow and twenty-one arrows, he [prepared].
O great king, he hurled it toward the chariot of Bharata.
Having cut all of them down, Bharata killed his charioteer.
And so he drove the four horses toward the abode of Yama.
Seeing Śailūṣa deprived of his chariot, the great army of the Gandharvas [surrounded him].
He rained down a shower of weapons, just as a cloud rains upon a mountain.
Having deluded Bharata, O King, he caused him to be released.
And having liberated the king, when the orb of the sun had set, [he departed].
Having withdrawn his forces, the lord of men then went to his camp.
Having slain the elephant-riders, chariot-warriors, and horsemen with his sharpened arrows, he reached the center of the host.
The hero of the Raghus also departed for his home, being honored by the lords of men upon the earth. || 21 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Sixth Day of Battle," in the account of the combat between Śailūṣa and Bharata, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 265 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, when the seventh day arrived, those two who were fierce in battle—
The two high-souled ones, Śailūṣa and Bharata, both met together.
Then Bharata spoke to Śailūṣa, who was fierce in battle.
What is the use of these dead soldiers for our army that has been mobilized? || 2 ||
Restrain your own army; I shall hold back my own.
Let the lords of the earth behold the duel between us two.
Your soldiers and those who are the lords of the gods, together with the immortals.
"Though I am angry, let them take pride in me; let the army fight as it pleases."
Or let him wage war in battle, for once you are slain, they shall be yours.
Having been addressed thus, he said, "So be it," and restrained the soldiers.
That king of the Gandharvas, Śailūṣa, and Bharata likewise [instructed] their own [disciples].
Then a battle commenced between those two, resembling that between the gods and the asuras.
While all the armies were looking on, even as the gods themselves looked on.
In that battle, the rays of the sun were shrouded by a vast net of arrows.
The two of them hacked at each other with straight-jointed arrows.
They were drenched in blood flowing from the mutual strikes of their arrows. || 8 ||
O Indra among kings, those two shone like two blossoming kimshuka trees.
Both were great chariot-warriors and heroes, both renowned for their prowess. || 9 ||
Likewise, both were excellent archers, and both were difficult to overcome in battle.
Both of them stood upon golden-limbed chariots, adorned with excellent banners.
Likewise, both were being fanned by two warriors with excellent whisks.
Then those two great chariot-warriors shone beneath the two umbrellas.
Both of them, by the prowess of their weapons, waged a tumultuous battle.
Having fought with missiles for a long time, they engaged in a battle with arrows.
When the battle with arrows had passed, the battle with missiles occurred again and again.
Thus, having fought for a day, the two of them had their mounts completely exhausted.
O King, they endured exhaustion in battles, having already conquered all fatigue.
Then, as the sun was hanging low, the king of the Gandharvas—
He manifested a tamasic illusion by which the world became blinded.
Then, when darkness had arisen, dreadful voices were heard.
Let Bharata be killed quickly; let him be devoured, or likewise cast down.
Snakes, scorpions, and crabs swarmed toward the descendant of Bharata.
Terrible monkeys, forest-dwellers, jackals, and likewise leopards;
Lions, tigers, boars, and those species that are carnivorous; || 17 ||
That righteous-souled Bharata was being tormented by those foul-faced men.
With the Soura weapon, that slayer of enemy heroes shattered that illusion.
Then that mighty-armed one created a great illusion.
A very great cloud arose, covering the surface of the sky.
And he rained down terrible nets of weapons many times over.
[He discharged] iron arrows, half-nārāca arrows, and likewise crescent-headed shafts.
Likewise, [arrows] with calf-tooth heads, as well as those with knots, hollow reeds, and cow-mouth heads.
As well as razor-edged arrows, crescent-shaped shafts, and those with the faces of boars.
Maces, bhushundis, spears, slings, and battle-axes.
Hubs, hubs with spokes, and hubs with many spokes, as well as wheels, swords, and other [weapons].
He rained down these and various other supreme weapons.
Being struck by those falling, terrible weapons, that descendant of Raghu—|| 23 ||
The slayer of enemies destroyed that illusion with the Vāyavya weapon.
Then, O Indra among kings, there arose the great Gandharva Parvata.
It was formidable with its flowing springs and possessed towering peaks.
The illustrious scion of Raghu [struck] that illusory Pārvatī with the Vajra weapon. || 25 ||
He caused them to perish, O king of kings, while the entire army looked on.
As his illusions were being destroyed, he created forms that were exceedingly terrible.
Of the yakṣas, the rākṣasas, the piśācas, and the winged creatures.
And likewise of lions, tigers, hyenas, and elephants. || 27 ||
In his wrath, Bharata shattered those illusions of his with divine weapons.
As his illusions were being destroyed, he [struck] Bharata in battle with agility.
O Indra among kings, that actor, arrogant in battle, caused him to be bewildered.
Bharata also hides himself within the tip of the bow and at the point of the arrow. ||29||
Again and again, [he was seen] at the tip of the banner, at the front of the chariot, and at the head of the horse.
O Yādava, he swiftly destroyed those Bharata arrows.
The descendants of Raghu, as well as the hosts of gods and daityas, were gratified by him.
The Asuras let out a terrible, most dreadful, loud laugh.
At the loud laughter of the Daityas, Bharata became exceedingly enraged.
Having joined the Nārāyaṇa weapon to an arrow with smooth joints, [he discharged it].
Out of anger, he desired to slay that gandharva who was arrogant in battle.
Knowing that the weapon had been withdrawn, he quickly returned to his own chariot.
And he desired to slay him with that terrible Rudrāstra weapon.
At that very moment, however, Bharata released an arrow.
It resembled the fire of cosmic destruction, and was likewise equipped with feathers and a tip.
It was adorned with the wings of Vainateya and served as the destroyer of enemies. || 35 ||
Having warded off the force of Rudra’s weapon from the king who stood upon his chariot.
O King, having pierced the golden armor, it then split his heart.
Having pierced the heart of the king and then the surface of the earth.
Having bathed in the waters of the netherworld, he quickly returned once more.
The king of the Gandharvas was struck by a straight-knotted arrow.
Having cast aside his bow from the seat of the chariot, that slayer of enemy heroes passed away.
Having seen her father slain in battle, the daughter of Śailūṣa [fainted].
To Bharata, who was fierce in battle, at the end of which he was overcome by anger and sorrow. || 39 ||
O best of monarchs, they pierced him with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Then, with weapons of various forms, they indeed [fought] upon the field of battle.
And they employed various illusions for the purpose of Bharata's downfall.
And the intermediate space was pervaded by them, raining down various excellent weapons.
And some great car-warriors showered Bharata with celestial weapons.
On account of the great variety of his warriors and the great power of his mighty weapons.
They have fallen into the greatest danger due to the power of the nets of weapons.
Then, O Bharata, he released the Sāṃvarta weapon, which is the weapon of Time.
Then, from that weapon, thousands of missiles issued forth.
The entire army of Gandharvas was struck back by those various weapons.
Some of those best of Gandharvas, having been decapitated by weapons, [fell].
O King, some marriages were performed, while others were dissolved into two parts.
Some were even married, O Yādava, and some were maimed.
And there were thirty million Gandharvas, skilled in battle.
In an instant, they were struck down by Bharata with the discharge of his missiles.
When the army of the Gandharvas had been destroyed, auspicious winds began to blow. || 47 ||
Then a rain of flowers fell upon the head of Bharata.
The quarters became clear, and the fear of the gods vanished. || 48 ||
Then the thousand-eyed god, together with all the hosts of gods, [approached].
Seated in his celestial chariot, he spoke these words to Bharata, who is devoted to righteousness.
Indra said:
Due to the intensity of his grandfather's boon, he was unslayable by the hosts of gods.
You have slain the actor, that thorn in the side of the gods and the brahmins.
Therefore, O descendant of Raghu, accept from me whatever boon you desire.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words from Śatakratu, Bharata spoke as follows.
Bharata said:
You are the lord of all the gods; this entire universe is yours.
Death will come before long because of the transgression of your command.
In this world, people such as I always serve as a sign for others.
Who in this world is capable of undoing the distinction established by Prajāpati? (53)
And if a boon is to be granted to me by you, O Lord, let it be bestowed.
On both banks of the ocean, I shall establish two cities.
In a region protected by Gandharvas, for the sake of both sons.
May he obtain that reward through the grace of Śatakratu. 55.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having said, "So be it," Vāsava then departed for the heavenly world.
When Vāsava had gone to heaven, King Citraratha then [ascended]. || 56 ||
The immensely radiant one among the Gandharvas addressed these words to Bharata.
Citraratha said:
The heroic Gandharvas, who have disobeyed my command, have been slain.
By you, who are constant in righteousness, those thorns to the gods and the brahmins have been removed.
That thorn has been extracted by me, and what was pleasing to the gods has been accomplished. || 58 ||
Therefore, having honored you, I shall go back once more to the third heaven.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then Bharata said to him: "The Gandharvas have been slain by me. (59)
Therefore, protect these people and their women.
The Gandharvas are to be protected; you are their protector.
Out of consideration for me, you ought to perform this specifically.
And the abode of all of them is likewise on Mount Gandhamādana.
Having departed, those who remain there shall uphold your command.
Having said, "I will do so," he embraced him while he was in pain.
The glorious Gandharva departed for the third heaven after seeing the omniscient Bharata. || 63 ||
The hero of the Raghus, too, having slain the enemies of Indra in battle, was joined with the granting of boons.
Shining with supreme glory, O King, he went to his own city, filled with joy.
Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Śailūṣa," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When the sun had set and the most dreadful hour of twilight had arrived.
Yudhājit turned back the chariot of Bharata.
Turning the chariot back, he spoke these words to Bharata.
Behold the field of battle created by yourself, O descendant of Raghu!
It was strewn with the limbs of Gandharvas and adorned with the ornaments of slain elephants.
The earth was crowded with throngs of horses and filled with those bearing excellent weapons.
With lips like the full moon and beautiful earrings, they were adorned.
The earth shines with heads whose brows are knit so tightly as to be difficult to behold. || 4 ||
Adorned with excellent armlets in the form of five-headed serpents.
O lord of the earth, the earth shines with the arms of heroes.
Likewise, the hands of the gandharvas have the shape of lotus petals.
The earth, pierced by his arrows, shines as if it were adorned with lotuses.
Likewise, by the hands of the gandharvas, which have the appearance of elephant trunks.
It shines, strewn with the earth and adorned with excellent sandalwood. || 7 ||
By means of elephants resembling massive boulders, pierced by your peerless arrows.
Behold the surface of the earth strewn with those whose lives have fled in utter confusion.
And likewise with horses whose teeth were bared and whose eyes were wide open.
Behold the earth in battle, covered with fallen horses.
She was resplendent with parasols possessing the luster of the moon and with yak-tail whisks.
With yokes, bits, saddles, blankets, and likewise with neck-ornaments; || 1.267.10 ||
With hair, staffs, bows, spears, swords, and battle-axes;
And with arrows of various kinds, auspicious, and marked with various names. || 11 ||
She was adorned with crowns, armlets, necklaces, and earrings.
O Raghunātha, behold the earth, which is enchanting even in its compassion.
And he saw Gandharvas being devoured by carnivorous beasts and birds.
Behold him, whose every limb is beautiful and who is adorned with all ornaments.
Being dragged into the depths of the battlefield by flesh-eating beasts amidst the stench of corpses.
With their limbs moving, O King, they appear as if they were still alive.
But the presence of the warriors caused their lotus-like hands to flee.
Marked by calluses from grasping the bow, and pecked at by birds.
With mouths half-devoured as well as completely devoured;
Behold the Gandharvas of evil conduct, as if they were kings fallen from their status due to a curse.
That which was performed in the past by the Gandharvas for the sinless lords of men.
Furthermore, that very same deed was done by you against the Gandharvas in battle.
O Raghava, behold the Gandharvas among the Piśācas on the field of battle.
Of yakṣas and rākṣasas by the hundreds and thousands.
[They were] constantly greedy for the flesh of gandharvas and eaters of blood. || 18 ||
The flesh-eaters, wives of the ocean, arrived, being exceedingly hungry.
Today, at the forefront of battle, you have brought these [demons] to ultimate satisfaction.
Behold the various forms of flesh-eating creatures in the battle!
Some were stout, some were thin; some were tall, and others were short.
Some had drooping eyebrows and protruding bellies, while others had flat noses.
Some had round eyes, some squinting eyes, some were protruding-toothed, and all were most terrifying.
And likewise, they had hair standing erect, great fangs, and enormous mouths.
The terrible ones are in front and at the two sides; the others are behind and at the two arms.
And likewise with faces resembling those of various kinds of sentient beings.
Wearing various disguises, they were fierce and possessed various deformed appearances. || 23 ||
Some wore garments of lion skins, and others likewise wore garments of tiger skins.
Some are summoned, others bite, and others carry away the supreme blood.
Others, having offered flesh and blood to Skanda, then returned.
They sport at their pleasure in the rivers of blood created by you. || 25 ||
Some were crushing them with blood, while others were making them drink gore.
Having smeared blood upon skulls, he placed them repeatedly upon his lap.
And others, together with their wives, drink blood in battle.
Likewise, other women caused him to drink, as did Rāma himself, the younger brother of Rāma.
Others drink blood from skulls held in the hands of their wives.
Others, with blood flowing profusely, drink from skulls that resemble the heads of elephants.
Others, having placed their children upon their shoulders, dance about, fully satisfied.
Others likewise dance, taking the hands of their wives. || 29 ||
Some were dancing, others were laughing, and likewise with distorted voices.
Some sing, others sleep, and still others quarrel.
Likewise, some cast away corpses, while others cast them upon the surface of the earth.
They desire to take others, and likewise they seize yet others. || 31 ||
And others, being base, engage in quarrels for the sake of a corpse.
Some, adorned with ornaments on their limbs, cut off and eat pieces of flesh.
And having eaten [the flesh], O Raghava, some even eat the bones and the marrow.
Others said, "We are satisfied by the grace of Bharata. || 33 ||
And having attained supreme joy, they spoke to one another.
May there be constant war among kings, as well as enmity and cruelty. || 34 ||
Strength, allies, and nourishment—by which we ourselves are satisfied.
Speaking thus, they sang with various melodies.
Likewise, others, overcome with affection and finding it exceedingly difficult to look upon, gazed at the chariot.
Thus did that illustrious Bharata [behold] what was shown by his maternal uncle.
Beholding the field of battle, he proceeded once more toward Rājagṛha.
He saw him near the city, bewildered by the Vāyavya weapon.
That army of the lords of kings was proceeding toward this foremost battle.
Having seen Bharata, all of them were covered with the dust of the battlefield. || 38 ||
The kings congratulated the heroic victor in battle.
Having approached those illustrious kings and embraced them, he—
And having consoled them, the righteous-souled one dismissed them to their camps.
Then he [reached] that maternal uncle’s capital city, which was delightful with its joyful warriors and noble women.
At night, the Lord of the Raghu dynasty entered while being praised with hymns by those who were like lions among men.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Battlefield," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When that night had passed, the people from the city of the Gandharvas [emerged].
And the sons and wives of the Gandharvas, as well as the wives of kings. || 1 ||
Having reached the field of battle, they wept, overcome with intense grief.
Oh, how powerful is Fate, by whom we have been rendered proud of our own strength! ||2||
Invincible to the hosts of gods, they have been struck down in battle.
There is no burden too heavy for destiny, nor is there anything impossible for it.
By whom the sons of the Gandharvas, possessing the strength of ten thousand elephants, were slain.
Those who formerly, intoxicated with pride, lay upon most excellent couches; || 4 ||
They do not find sleep; today they lie upon the bare ground.
Those who were fanned by the breezes from palm-leaf fans and by beautiful women; ||5||
Today they lie fallen upon the surface of the earth, fanned by the wings of vultures.
Those who had assembled there shone, their limbs anointed with the most excellent sandalwood paste.
Smeared with blood upon the great earth, they all no longer shine today.
In the past, women with beautiful thighs and hips used to sleep while embracing him. ||7||
Those who today, embracing the earth as their bed, lie upon couches of suffering.
"O King, destroyer of the pride of the gods! O King, lover of your servants! (8)
"Alas, O King, whose every limb is beautiful! Alas, O King, who are so affectionate toward your charioteer!"
O Lord of Men, under whose protection do we now stand, having lost the shade of your arms? (9)
Free from fear, we shall dwell at our ease among the gods and the daityas.
With faces like the full moon, surrounded by millions of sons.
Seeing him situated in such a precarious position, we shall go to the abode of Yama.
Not seeing you seated in the assembly, we shall go to the abode of Yama.
While the people were thus afflicted with grief and lamenting piteously, then—
Those most captivating women were the wives of the sons of the Gandharva kings.
Then, afflicted by pain and grief, they remained established in great compassion.
A certain woman [beheld] her husband deprived of his head and bereft of his arms.
Likewise, another was cut in two, while yet another had been devoured by carnivorous beasts.
Seeing this, a certain woman, afflicted by grief, wept; she could not even find [consolation].
Stumbling over corpses, they wandered there in great distress.
Beating their breasts with their hands and tearing out their hair. || 15 ||
In whose dwellings, even the sun formerly did not obtain a sight.
Then all the people beheld them, suffering and with their hair disheveled. || 16 ||
Some fall upon their husbands, while others embrace them.
Likewise, O King, others wept with sweet voices, uttering cries of distress. || 17 ||
While they were thus weeping, the queens were also deeply afflicted with grief.
O King, they wept piteously, their hair disheveled.
Alas, my beloved! Alas, great king! Alas, you who are dear to the people!
Alas, O destroyer of the pride of the Lord of the Gods! Alas, O you whose face resembles the moon! 19.
"O husband, by whom has your mind been led toward death?"
"Alas, O King! You embrace this earth as if she were your beloved."
Do you not feel shame in this assembly for holding the earth with your beloved arms?
Why do you lie before us, especially while we are in our menses? ||21||
O King, even though you are a sky-walker, the earth is always dear to you.
For those words of Nārada were not listened to by you for your own benefit.
O King, although the earth is dear to you, nevertheless [it is so] toward us as well.
For it is indeed right that you should show courtesy, since you are born of my own lineage.
We have been deeply distressed by your departure, which was made without our anticipation.
O destroyer of enemies, grant us consolation with mere words.
It is not fitting for a king to sleep upon the bare surface of the earth.
Therefore arise, O Indra among kings; resort to your bed no longer. ||25||
We have been struck down, O Great King, by passion and by intoxication.
"O Lord of Men, deprived of you, whom indeed shall we embrace around our necks? (26)
O King, the powerful Kṛtānta has drawn you away today and leads you away.
If you had followed the words of Nāḍāyana, [this would not have happened]. || 27 ||
O lord of men, there would have been no separation from you for us.
"O King, why do you sleep today on the bare ground with your limbs motionless? (28)
Having risen, O hero, you did not embrace us or kiss us.
Having conquered the heroes in battle and slain the lords of the earth. || 29 ||
How was it that you were struck down in battle by a single mortal?
Where is your body? Where is your splendor? Where is that beauty? Where is your strength? (1.268.30)
Where is that pure umbrella of yours, and where are those excellent yak-tail whisks?
O Lord, where is that seat of passion, and where is your daughter? (31)
Where is that grace, where is that splendor, and where are those excellent panegyrists?
And where are those supreme women who bear the excellent chowries?
Deprived of you this very day, we long for you this very day.
"O beloved of the people, you have departed; you are to be remembered this very day. (33)
"O Indra among kings, the women in heaven are surely even more beautiful."
O sinless one, having abandoned your own kinsmen, you have instead fixed your delight upon him.
By whom, acting according to their own will, has this mindset been cultivated that is frequented by heroes?
By you, in making this request, the desire for battle has been increased in the world. ||35||
Of this beloved person who has been so cherished by you.
On a long journey, one should offer assistance even by means of mere words. ||36||
Dismiss the people, O King; let us sport together with you.
In various gardens, forests, and groves. ||37||
We do not harbor envy while all the world looks on.
Surely this heart has been made very firm, with the essence of a diamond.
Even seeing you lifeless, that it does not shatter into a hundred pieces—[this is a marvel].
O you whose limbs are moist with camphor and sandalwood paste, who are accustomed to a costly couch! 39.
O Indra among kings, you shine resplendent upon the surface of the earth, drenched in blood.
Where are those elephants with their shattered temples, and where are those horses and tuskers?
O King, where have those warriors of yours gone, who vied with Śakra in battle?
Standing in the great army, he held a sword, arrows, and a bow. || 41 ||
O King, how did Rāghava lead you away to the other world?
O lord of men, your trembling arises precisely from the sight of the God of Death.
How was he struck down today in battle by a mere human?
Therefore, what shall we do, being hopeless for your life?
I have no conceptual construction, nor do I have any view; there is no association with views in me.
Thus lamenting were those women of the actor. || 44 ||
O King, embracing him again and again, they fall upon the surface of the earth.
They strike down their heads and likewise beat their arms. || 45 ||
They beheld that hero once more upon the ground, his life having departed.
And having seen it, they fell again upon the surface of the earth, unconscious.
The sound of their weeping pervaded the entire surface of the earth.
The learned brahmin Nāḍāyana offered them consolation.
At that very time, however, Aparājita went to that region.
The lord of the Gandharvas arrived, impelled by Bharata.
Then, having approached that place, he [instructed] all the people according to the prescribed rule.
Then King Citraratha slowly comforted him.
He caused the actor, together with his sons, to receive due honor.
Then those Gandharvas were urged on by King Citraratha.
Then they constructed the king's funeral pyre with many well-dried logs.
Of all his sons and of all his warriors without exception.
With logs of sandalwood, agallochum, and likewise of kālīyaka. ||51||
And having set the funeral pyre ablaze with perfumes, oils, and ghee, they—
Having consecrated all of them, they set out for the city.
Then, at the word of the king of the Gandharvas, all the great multitude [acted].
Placing Nārada at the head, he set out for Gandhamādana.
He established his camp there on the slope of Mount Rāma.
Having established their dwellings there, all of them acted by the command of Citraratha.
O Great King, we have lived happily, being protected by that high-souled one. || 54 ||
O King, even there, in that preeminent city, the grandson of Śailūṣa became the leader of the people.
But the king of the Gandharvas provided protection for him, at the command of the chief of the Raghavas.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Lamentation of the Gandharva Woman," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, at the conclusion of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha.
The five-day festival of the lords of the thirty-three gods has come to an end. || 1 ||
The Blessed Lord Madhusūdana has his bed upon the ocean of milk.
Then, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, he entered into yogic sleep.
Bharata, too, having celebrated a festival and worshipped Janārdana, [departed].
Having likewise performed the gift of land, one should eat only at night for five days.
And when the Cāturmāsya period has ended, [one may eat] honey and meat.
Having honored the lords of the earth, he dismissed them from his palace.
Having spoken with various kinds of consoling words and having embraced him very tightly.
Having divided the accumulated wealth obtained like that of a city of the Gandharvas.
Having honored his own military forces during the rainy season, he...
Having consulted together, he sent [him] with longing toward his beloveds.
Having dispatched his men, he proceeded with a small remnant of his own troops.
He dwelt in his maternal uncle's house like a king of the gods among the Bharatas.
The best of the Raghus stayed there for four months with delight.
Then, having reached the month of Kārttika, at the conclusion of the bright fortnight.
Having obtained five days, he celebrated a grand festival.
The awakening of the God of gods during the great festival of the thirty deities.
Having given great gifts to them, especially on the full moon day of Kārttika.
Having worshipped the Lord of the World, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
On an auspicious day and under a favorable constellation, having worshipped the most excellent of the twice-born,
Placing the astrologer and the master builders at the forefront, that descendant of Raghu [proceeded].
He established two cities on both banks of the ocean.
Puṣkara at Puṣkarāvatī, and Takṣa toward Takṣaśilā. || 12 ||
Having made preparations for the two cities and having consecrated both his sons, he departed.
In both cities, O Great King, he duly gave abundant sacrificial fees.
O Yādava, Puṣkara then begot a son named Puṣkara and also Takṣa.
The city was crowded with merchants as well as Brāhmaṇas. || 14 ||
And by artisans, O Great King, who subsist upon various crafts.
It was strewn with heaps of houses and adorned with temples. || 15 ||
Then, O Bharata, the kingdom was established under the rule of his two sons.
Having divided the wealth, jewels, horses, and elephants between his two sons.
When Yudhājit had departed after entrusting [them] to him, a year had then passed.
In the past month of Kārttika, under an asterism endowed with auspicious qualities.
The illustrious Bharata went to see Rāma, O lord of men.
The hero was followed by his sons and by his maternal uncle, Yudhājit.
On the shore of his own domain, he sent his two sons back home, and having embraced his afflicted maternal uncle Yudhājit, he dismissed him as well.
Bharata, his eyes filled with tears, [set out] with a fourfold army.
And thus he went forth in a small chariot adorned with gold.
And having restrained him from his chariot, they then followed Bharata as he was departing.
With dejected minds and somewhat overcome by confusion, they gazed [upon him]. || 21 ||
Turning back again and again, Bharata somehow managed to go on.
Not seeing one another, they proceeded in such haste. || 22 ||
Bharata likewise [traversed] countries, regions, and rivers.
Having bypassed villages, towns, and settlements, he went to the city.
Then, having been away for a long time, he reached Ayodhyā.
Having entered that city, which was crowded with banners and flags, [he proceeded]. || 24 ||
The palace, white as nectar, was sprinkled with sandalwood water.
Everything was done according to Rāma’s command, and the divine child was worshipped.
Accompanied by a fourfold army, he set out ahead of him.
By Rāma’s command, the highly resplendent Lakṣmaṇa, together with the citizens, [departed]. || 26 ||
Seeing Bharata, who had been away from home for a long time, Lakṣmaṇa...
He greeted him with affection, placing his head upon the surface of the earth. || 27 ||
Bharata, having smelled his head and embraced him tightly, [spoke].
Having everywhere made inquiries regarding his welfare according to the prescribed rule, [he spoke].
He honored the city-dwellers according to their merit.
She addresses others with a smile, employing inquiries concerning their welfare. || 29 ||
He was being honored again and again by that multitude of people.
The illustrious Bharata entered the city, mounted upon the neck of an elephant.
But by one situated at the windows of palaces, mansions, and towers.
While being gazed upon with longing by the women, the one of great splendor— || 31 ||
The one of great splendor reached the long-stretched gateway of the king's palace.
There, the sound of musical instruments was great, as was the tumultuous clamor.
Then, having reached the royal gate, he descended from his excellent elephant.
Taking Lakṣmaṇa by the hand, he then entered the assembly hall.
There, upon that lion-throne, he beheld Rāma, the mighty-armed one.
His limbs were anointed with sandalwood paste, and he was adorned with all kinds of ornaments.
With a face like the full moon and eyes like the petals of a blue lotus.
Upon seeing Rāma, Bharata placed his head upon the ground.
The one of great splendor fell down, especially because of Lakṣmaṇa.
Rāma also, seeing Bharata, raised up the mighty-armed one.
He embraced him, who was distressed, and smelled his head repeatedly.
Having inquired after his inexhaustible welfare, he assigned him a seat.
Having presented the finest jewels to the Gandharvas, that descendant of Raghu—
Just as she had provided a noble seat for Rāma, who was ever devoted to righteousness. || 38 ||
Having been questioned by Rāma, that hero among men reported the events exactly as they had occurred.
Dismissed by him, he went home and then worshipped Viṣṇu.
In that dream, the hero, unconquerable in battles, likewise dwelt having reached the feet of Rāma.
Rāma also, having completely destroyed the faction of his enemies, ruled the kingdom together with him in a proper manner.
Then, in the fourth year, Rāma heard of the prowess of the two city-dwellers.
Having performed this for his two sons, Bharata, being greatly delighted, attained supreme joy from Viṣṇu. || 41 ||
Today, I have proclaimed this victory of the joy of the Raghus upon the field of battle.
This, which is delightful through its wisdom, virtue, purpose, and fame, must certainly be heard by a man.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Meeting of Śrī Rāmacandra and Bharata," in the first section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara* within the second part of the *Śrī Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra. || 269 ||
And this first section is completed.
